United Airlines’ Oldest Aircraft Is Over 30 Years Old & It’s Still Going Strong In 2026

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1434 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Simpleflying

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that united Airlines is keeping a large contingent of three-decade-old widebodies flying across long-haul skies in 2026, led by active flagship N641UA at 35.72 years old.
  • How can three-decade-old widebodies remain central to a major global carrier's network in 2026 when newer twinjets are already in service and improve on every metric?
  • It has been revealed that according to ch-aviation fleet records from November 19, 2026, 20 of United Airlines's 767-300ER airframes are aged 30 years and older, spanning from 33.27 years up to 35.72 years.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that united Airlines is keeping a large contingent of three-decade-old widebodies flying across long-haul skies in 2026, led by active flagship N641UA at 35.72 years old. Data from ch-aviation lists 37 Boeing 767-300ER aircraft in United's fleet, with 20 airframes aged 30 years and older, 18 active, one in maintenance, and one in storage. It would be so easy to go and sideline these seasoned twin-aisle jets, but United continues to rely on them for demanding international and domestic flying.

How can three-decade-old widebodies remain central to a major global carrier's network in 2026 when newer twinjets are already in service and improve on every metric? Looking at ch-aviation fleet records alongside recent flight activity and industry coverage, this article examines United's 30-plus Boeing 767-300ER airframes, cabin configurations, retirement plans, rival widebody comparisons, and the operational economics keeping them airborne.

It has been revealed that according to ch-aviation fleet records from November 19, 2026, 20 of United Airlines's 767-300ER airframes are aged 30 years and older, spanning from 33.27 years up to 35.72 years. At the top of that age bracket sits active flagship N641UA at 35.72 years, followed closely by active N642UA at 35.61 years and active twins N644UA and N643UA at 35.58 years apiece. Seventeen other airframes in this cohort sit between 33.27 and 34.69 years, with 18 of the 20 aircraft active, N648UA in maintenance at 34.41 years, and N659UA in storage at 33.7 years.

Closely following specific tail numbers from this 30-plus group shows how actively these airframes still work long-haul and domestic rotations in late 2026. FlightAware records show N641UA operating long-distance flights such as Houston (IAH) to Santiago (SCL), a 4,669-mile (7,514-km) sector, and Amsterdam (AMS), while FlightAware shows N642UA rotating between Washington Dulles (IAD), Houston, Amsterdam, and South America. Even N644UA returned to active line flying in November 2026 after diverting to St. John's (YYT) over an engine issue on a Washington Dulles–Amsterdam flight in October 2026.

Industry observers note that having 18 30-plus 767-300ERs actively flying alongside two others in maintenance or storage highlights how central older aircraft are to daily dispatch reliability. Routine maintenance checks on jets like N648UA and occasional short-term storage on N659UA form a normal part of running a mature fleet rather than suggesting an immediate fleetwide grounding.

Recent findings suggest that united Airlines has outfitted its fleet of 767-300ERs with modern long-haul cabins tailored to high-yield demand. According to United Airlines's fleet specifications, the carrier operates two distinct three-cabin layouts on the type, combining lie-flat Polaris business seats with United Premium Plus, Economy Plus, and standard economy. Even on older fuselages, passengers get onboard WiFi, in-seat power outlets, USB ports, and seatback audio-video on demand across every cabin.

The flagship high-J configuration packs 167 seats into the fuselage, led by 46 Polaris suites with 77 inches (195 cm) of sleeping space, 22 Premium Plus recliners offering 38 inches (96 cm) of pitch and six inches (15 cm) of recline, 43 Economy Plus seats and 56 economy seats arranged in a passenger-friendly 2-3-2 layout. A second 203-seat version caters more to corporate and leisure demand with 30 Polaris seats, 24 Premium Plus seats, and 149 Economy seats, where Economy Plus offers 34 inches (86 cm) of pitch and standard economy provides 31 inches (79 cm) of pitch with 18.5-inch (46.9-cm) seat widths.

Industry observers note that that cabin mix makes the 767-300ER uniquely suited to transatlantic and secondary international routes where larger twinjets would carry too many empty seats. Deploying the 167-seat premium-heavy variant on business-dense European routes out of hubs like Newark and Chicago while assigning the 203-seat version to mixed leisure-and-corporate corridors, United extracts strong revenue per departure. Combined with its comfortable 2-3-2 cross-section, the modernized interior explains why passengers and schedulers alike still value the type.

In a recent development, united Airlines plans to be well into retiring its 767 fleet around 2030, setting a clear multi-year horizon for winding down the type. The aircraft will not be grounded abruptly, as management has framed the exit around fleet renewal and long-haul capacity growth as newer twinjets enter service. That timeline gives United room to extract remaining value from its 767s while preparing replacement capacity.

Recent findings suggest that boeing 787 Dreamliners sit at the center of that transition as United's primary long-term widebody replacement, an aircraft that has been integral to the airline's growth in recent years. With 787-9 and expanded 787-10 deliveries rolling out across upcoming fleet waves, resulting in the airline becoming the largest 787 operator globally, United gains far better fuel efficiency, lower operating costs, and upgraded premium cabins than older twin-aisle jets can match. Shifting transatlantic and trunk widebody flying onto Dreamliners lets United retire aging airframes a step at a time, not infringing on long-haul frequency.

Deliveries and widebody fleet planning still carry moving parts as United looks toward the end of the decade. Supply-chain pacing, aircraft delivery schedules, and long-range fleet choices, including whether United ever firms up its long-delayed Airbus A350 order around 2030, will shape how quickly 767s exit, though that seems highly unlikely as of November 2026. Until enough replacements arrive in full volume, the 767 is integral to the United fleet.

In a recent development, united Airlines is far from alone in flying mature 767-300ERs, with Delta Air Lines running a similarly seasoned widebody subfleet. Across 37 Boeing 767-300ERs, Delta's average fleet age stood at 29.7 years in September 2026, closely tracking United's 29.8-year average across 37 aircraft of the same variant at the end of 2025, as per data from AeroCorner.

Recent findings suggest that other airlines show contrasting ways of handling aging 767s as market demand and upcoming deliveries shift. Air Canada retired its passenger 767s in 2020 before moving to reintroduce two stored 767-300ERs as short-term capacity insurance while adjusting 767 freighter plans around incoming Dreamliners and Airbus widebodies. Meanwhile, lease-heavy low-cost carriers such as Frontier rely on operating leases to keep average fleet ages young rather than holding decades-old jets.

Comparing United against Delta, Air Canada, and lease-focused rivals helps to show more clearly how ownership structure and hub economics drive widebody longevity. Where ultra-low-cost operators avoid ownership exposure and rapid-growth airlines lean on newer deliveries, legacy carriers with established transatlantic and long-haul hubs can squeeze extra years out of 767-300ERs. That contrast highlights why United's approach looks distinctly legacy-carrier-like.

Keeping 30-year-old 767-300ERs flying is not as straightforward as it is with newer aircraft. Older airframes demand thorough heavy checks, corrosion inspections, and component overhauls as flight hours and cycles climb, but paid-off ownership and lower capital charges can still make them profitable on seasonal or peak-demand routes. When peak revenue outpaces incremental fuel and maintenance spend, keeping an older widebody on the line makes a lot of financial sense.

According to recent reports, at the same time, the broader 767 program is entering its final commercial chapter as Boeing winds down commercial 767 production in 2027 after completing remaining freighter orders. Even as commercial assembly ends in Everett, while KC-46A tanker production continues, hundreds of existing 767s will remain active in passenger, freighter, and converted cargo service for many years. Spare-parts support and mature maintenance ecosystems are naturally vital for operators running the type deep into its fourth decade.

For long-haul twinjet flying more broadly, the 767-300ER's staying power shows how mid-sized widebodies fill a practical niche between narrowbodies and larger twinjets. Where replacement widebodies face tight delivery slots or higher upfront acquisition costs, well-maintained 767-300ERs buy airlines schedule flexibility and capacity cushion. That combination of proven range, familiar operations, and practical economics explains why 30-plus-year-old airframes are still going strong in 2026.

United Airlines's 30-plus 767-300ER fleet demonstrates that age alone does not sideline a well-supported widebody when economics and network fit align. Across 37 airframes in ch-aviation records, 20 aircraft aged 30 years and older, led by active flagship N641UA at 35.72 years, continue flying demanding routes thanks to updated Polaris and Premium Plus cabins, paid-off ownership, and practical mid-sized widebody economics. Many airlines would see these aircraft as simple stopgaps, but these veteran twinjets carry real commercial weight on routes where larger twinjets would carry excess capacity.

According to recent reports, the 767 story at United is unfortunately not forever lasting. Boeing is winding down commercial 767 production, and around 2030, United targets retiring its 767 fleet as 787 Dreamliners take over. Only time will tell how smoothly those Dreamliner deliveries ramp up, how spare parts and maintenance support hold up after commercial assembly ends, and how reliably 30-plus airframes perform across upcoming seasons.

In a recent development, chase and Hyatt have a pretty straightforward co-brand card portfolio, as there’s one personal card and one business card. Specifically, I’m talking about the World of Hyatt Credit Card and the World of Hyatt Business Credit Card.

In this post, I’d like to compare the two cards, and talk about which is better. First let’s cover the details of both products, and then I’ll share my take on which is worth applying for. This is an especially good time to pick them up, given the current welcome offers.

Link: Learn more about the World of Hyatt Credit Card or World of Hyatt Business Credit Card.

According to recent reports, to start, let’s cover the details of Hyatt’s two co-branded credit cards. Below is a chart with the basics, and I’ll go into a bit more detail below.

The World of Hyatt Credit Card (learn more) is Hyatt’s personal credit card, with a $95 annual fee. Hyatt’s personal credit card offers a variety of perks, including the following:.

The World of Hyatt Business Credit Card (learn more) is Hyatt’s business credit card, with a $199 annual fee. Hyatt’s business credit card offers many benefits, including the following:.

If you’re considering applying for a Hyatt credit card and would be eligible for a business or personal card, which should you apply for?

The first thing to understand is that the World of Hyatt Card and World of Hyatt Business Card aren’t mutually exclusive. You could apply for both cards, and also earn the welcome bonus on each. So in some ways, it’s worth assessing the value of the cards independently, since you don’t actually have to decide between them.

If you ask me, the World of Hyatt Card is a slam dunk if you stay at Hyatts with any frequency. The card has a reasonable annual fee, and it’s worth holding onto even if you don’t spend a dime on it.

The annual free night award alone more than justifies the annual fee, and the five nights toward elite status with no spending requirement is a great perk as well. On top of that, I think there’s merit to spending $15,000 on the card per year, to earn a second annual free night award, plus to earn an additional six elite nights toward status.

Sources indicate that the math on the World of Hyatt Business Card isn’t quite as straightforward. The card has a different welcome bonus than on the personal card, so there’s merit to picking up the card for that. But beyond that, the main reason you’ll want to get this card is because it offers the best rate of return on spending in terms of earning elite nights.

With the business card, you can earn one elite night for every $2,000 spent, while with the personal card, you can get one elite night for every $2,500 spent (though the increments for earning elite nights differ).

Recent findings suggest that so my best consolidated advice would be that the World of Hyatt Card is more valuable and is easier to justify, and is the best for the first $15,000 in spending annually. Beyond that, though, the World of Hyatt Business Card is best for helping to earn Hyatt status, especially if you’re a major spender. Furthermore, it can be worth picking up the card in part for the huge bonus.

Hyatt has both a personal and business co-branded credit cards. The products are totally different, and there’s potentially merit to both. The World of Hyatt Card is much easier to justify — the card has a lower annual fee, offers an annual free night award, provides five nights toward status without a spending requirement, and more.

That being said, you don’t have to decide between the two cards, and there’s also merit to getting the World of Hyatt Business Card. The card has a better welcome bonus, and has the potential to be more rewarding for spending.

House Ethics panel adopts changes aimed at speeding up investigations

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (650 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that ethics Chairman Michael Guest, left, and ranking member Mark DeSaulnier arrive for a committee meeting on Capitol Hill in April.
  • In a year roiled by sexual misconduct allegations in the House, the Ethics Committee approved a series of changes Thursday that its members say are intended to improve how the panel handles its investigations.
  • In a rare public meeting lasting less than 10 minutes, the committee discussed proposed tweaks aimed at speeding up its processes, after some observers have criticized its pace.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that ethics Chairman Michael Guest, left, and ranking member Mark DeSaulnier arrive for a committee meeting on Capitol Hill in April. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

In a year roiled by sexual misconduct allegations in the House, the Ethics Committee approved a series of changes Thursday that its members say are intended to improve how the panel handles its investigations.

In a rare public meeting lasting less than 10 minutes, the committee discussed proposed tweaks aimed at speeding up its processes, after some observers have criticized its pace.

“My problem with the Ethics Committee is it just takes too damn long,” Rep. Madeleine Dean, D-Pa., said earlier this year.

The internal rule changes were adopted in a voice vote by the committee, which is evenly divided between Republicans and Democrats.

“We believe that these rule changes will provide more transparency. They will expedite our investigative process while maintaining protections for witnesses and victims, while also making sure that … due process is protected,” Chair Michael Guest, R-Miss., mentioned during the meeting.

When former Reps. Eric Swalwell, D-Calif., and Tony Gonzales, R-Texas, resigned earlier this year amid misconduct allegations, it sparked outrage as some called to rethink how the House polices bad behavior. Both men were on the radar of the Ethics Committee at the time, but such investigations have tended to move slowly.

“I want the Ethics Committee to move faster,” remarked panel member Rep. Suhas Subramanyam, D-Va., back in April.

The committee did not immediately make available the exact text of the changes it adopted Thursday. But a summary sent in a news release earlier this week included one proposal aimed at “consolidating deadlines” for a member to respond to an investigative subcommittee’s findings. Another tweak aimed at speeding things up would give the chair and ranking member subpoena power on behalf of the committee, rather than requiring a full committee vote.

The summary described “codifying the Committee’s policy of publicly disclosing any findings that a Member engaged in sexual harassment or other sexual misconduct” while “prohibiting publication of the identity of any victim.”.

Also on the list: “Expanding the circumstances under which fines and denials of privileges are considered an appropriate sanction to include any abuses of position.”.

Industry observers note that it comes as women on both sides of the aisle have formed a partnership aimed at reviewing how Congress deals with sexual misconduct and suggesting concrete ideas for an overhaul. Rep. Teresa Leger Fernández, D-N.M., has been co-leading that effort as the chair of the Democratic Women’s Caucus alongside Republican Women’s Caucus head Kat Cammack, R-Fla.

According to Leger Fernández, the Ethics Committee has “consulted” with her group as it weighed the changes to its internal rules.

“The Ethics Committee was clearly listening to women staffers, and has been a great partner in our work. We appreciate how they’ve consulted DWC and that these proposals will improve transparency and help protect the identities of those who report alleged misconduct. Together with RWC, we will continue to work on additional legislation in our sexual misconduct reform agenda,” she noted in a statement earlier this week.

Cammack stated that, while “the entire system on Capitol Hill has been designed to create a chilling effect for victims,” the Ethics committee rule changes would help.

“Putting public disclosure of misconduct findings in writing, while protecting every victim’s identity, gives staffers a commitment they can count on. Faster investigations mean they get answers in time to matter,” Cammack said in a statement. “This is exactly the kind of change our bipartisan task force has been pushing for.”.

Ethics ranking member Mark DeSaulnier, D-Calif., said everyone in the House should have “zero tolerance” for sexual harassment.

“We’ve worked very hard to look at ways that we could make the committee’s process fair, transparent and accountable, and I think we’ve done that,” he mentioned at Thursday’s meeting.

Tech Report: Royal Air Maroc Business Class Boeing 737 Review: Good For A Short Hop

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • To kick off the return portion of our Orient Express adventure via Africa trip, we flew Royal Air Maroc’s Boeing 737-800 business class on the 45-minute flight from Malaga (AGP) to Casablanca (CMN).
  • I must admit, Royal Air Maroc has a really solid short haul product.
  • In a recent development, admittedly the flight attendant serving us didn’t have much personality, and the cabin wasn’t in great condition.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

To kick off the return portion of our Orient Express adventure via Africa trip, we flew Royal Air Maroc’s Boeing 737-800 business class on the 45-minute flight from Malaga (AGP) to Casablanca (CMN).

I must admit, Royal Air Maroc has a really solid short haul product. While there’s no Wi-Fi or seat back entertainment, I appreciate that the airline has “proper” business class seats, the inflight meal service was outright generous for such a short flight, and I also appreciated the dedicated business class bus upon arrival.

In a recent development, admittedly the flight attendant serving us didn’t have much personality, and the cabin wasn’t in great condition. But still, those are hardly huge issues. For that matter, it has to be acknowledged how the airlines of northern Africa really lower the bar when it comes to the quality of the inflight experience (hi, Air Algerie!), so on a relative basis, this was rather excellent.

In a recent development, ford and I booked an itinerary on Royal Air Maroc all the way from Malaga to Miami via Casablanca. The reason was because the airline offered the best schedule that would get us home the same day after our Orient Express Sailing Yachts cruise.

Royal Air Maroc often makes only one business class seat available, so I had to get a bit creative to make this work. I ended up booking one ticket using 57,500 American AAdvantage miles plus $85.72 in taxes & fees, while the other ticket was booked with cash, at the cost of $1,620, with the following itinerary:.

10/09 AT989 Malaga to Casablanca departing 2:15PM arriving 1:30PM10/09 AT204 Casablanca to Miami departing 3:00PM arriving 7:45PM.

Obviously paying cash for a ticket wasn’t ideal, but that still ended up being less out of pocket than flying British Airways business class through London on awards, factoring in the carrier surcharges.

Industry observers note that we arrived at Malaga Airport at around 11:30AM, plenty early for our 2:15PM flight. We headed through security and then cleared passport control… only then did I realize that the non-Schengen lounge is currently closed, so we had no lounge option there.

Recent findings suggest that I guess we could’ve exited passport control again to access the lounge in the Schengen area of the terminal, but we figured that wasn’t worth it, so we just decided to grab a seat. I have to say, the non-Schengen portion of the Malaga Airport had quite the scene. Virtually every other flight departing around the same time was on Jet2, and it was definitely a “festive” spirit in the terminal. Based on the passengers, you’d think the airport had banned close-toed shoes.

In a recent development, boarding for our flight was scheduled for 1:30PM, 45 minutes before departure, from gate B16. Sure enough, that’s exactly when boarding started, with business class passengers being invited to board first.

Recent findings suggest that we boarded the Royal Air Maroc Boeing 737-800 through the forward door, and then turned right into the business class cabin. Royal Air Maroc’s 737s have 12 business class seats, spread across three rows, in a 2-2 configuration.

Royal Air Maroc’s 737 business class seats are particularly spacious, as they boast 43″ of pitch and 21″ of width, with 6″ of recline. So this is significantly more spacious than what you’d find in domestic first class within the United States, where pitch is more commonly around 37-38″ — an extra 5-6″ is definitely noticeable!

According to recent reports, these seats have little foot bars that fold down from the seat in front, for extra support while inflight. These were also old style seats, in terms of having large, deep, leather pockets on the seat back.

The tray table folded out from the side of the seat, and had to be flipped over to be fully extended. It was a bit flimsy, as the cabin definitely felt a bit past its prime.

There was a center console where drinks could be placed during the flight, along with additional little drink trays that could be extended, acting as “wings” to the center console.

On the front side of the center console were the AC charging outlets, which were the extent of the charging options there — there were no USB-A or USB-C charging options.

There were also little channel and volume controls, along with a headphone jack, for tuning into the inflight entertainment.

Perhaps the most modern part of the cabin was the overhead consoles, which had the more modern Boeing overhead lights and air nozzles.

While the cabin definitely felt tired and wasn’t in great shape, the comfort was otherwise great, when compared to what you’ll otherwise find in the region. I mean, my previous two regional flights on airlines from northern Africa were on junky wet leased planes, so this was luxurious by comparison.

Unfortunately this Royal Air Maroc 737 didn’t have any sort of Wi-Fi or streaming entertainment. Instead, there were monitors that folded down from the overhead consoles, which had some programming during the flight — on this flight, there were cartoons.

It has been revealed that so the entertainment situation was disappointing, but of course on a flight of this length, it wasn’t an issue. But if I were on a three or four hour flight on one of these 737s, I’d of course have a different impression.

During boarding, the crew came around with pre-departure drinks, including the choice of water or lemon mint juice, and we got one of each. They were served in proper glassware — I love the branding!

One thing I have to mention is that the cabin was insanely hot during boarding — I imagine the APU wasn’t working, or something, so we were sweating our you-know-whats off.

Airlines of northern Africa are always a bit funny when it comes to safety. At 1:55PM the safety video was screened, while the door was still open, and before all passengers had boarded.

In a recent development, at 2:05PM the main cabin door closed, with seven of the 12 business class seats occupied. At 2:10PM we began our pushback, and at 2:15PM we began our taxi. There were zero security checks during the taxi out, and a couple of people in business class had their seats reclined.

The captain sure was a good multi-tasker, or at least so I assume — he made his welcome aboard announcement while also taxiing us out and making some turns (at least I assume that at Royal Air Maroc taxiing is a captain-only function, but maybe that’s not the case?).

Sources indicate that it was just a quick taxi out to runway 13, where we were second in line for takeoff, behind a Ryanair 737. We were cleared for takeoff at 2:20PM, with some nice views on the climb out.

The seatbelt sign was turned off just five minutes after takeoff, at which point the crew sprung into action, starting by closing the curtain between the cabin and the galley.

After takeoff, the crew distributed some warm towels, which had a nice scent to them.

In a recent development, A few minutes later, the inflight meal was brought out. For a flight of this length, I was impressed. The main dish had some prawns, burrata, and veggies. Then there was a cheese plate, a slice of cake, and a piece of bread. Unlike on Air Algerie, a little thought was also put into presentation.

According to recent reports, the crew passed through with water, while other drinks had to specifically be requested. I asked for a cup of tea, which was also promptly served. By the time I finished my snack, we were already well into our descent.

For a flight of this length, this kind of snack is really tough to beat.

Sources indicate that just before landing, I checked out the business class lavatory on the Royal Air Maroc 737. It was a pretty standard previous generation 737 lavatory, and had definitely seen better days. Among other things, the toilet seat just wouldn’t stay up unless you held it open the entire time.

There were no special amenities, other than Royal Air Maroc branded hand lotion.

The lead flight attendant on this flight was a nice older guy. We didn’t interact with him much, but he seemed generally charming. For example, I saw him kindly bring some toys to a kid seated in business class, and engage nicely with him.

Sources indicate that the primary flight attendant working in business class was a younger lady. She wasn’t rude, but had zero outward personality. She didn’t smile, and if we exchanged five words, that would’ve been a lot. But at least she was efficient and on top of things, and compared to Air Algerie, she was basically a Singapore Airlines flight attendant.

At 1:50PM Casablanca time (there was a one-hour time change from Malaga, so this was 30 minutes after takeoff), the seatbelt sign was turned on, as we were well into our descent to Casablanca. At that point the pre-landing announcement was made, but again, there was nothing in the way of safety checks, and the person seated in front of me even still had a glass at their seat.

The views on the approach were lovely — Morocco really is a beautiful country.

We ended up landing at Casablanca Airport at 1:05PM, on runway 35L.

From there we had a short five-minute taxi to our arrival stand, where we’d have to get on a bus to get to the terminal.

On the plus side, this gave us a great view of the 737 we had just flown, which was in the special oneworld livery.

Industry observers note that as we deplaned, the lead flight attendant and captain kindly bid farewell to everyone. The airline did have a special bus for business class passengers, which is at least a nice aspect of the passenger experience, as it shows some effort.

It was a roughly five-minute ride to the terminal, then we cleared security, and then we boarded our Royal Air Maroc 787 business class flight to Miami a short while later.

Recent findings suggest that I had a pleasant flight in Royal Air Maroc’s 737 business class. For a 45-minute flight, it sure is nice to get real business class seats and a proper, tasty snack. The flight also operated on schedule, so I really have no complaints, especially when you consider the typical airline experience in the northern part of Africa.

In a recent development, to be fair, though, the cabin was definitely a bit tired, and the lack of Wi-Fi and streaming entertainment would prove more frustrating on a longer journey. Furthermore, the primary flight attendant working business class just didn’t have any personality.

What do you make of Royal Air Maroc’s 737 business class?

#226020. Air France Economy Class: Impressions From A Flight Across The Atlantic

📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1786 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Onemileatatime ↗ Open Full Page

Air France Economy Class: Impressions From A Flight Across The Atlantic

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1786 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Onemileatatime

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In the spirit of trying out upcoming ideas and topics here at OMAAT, and having learned that many of you are interested in reading about economy, here are some thoughts about how well Air France does the job.
  • I’ll focus on the daytime return flight from Dublin (DUB) back to Rio (GIG) via Paris (CDG), as I slept through as much of the outbound overnight as I could.
  • Industry observers note that after completing this trip, I’ve flown back and forth between Brazil and France in all four of Air France’s cabin classes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In the spirit of trying out upcoming ideas and topics here at OMAAT, and having learned that many of you are interested in reading about economy, here are some thoughts about how well Air France does the job.

I’ll focus on the daytime return flight from Dublin (DUB) back to Rio (GIG) via Paris (CDG), as I slept through as much of the outbound overnight as I could. This is not a full review — rather, it’s some general comments on the seats, food, and tech, in Air France’s economy offering.

Industry observers note that after completing this trip, I’ve flown back and forth between Brazil and France in all four of Air France’s cabin classes. Yes, including La Première – I do fly in the pointy end sometimes. 😉.

Having transited through Paris Charles de Gaulle so many times now, I’m actually starting to learn my way around the crazy maze of terminals.

Industry observers note that on this occasion, the transfer was on the simpler side, as both flights used gates in Terminal 2E. That remarked, I still had to catch the light rail transit from Hall K to Hall L and pass through a full security screening before entering the departures area. Not all airports in Europe require this, and I hope it’s taken into account when CDG simplifies its terminal numbering, which is expected in March 2027.

Thanks to my Flying Blue Gold status, I had access to Air France’s Hall L Lounge, which is presently undergoing some refurbishments.

Getting a post- or pre-flight facial would have been amazing, but, like my five previous visits to Air France’s lounges in Paris, I’ve had no luck at getting a slot.

Either there were simply no slots left, or, as on this visit, the remaining slot(s) were after my departure time.

Sources indicate that speaking of lounges, I took this photo from Air France’s lounge in Terminal 2E, Hall K, on a previous trip. According to a staffer I spoke with, the construction outside will eventually be a huge upcoming flagship Air France lounge for Terminal 2E.

I sent this photo to Ben before I boarded, and he was surprised to see that the board specifically referenced pre-boarding for Flying Blue Ultimate members. In case you didn’t know either, now you do.

Here’s one final pic for the AvGeeks: even though Air France’s version of the A380 wasn’t particularly loved, the elevated jetbridge above the Boeing 777-300ER in this pic was a nostalgic reminder of the airline’s former superjumbos.

If you’re locking in for 10+ hour flight in economy, there’s only a limited level of comfort that any airline would be able to offer. I wasn’t envious at all walking through the premium economy cabin during boarding….

It has been revealed that thanks to my Flying Blue Gold status, I was able to choose any seat in the cabin from 72 hours before departure. Contrary to my avoidance of bulkhead/exit row seats and their fixed armrests on night flights, I picked bulkhead window seat 21L in the front row of the economy cabin.

It has been revealed that the legroom here was more than I needed for this day flight. My proposal was to spend most of the flight working, so this seat also avoided anyone reclining into my laptop.

Recent findings suggest that of Air France’s three Airbus A350-900 configurations, this was the newest 292-seater version that has been rolling out since 2023. The economy cabin has 212 seats in a 3-3-3 layout, which I know isn’t usually a favorite of families of four. Non-bulkhead/exit row seats have a pitch of around 31 inches.

I didn’t move the four-way adjustable headrest at all during the flight, and the recline is listed as being around 118 degrees.

No matter where I’m sitting, I can’t help but marvel at that wingtip.

Of the 29 flights I’ve taken with Air France, I can only remember one meal that wasn’t good. In fact, it was terrible, and was actually when I was flying premium economy from Paris to Zanzibar (ZNZ) in 2024.

Of the two meal choices, I went for the chicken pasta (I didn’t note down the second option as I only decided to write about this after the flight).

I thoroughly enjoyed the main dish. It had lots of protein, the sauce was flavorful, and the little mini pasta pieces weren’t dry at all. Given the several accompaniments, I consider this a generous helping of food. The Président camembert cheese was a nice premium touch, and the bread roll was quite the opposite of stale. I can’t tell you how good the mini apple tart was, as I’m intolerant to apples.

I wish there had been a menu so I could know for sure what was in this really tasty salad. I’m pretty sure it was a mix of mainly carrots, potato, and barley, in what I guess was a honey mustard sauce.

For those who don’t know, Air France differentiates itself by serving Champagne in economy. Partial though I can be, I stuck to Coke Zero for the caffeine.

I like the intention of using wood instead of plastic for cutlery; I just wish the knife could actually cut!

It has been revealed that despite the hefty lunch serving, I got very hungry midway through the flight as I didn’t eat a proper breakfast. I went to raid the snack baskets at the rear-most galley. The area very busy with lots of passengers lingering, and there was some kerfuffle over a medical issue, so I didn’t take any pictures.

I did, however, get a snap of my snack haul. A mini ice cream, a couple of chocolate truffles, a packet of savory biscuits, and half a cheese sandwich. While the snacks might have lacked in nutrition, it’s nice to know that you won’t go hungry on Air France’s economy flights.

Sources indicate that I was so tired after the 3:30 a.m. alarm that I skipped the pre-landing light meal on the return flight in favor of a nap.

Sources indicate that neither did I touch the box containing a very beige selection of a bread roll and a pastry on the flight to Paris from Rio. Craving caffeine after a patchy night of sleep, I attempted the drip-style coffee, but a sip was enough to turn my nose up. Yes, I am a coffee snob, and I’m proud of it.

Air France made a great choice to mount the IFE screens on the bulkhead. Only the screen in the aisle seat in my row of three was in that annoying underseat position that needs to be folded away for takeoff and landing.

In a recent development, I could just about reach the very tactile screen when leaning forward. Otherwise, there was a mousepad-style remote.

The 13.3-inch screens are among the largest in the industry, and are the same size as those in the premium economy cabin on this plane.

I counted four charging outlets: a USB-C and a USB-A port in the IFE screen, and, under the seat, a regular power outlet and a second USB-C port.

In a recent development, as for Wi-Fi connectivity, there were no disruptions to the complimentary Starlink for the duration of the flight. However, the whole IFE system had to be reset shortly after we took off. Then, a few hours into the flight, the vast majority of the movies disappeared from the system, including the one I was halfway through. I was able to connect my AirPods to the screen with no issue.

Other amenities, so to speak, were a rather coarse pillow, a blanket, and over-the-head headphones.

One of my favorite things about flying and traveling is meeting newly introduced people, including cabin crew, though due to the busyness of economy cabins, that can be tough.

It has been revealed that if I have time, I also try to bring a sweet treat on board for the crew to enjoy during the flight, no matter which cabin I’m flying in, as it is usually a great way to build rapport. It worked on this flight, as several crew members came to thank me for the mince pies. Mattieu, to whom I handed them during boarding, brought me a little note to say thanks for both the pies and my Flying Blue loyalty.

It has been revealed that over the course of the flight, I noticed crew in the economy cabin engaging enthusiastically with passengers. At the start of interactions during meal service, I even heard crew asking passengers whether their preferred language was English or French. On at least three occasions, I noticed crew walking through the cabin offering water.

In a recent development, after being spoiled with lots of lie-flat beds over the years, I’ll admit the pre-flight excitement isn’t quite the same when boarding a long-haul flight in economy. This return trip in Air France economy was perfectly fine, with the pros certainly outweighing the cons.

Whether you only fly business class, or a frequent economy class flier, I hope you gained some insights into the Air France economy experience.

When was the last time you flew long-haul in economy, and how was the experience?

Why should the terminal renumbering affect security control? They're literally just changing signs, the layout stays the same. Some gates allow arrivals from safe countries to disembark airside, but others don't simply because the passenger flow is mixed with arrivals from "unsafe" countries.

Looks a very nice economy product. The idea of giving the crew treats is totally bizarre to me.

I agree with others here. Thanks Dan for a great review. Looking forward to seeing many more reviews like this. This is far better than the previous opinion-based articles.

Interesting that you refer to President Camembert as a "Premium" :-) More seriously, it's great to see Economy reviews. As much as I'd like to always fly business, nearly all my long-haul trips are in Economy.

Tech Report: Iran resolution blocked in first war powers vote since midterms

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Tim Kaine, D-Va., seen here at the Capitol on June 17, stated additional war powers votes are under discussion for when Democrats control both chambers in the 120th Congress.
  • The Senate rejected a resolution Thursday meant to rebuke President Donald Trump over the Iran war weeks after the midterm elections demonstrated the depth of public anger about the war and its effects on the U.S.
  • Sources indicate that senators voted 48-51 against adopting the Iran war powers resolution that the House previously adopted in mid-September that would direct the president to withdraw U.S.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sen. Tim Kaine, D-Va., seen here at the Capitol on June 17, stated additional war powers votes are under discussion for when Democrats control both chambers in the 120th Congress. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call).

The Senate rejected a resolution Thursday meant to rebuke President Donald Trump over the Iran war weeks after the midterm elections demonstrated the depth of public anger about the war and its effects on the U.S. economy.

Sources indicate that senators voted 48-51 against adopting the Iran war powers resolution that the House previously adopted in mid-September that would direct the president to withdraw U.S. forces from the war.

It has been revealed that as they have previously with similar measures, GOP Sens. Susan Collins of Maine, Lisa Murkowski of Alaska and Rand Paul of Kentucky broke with their party to support the resolution, while Democratic Sen. John Fetterman of Pennsylvania broke with his party to oppose it. Departing GOP Sens. Thom Tillis of North Carolina and Bill Cassidy of Louisiana, who have at times voted in support of similar measures, this time voted against the resolution.

Even if the resolution was adopted in both chambers of Congress, it would be largely symbolic since, as a concurrent resolution, it would not go to the president for his signature.

But the vote afforded senators the opportunity to register their complaints about the war for the first time since Democrats routed Republicans in the midterm elections.

It also comes amid a larger debate within the Democratic Party on how best to fulfill their campaign promise of ending the war as they prepare to take control of Congress next year.

According to recent reports, democrats have become increasingly interested in trying to cut off funding for the war rather than continuing to hold war powers votes. But they are divided on whether to demand an immediate end to funding in the next government funding bill in December or to wait until they take power in January.

Recent findings suggest that “When we have the gavels, we are contemplating other things, and we're actually contemplating things in connection with the CR discussion,” Sen. Tim Kaine, D-Va., told reporters Thursday in an apparent reference to the debate among Democrats.

According to recent reports, as of Nov. 13, the war has cost at least $48.3 billion, up from $47 billion last month, the nominee to be Navy comptroller, Arthur Miller, told the Senate Armed Services Committee at his confirmation hearing Thursday.

According to recent reports, as with previous estimates, the number Miller cited Thursday includes munitions, equipment replacement costs and operational costs but does not factor in the cost of damage to U.S. bases, which alone is likely to run in the billions.

Last week, a trio of Senate Democrats unveiled legislation to prohibit funding for offensive military operations in Iran that they stated they intend to introduce as an amendment to the next government funding bill, which Congress will need to pass to avoid a government shutdown after Dec. 11.

Industry observers note that on Thursday as the Senate voted on the war powers resolution, Sens. Tammy Duckworth, D-Ill., and Kirsten Gillibrand, D-N.Y., two of the sponsors of the proposed amendment, demanded it be included in the next funding bill.

“We’ve already tried tool after tool to get the president to rein in this conflict. Nine months in, defunding the war is the only way to force Trump to end it,” Duckworth, who vowed to vote against any continuing resolution that doesn’t include the amendment, mentioned at a news conference.

Sen. Michael Bennet, D-Colo., unveiled his own proposed amendment Thursday to bar any future and previous funding from being used to “support directly or indirectly combat activities by United States personnel in or over Iran, or in Iranian territorial waters” unless specifically authorized by Congress.

His legislation is modeled off of language Congress passed in 1973 to cut off funding for the Nixon administration’s bombing campaign in Cambodia, Bennet’s office noted in a news release.

“When we vote on short-term spending in the near future, we can fund the government and end this war. It is what the American people demand, and what they deserve,” Bennet noted in a statement.

Meanwhile, the House is likely to vote again on a war powers resolution before year’s end.

Industry observers note that “Before the lame duck’s over, I hope to enforce a war powers resolution vote, and it’ll be a chance for Republicans to say whether they did or didn’t get the message on Nov. 3,” Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., said Thursday in a brief interview, referring to the date of the elections.

As with previous resolutions, Massie’s would direct the president to remove U.S. military units from hostilities against Iran unless specifically authorized by Congress or needed to defend against an imminent attack.

The resolution was filed Nov. 10, and under the 1973 War Powers Resolution, Massie can force a vote 15 calendar days after its introduction.

John M. Donnelly and Lauren Green contributed to this report.

Breaking: Traveler Says American Pilots Should Have Just “Had A Cup Of Coffee” Instead Of Following Federal Law

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1180 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Onemileatatime

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • There’s no denying that traveling by air can be stressful, and that it’s extremely frustrating when things go wrong.
  • So that brings us to a complaint from last night from an American Airlines passenger.
  • Late last night, a social media user posted a picture of two airline pilots on X, with the following caption:.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

There’s no denying that traveling by air can be stressful, and that it’s extremely frustrating when things go wrong. Furthermore, not everyone is a frequent traveler, and understands the ins and outs of how the airline industry functions.

So that brings us to a complaint from last night from an American Airlines passenger. The complaint is so incredibly off base in the first place. But what’s even worse is that when this person is confronted with reality, he just doubles down and keeps going. This person deserves to be roasted, and if you ask me, should be banned from the airline.

Late last night, a social media user posted a picture of two airline pilots on X, with the following caption:.

It has been revealed that I won’t be seeing my family this Thanksgiving because a couple pilots couldn’t drink a cup of coffee and get us home. They clocked out in two hours, but we had 3 hr flight. Thanks @AmericanAir.

I won't be seeing my family this Thanksgiving because a couple pilots couldn't drink a cup of coffee and get us home. They clocked out in two hours, but we had 3 hr flight. Thanks @AmericanAir pic.twitter.com/q1I8pjsM3w.

According to recent reports, I can totally appreciate how frustrating it is when a flight is canceled, but this is actually very simple — federal regulations dictate the maximum number of hours that pilots can fly, and that’s for good reason. The airline industry operates with the goal of putting safety above all else, and pilot fatigue has been a contributing factor to many accidents over the years.

Sources indicate that I totally get it, you want to be home for Thanksgiving, and it sucks things went wrong, but those are the facts. This is federal law, and on top of that, we should want pilots to be well rested, rather than just saying “keep working, just have another cup of coffee.”.

Recent findings suggest that I’d like to point out what makes this even worse — this was a flight out of Miami last night, and the airport had shut down due to a ground stop, because a FedEx MD-11 ran off the runway. That was an absolute pain for all passengers out of the airport, and I can assure you that American also wasn’t happy about that happening, and the impact it had on its operations.

All would be forgiven if this traveler either just didn’t say anything further, or acknowledged “ah, I wasn’t aware of that.” Instead, he has had dozens and dozens of posts, just going on and on and on.

He posted about how American claimed the cancelation was the airport’s fault, but insisted “it’s actually these pilots fault,” and suggested “pilots will lie to save money for their company.”.

Recent findings suggest that @AmericanAir will cancel your flight the day before Thanksgiving and say it's the airports fault. It's actually these pilots fault. pic.twitter.com/v4t8KPSojR.

@AmericanAir pilots will lie to save money for their company @AmericanAir pic.twitter.com/7VmOKILwCL.

He then attacked American’s rebooking lines at Miami Airport. Look, I’ll be the first to call out American when they fall short (and they often do!), but if you really can’t figure out why rebooking lines “wrap around the corner” on one of the busiest travel days of the year when there was an accident that shut down an airport, then you really aren’t trying very hard to understand things.

In a recent development, @AmericanAir why do your rebooking lines always wrap around the corner? How bad are your operations? pic.twitter.com/Id8AaTiom1.

He also has an matter with bathrooms at Miami Airport, which I get, but goodness, he’s repetitive.

Why do you have the most disgusting bathrooms @iflymia.

Why are your bathroom so nasty @iflymia.

Why are your bathroom never clean@iflymia.

Why are your bathrooms such a health hazard @iflymia.

You should hire people to clean your bathrooms@iflymia.

Kimpton Social Password Winter 2026-2027: “This Calls For Something”

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (881 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Onemileatatime

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Kimpton has a pretty cool “social password” concept, whereby you can receive extra perks for sharing a phrase at check-in.
  • I’d like to talk about what the upcoming password is, share my experience using it, and also pose a question to Kimpton regulars about the least cringeworthy way to go about saying it.
  • Kimpton is one of the cooler IHG hotel groups, and there are a variety of things that set Kimpton apart from other IHG brands.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Kimpton has a pretty cool “social password” concept, whereby you can receive extra perks for sharing a phrase at check-in. Kimpton generally has this promotion a couple of times per year — we last saw this in summer, and there’s now a new password for winter.

I’d like to talk about what the upcoming password is, share my experience using it, and also pose a question to Kimpton regulars about the least cringeworthy way to go about saying it.

Kimpton is one of the cooler IHG hotel groups, and there are a variety of things that set Kimpton apart from other IHG brands. One of those things is the social password. The idea is that seasonally, Kimpton provides a phrase through social media that you’re supposed to say when you check-in, and if you do that, you’ll receive something extra.

The upcoming Kimpton password is “this calls for something,” and it’s valid for stays between November 27, 2026, and February 28, 2027. So just say that when you check-in at a Kimpton property during the promotion period, and you’ll receive a surprise.

In a recent development, for those curious about what happens when you say the Kimpton password, I stayed at the Kimpton EPIC Miami some time back, which was my first Kimpton stay in quite a while (and I haven’t stayed at one since either). It was a good value as well, as I was able to use a free night award earned with the Fresh IHG One Rewards Premier Credit Card (learn more).

I was curious what the benefit would be for using the password. So I shared the password with the front desk agent. At the conclusion of the check-in experience, he brought out a game show-style wheel. I might have spun too hard, as it must have gone around for about 30 seconds. Go figure I landed on the tile that just had me spin again.

Sources indicate that then I spun again, and the prize was free parking. I had a car and was staying for two nights, and parking costs $44 per night. So using the Kimpton password saved me nearly $100 — score!!

Recent findings suggest that based on looking at the wheel, it seems that some of the other prizes include a free welcome drink, free breakfast, free snacks, and a free movie. There were also a few empty squares, where I guess you don’t win anything. And I’m not sure what the alarm clock, car tipping over, or postcard of Miami get you. Regardless, I’d say those are some awesome prizes, and I got a great reward.

It’s cute how the Kimpton EPIC Miami makes a game of this. I know there’s a lot of inconsistency when it comes to this benefit across Kimpton properties. Some hotels provide meaningful perks (an upgrade, free, parking, etc.), like I got here, while other hotels provide a 19 cent branded koozie.

In a recent development, it’s great that this has stuck around, given that it has presumably become increasingly popular. Years ago not everyone was on social media, so it was a good way to encourage people to follow Kimpton on X, Facebook, Instagram, etc. With the way the internet has evolved, times have changed a bit.

Recent findings suggest that I’m sure I’m not the only one who finds the concept of saying a password at check-in to be kind of weird. So I think it’s fun to compare notes about how people share the password at the front desk. I find it awkward to just blurt out the password out of nowhere.

So when I used this for my stay, I noted “I guess I’m supposed to say [social password] as the social password?” That did the trick, but I’d be curious to hear how other Kimpton regulars go about this!

Between November 27, 2026, and February 28, 2027, Kimpton’s social password is “this calls for something.” Just state that phrase when you check-in at a Kimpton, and you should get some sort of a surprise. The gift will vary by property, so there’s no reason not to take advantage of this if staying at a Kimpton.

The last time I used the password I got to spin a wheel at check-in, and then I ended up getting free parking, which was a value of $44 per night.

If you’ve used the Kimpton password, what was your experience like?

  • TSA reportedly told United Airlines to suspend a pilot accused of supporting a terrorist group, after the pilots union resisted action according to a federal government source cited by TV news reporter Mike Wagenheim.
  • The latest report claims the intervention happened last week.
  • Mike Wagenheim’s November 24 enhancement on the reported TSA intervention.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

TSA reportedly told United Airlines to suspend a pilot accused of supporting a terrorist group, after the pilots union resisted action according to a federal government source cited by TV news reporter Mike Wagenheim. The fresh report says the intervention happened last week. The pilot hasn’t been named. Neither has the terror group he allegedly supported. Mike Wagenheim’s November 24 enhancement on the reported TSA intervention Wagenheim’s earlier report cited two sources saying United knew of up to six additional crew members who’d expressed support for terrorist groups. United’s pilots union spokesman declined to discuss individual cases. He remarked the Air Line Pilots Association has a professional standards committee and legal team that assess accusations against its ethics code and United’s workplace guidelines. The Pilot Israel Barred Was Already On Leave In October, Israel prohibited flights with Sina Amjadian serving as crew from arriving in the country. Israeli officials confirmed the restriction after receiving allegations that he’d expressed support for Iran’s Revolutionary Guards and Hezbollah. But United said he wasn’t presently flying, having been on leave since 2024. He flew Boeing 737s and wasn’t qualified on long haul aircraft. Apparently there was material showing Iranian leadership imagery and mourning civilians killed in strikes. There are claims of Hezbollah support and that there was a video of him kissing the regime’s emblem. United Pilot Celebrated October 7 Rapes And Murders As ‘Bravery’ I first wrote about Ibrahim Mossallam in November 2023, after his Facebook description of the October 7 attack as “resistance by a brave people.” United removed him from service with pay but he was reported back flying. On October 6, 2026, after the flydubai pilot sought to use his plane as a missile to attack Israel, United told me: We have withheld this pilot from service pending an ongoing review. There were also reports that he returned after just a day, and that two colleagues had given up first class seats to monitor him in the cockpit. United subsequently denied both accounts. A reported claimed the union blocked his firing. TSA Can Order A Pilot Out Of The Cockpit It was striking that the reported order came from TSA. It has authority that extends well beyond passenger checkpoints. Under federal law, a TSA determination that a pilot poses, or is suspected of posing, a terrorism or passenger safety threat requires the Federal Aviation Administration to take action against the pilot’s certificate. TSA can request that the action take effect immediately. It can also glitch mandatory security directives to airlines. However, it isn’t clear from the report what legal mechanism is claimed to have been used and doesn’t report an FAA certificate action. It says the pilot’s “TSA credential” was revoked and describes that as Known Crewmember access. TSA can require an airline to remove someone’s access, but losing that privilege doesn’t mean losing a pilot’s license. Flydubai Highlights Why The Concern Is Real I don’t need to know a pilot’s politics. But I wouldn’t want someone who celebrates the killing of civilians at the controls of my flight. That calls their judgment into question even without evidence they’ve planned an attack themselves. The September 30 flydubai cockpit attack makes the concern concrete. The co-pilot of that flight planned a suicide attack on the Tel Aviv airport, attacking the captain with an axe to take over the aircraft. He had satisfied the licensing, good conduct and security requirements for the job, and those checks had failed to uncover his extremist intentions. The values of the person in control of an aircraft matter. 💡 Key Takeaways
  • American Airlines is at the moment offering a rare elevated promotion on purchasing AAdvantage miles.
  • While that’s not a price at which I’d proactively pick up miles, there are definitely some situations where that could represent a good value, if you have an immediate use in mind, especially for first and business class travel.
  • Note that offers like this are extremely rare — while American offers a 40% off promotion on buying miles consistently, the 50% off promotion seems to come around just once or twice per year.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

American Airlines is at the moment offering a rare elevated promotion on purchasing AAdvantage miles. Through December 2, 2026, AAdvantage members can purchase miles with up to a 50% discount, which is potentially an opportunity to buy miles for 1.88 cents each.

While that’s not a price at which I’d proactively pick up miles, there are definitely some situations where that could represent a good value, if you have an immediate use in mind, especially for first and business class travel.

Note that offers like this are extremely rare — while American offers a 40% off promotion on buying miles consistently, the 50% off promotion seems to come around just once or twice per year.

Link: Buy American Airlines AAdvantage miles with a discount.

Sources indicate that between 12:01AM CT on November 27 and 11:59PM CT on December 2, 2026, American AAdvantage is offering up to a 50% discount (or 100% bonus, if you prefer) on buying miles. The offer is tiered, and you get a bigger discount the more miles you buy, as follows:.

As you can see, you need to buy a lot of miles to get the best price!

In a recent development, ordinarily American sells AAdvantage miles for 3.5 cents each pre-tax, or 3.76 cents after factoring in the 7.5% federal excise tax. That’s before any discounts or bonuses. In this case if you max out the promotion and buy 500,000 AAdvantage miles, you’d pay a total of $9,406.25, which comes out to 1.88 cents per mile (that factors in the 7.5% tax).

Sources indicate that keep in mind that American Airlines mileage purchases are non-refundable, and buying AAdvantage miles doesn’t count toward your Loyalty Points total (other than any amount you may spend on an eligible credit card). Purchased miles typically post nearly instantly, but in some cases, it can take up to four hours for them to post.

According to recent reports, the 50% discount is the best price we’ve seen from American AAdvantage in recent years, and again, it only comes around once or twice per year. With the standard 40% off promotion on buying miles, you’d ordinarily pay 2.26 cents per mile.

The American AAdvantage program ordinarily allows members to buy at most 300,000 miles per account per calendar year, before factoring in any bonuses. However, during this promotion, that cap has been increased to 500,000 miles. AAdvantage accounts less than 30 days old aren’t eligible to buy American Airlines miles. Miles can only be purchased in 1,000-point increments.

Recent findings suggest that the process of buying American Airlines miles is easy — the easiest way is to simply follow this link. Alternatively, you can go to aa.com, click on “AAdvantage” at the top of the page, and then click on “Buy, gift or transfer miles.”.

In a recent development, yes, you absolutely can buy American Airlines miles, you just have to be aware of a few restrictions. For one, your account needs to be at least 30 days old. On top of that, you have to stay within the annual cap.

It’s possible to buy miles for yourself or others, but you’ll need to be sure you use the right account to make the purchase.

Is this a good deal? At 1.88 cents per mile, the current promotion is 50% below the standard price. That matches the best deal we’ve tracked. It’s 0.38 cents above our 1.5-cent valuation of AAdvantage miles.

Among the “significant three” carriers in the US, I tend to think AAdvantage has the best redemption opportunities.

I find the cost of business class redemptions to be excellent in many cases. There are instances where it could make sense to pick up miles during a promotion with a short term use in mind. For airlines like Cathay Pacific, Etihad, and Qatar Airways, the airlines now largely restrict premium awards to members of their own frequent flyer programs. So definitely do your research before buying any miles.

In a recent development, another thing worth mentioning is that if you redeem for travel on British Airways, get ready to pay huge carrier imposed surcharges, which could be hundreds of dollars on a long haul premium cabin trip. So that wouldn’t be my preferred use of American Airlines miles.

American Airlines belongs to the oneworld alliance, so you can redeem AAdvantage miles on all oneworld airlines.

On top of that, you can redeem miles on some of American’s other partner airlines, including Aer Lingus, Air Tahiti Nui, China Southern, Etihad Airways, and GOL Airlines, among others.

Industry observers note that everyone will value mileage currencies differently, and based on my latest miles & points valuations, I consider AAdvantage miles to be worth 1.5 cents each. However, I tend to value points pretty conservatively, and there are many ways to get way more value from AAdvantage miles than that.
