    #225997. Your Flight Takes 10 Minutes Longer Than It Used To—And That’s A Luxury Worth Paying For

    📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2235 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Viewfromthewing ↗ Open Full Page

    Your Flight Takes 10 Minutes Longer Than It Used To—And That’s A Luxury Worth Paying For

    📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2235 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Viewfromthewing

    ⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that flying takes longer than it used to – and, retirement of the Concorde notwithstanding, it’s not because planes aren’t as fast.
    • It has been revealed that by one estimate flights have gotten 8% longer.
    • In a recent development, airlines are often chided for ‘schedule padding’ – claiming that flights take longer than they should.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that flying takes longer than it used to – and, retirement of the Concorde notwithstanding, it’s not because planes aren’t as fast. There are more than twice as many commercial flights as there were at the time of airline deregulation, and air traffic control hasn’t been upgraded very much. There’s congested airspace and also congested airports. We also don’t build major upcoming airports – the last one was Denver, 30 years ago. (Austin’s new 1999 airport was a converted military base, and there were others like that in the 90s.) By one estimate flights have gotten 8% longer. That means a two hour flight is 10 minutes longer than it used to be. And the single biggest factor is often tagged as strategic padding of schedules. Airlines are often chided for ‘schedule padding’ – claiming that flights take longer than they should. Often, this just reflects the reality of telling customers when they can expect to arrive – although there’s greater variance than there used to be, which isn’t great for having a gate available when you land early. Airlines do not like this! Though real airfares (even including fees) are down significantly since deregulation, longer flight times are expensive for staffing, fuel and efficient use of $50 – $100 million planes. And longer travel times historically disadvantaged an airline trying to sell tickets, because it meant their flights were displayed lower on the screen that travel agents and later passengers directly saw – which translates into fewer sales. A new study finds that airlines with more “padding” in their schedules tend to charge higher fares. That sounds like passengers paying more for a slower trip. But those extra minutes can also let United hold your plane with ConnectionSaver and get you home that night, and still arrive on time. It also means fewer delays and missed connections. So that ‘premium’ is actually a more valuable product to many consumers. I’ve argued for years that schedule padding often isn’t really padding. Sometimes an airline is finally admitting how long the trip takes. Customers can proposal around an honest arrival time. There’s a new chapter by Embry-Riddle’s Jules Yimga, “The Price of Punctuality,” in The Economics of Airline Pricing. It combines 2019 flight time data with the government’s ticket price survey. It compares schedules against different percentiles of actual flight times, then examines how the resulting measures relate to fares. More padding is associated with higher fares, especially when the comparison uses the faster end of actual flight times. The relationship appears in both competitive and concentrated markets. The abstract itself allows that reliability could be a service customers value. (Interestingly, Yimga’s earlier research on schedule padding attributed higher prices primarily to higher costs rather than higher margins.) Even scheduling to the median arrival time means roughly half of trips take longer than published. It’s often better for a customer if an airline underpromises and overdelivers – or arrives ‘on time’ rather than late. Predictability matters when you’re scheduling connections or trying to arrive in time for a meeting. An airline that leaves little buffer is going to appear less reliable, so customers book earlier flights and longer layovers or even fly in the night before an important meeting. Then the buffer hasn’t disappeared, it just changes who’s scheduling it. That’s why I argued American’s investment in more realistic schedules could pay for itself. Avoiding rebooking, mishandled bags and aircraft and crews getting out of position can justify spending running an on-time schedule even before a customer chooses the airline again because the trip met expectations. American’s Dallas – Fort Worth overhaul that began in April combined longer scheduled flight times with a move from nine daily banks of flights to thirteen. Spreading flights into smaller waves reduced congestion that made some of the extra time unnecessary. One plane waiting for a gate can delay its passengers, its next departure, and other flights whose crews are stuck on board. Giving the operation room to recover can prevent that problem from cascading. In January, I covered American network planning chief Brian Znotins explaining that bookings for 40–54 minute connections at DFW were 4% below what its model predicted. Bookings for 55–84 minute connections were 8% above prediction. Customers have actually started choosing longer connections because they feel more reliable and less likely to leave them stranded. When I covered United’s media day in 2019, Greg Hart explained that 25% of its flights each day were expected to arrive ten minutes early. That gave United room to use ConnectionSaver to hold flights for connecting passengers and still arrive on time. Of course there’s such a thing as too much slack. An airline can improve its reported punctuality by moving the promised arrival later without getting anyone anywhere sooner. Excessively long connections waste customer time. And routinely beating an absurdly generous schedule doesn’t make an operation excellent. Not all padding is something customers will pay a premium for. Avoiding rebooking, mishandled bags and aircraft and crews getting out of position can justify spending running an on-time schedule even before a customer chooses the airline again because the trip met expectations. American’s Dallas – Fort Worth overhaul that began in April combined longer scheduled flight times with a move from nine daily banks of flights to thirteen. Spreading flights into smaller waves reduced congestion that made some of the extra time unnecessary. One plane waiting for a gate can delay its passengers, its next departure, and other flights whose crews are stuck on board. Giving the operation room to recover can prevent that problem from cascading. In January, I covered American network planning chief Brian Znotins explaining that bookings for 40–54 minute connections at DFW were 4% below what its model predicted. Bookings for 55–84 minute connections were 8% above prediction. Customers have actually started choosing longer connections because they feel more reliable and less likely to leave them stranded. That gave United room to use ConnectionSaver to hold flights for connecting passengers and still arrive on time. Of course there’s such a thing as too much slack. An airline can improve its reported punctuality by moving the promised arrival later without getting anyone anywhere sooner. Excessively long connections waste customer time. And routinely beating an absurdly generous schedule doesn’t make an operation excellent. Not all padding is something customers will pay a premium for. So that ‘premium’ is actually a more valuable product to many consumers.

    I’ve argued for years that schedule padding often isn’t really padding. Sometimes an airline is finally admitting how long the trip takes. Customers can plan around an honest arrival time.

    There’s a new chapter by Embry-Riddle’s Jules Yimga, “The Price of Punctuality,” in The Economics of Airline Pricing. It combines 2019 flight time data with the government’s ticket price survey. It compares schedules against different percentiles of actual flight times, then examines how the resulting measures relate to fares.

    Recent findings suggest that more padding is associated with higher fares, especially when the comparison uses the faster end of actual flight times. The relationship appears in both competitive and concentrated markets. The abstract itself allows that reliability could be a service customers value. (Interestingly, Yimga’s earlier research on schedule padding attributed higher prices primarily to higher costs rather than higher margins.).

    Recent findings suggest that even scheduling to the median arrival time means roughly half of trips take longer than published. It’s often better for a customer if an airline underpromises and overdelivers – or arrives ‘on time’ rather than late. Predictability matters when you’re scheduling connections or trying to arrive in time for a meeting.

    #225996. Sweeping permitting overhaul passes Senate, on to House

    Sweeping permitting overhaul passes Senate, on to House

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1483 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, from left, Sens.
    • The Senate passed a bill Thursday evening that would overhaul the federal permitting system for electric power lines, power lines wind and solar farms, hard rock mining and oil drilling projects and more.
    • In a recent development, it's the culmination of a yearslong effort intended to address industry concerns that it is too difficult to build any major infrastructure project in the United States.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, from left, Sens. Mike Lee, R-Utah., Shelley Moore Capito, R-W.Va., Martin Heinrich, D-N.M., and Sheldon Whitehouse, D-R.I., hold a news conference on the measure in the Capitol on Sept. 30. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call).

    The Senate passed a bill Thursday evening that would overhaul the federal permitting system for electric power lines, power lines wind and solar farms, hard rock mining and oil drilling projects and more.

    In a recent development, it's the culmination of a yearslong effort intended to address industry concerns that it is too difficult to build any major infrastructure project in the United States. Supporters overcame opposition from more than half the Democratic Caucus, which will be a factor when the bill moves to the House after the Thanksgiving recess.

    The bill passed on a 62-33 vote, with 31 Democrats joining two Republicans, Josh Hawley of Missouri and Mike Rounds of South Dakota, in opposition.

    Shortly after the post-cloture time expired late Thursday, the Senate voted on passage of the legislation, including a substitute amendment consisting of revised text of the original permitting bill that the bipartisan authors unveiled before the midterm elections.

    However, the chamber did not consider any additional amendments to the bill, as initially planned by the sponsors, including Environment and Public Works Chairman Shelley Moore Capito, R-W.Va., panel ranking member Sheldon Whitehouse, D-R.I., Energy and Natural Resources Chairman Mike Lee, R-Utah, and panel ranking member Martin Heinrich, D-N.M.

    The bill includes changes to how reviews are conducted and permits are issued under the National Environmental Policy Act, National Historic Preservation Act, Endangered Species Act, Federal Power Act and Clean Water Act.

    It includes provisions intended to ensure electricity ratepayers are not saddled with the costs of bringing power to data centers, and would give the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission new authority over interstate transmission lines.

    Sources indicate that it also would provide legal recourse when administrations discriminate against certain forms of energy or seek to revisit permits on ideological grounds. That's intended in part to address the Trump administration’s actions to delay or block solar and wind energy projects.

    Sources indicate that democrats walked away from negotiations last year due to Trump administration actions to block offshore wind construction. However they ultimately said they received sufficient assurances that the administration would let stalled wind and solar projects move forward.

    The "massive four" senators on the permitting bill solicited feedback and changes sought by various lawmakers on both sides of the aisle, and were open to votes on additional amendments — so long as they didn't undo the measure's core tenets.

    "This bill has threaded a needle the likes of which this chamber has not seen in a while, and we’ve got to take advantage of this opportunity," Capito remarked before passage.

    In a recent development, ultimately, Oregon Democratic Sens. Jeff Merkley and Ron Wyden would not consent to a time agreement allowing consideration of a finite number of amendments because Republicans wouldn't allow up-or-down votes at a simple-majority threshold on some of theirs. Merkley then objected to a unanimous consent request to consider amendments on the floor.

    Wyden was pushing for a vote on an amendment that would prohibit construction of data centers on federal public lands. Merkley was pushing for amendments that included barring data centers from benefiting from “project certainty” protections against future presidents revoking their permits, and limiting presidential power to impose tariffs on clean energy project components, like wind turbines.

    The Senate had already adopted the substitute amendment introduced by the bill’s sponsors during a procedural vote on Wednesday. But the lack of a unanimous consent agreement to take up more amendments meant that an additional manager's package of changes to the substitute fell by the wayside.

    That amendment would have narrowed the instances where exemptions from National Historic Preservation Act reviews would be allowed, increased the annual authorization for the Historic Preservation Fund by 50 percent, and addressed concerns about the use of eminent domain when permitting transmission projects raised by Hawley and Rounds.

    The sponsors introduced an updated version of their manager’s amendment Thursday afternoon that would refine exemptions from the ratepayer projection provisions so that artificial intelligence "hyperscalers" can't escape through a loophole.

    The original manager's amendment sought to exempt internet and telecommunications providers' facilities, but the language was broad enough that cloud storage and other "information services" exclusions could potentially benefit data centers.

    None of those changes made it into the bill as a result of the stalemate over amendments, and Merkley objected on the floor to incorporating just the manager's package.

    It has been revealed that the bill has been endorsed by a wide range of industry groups, who argue that the current federal permitting regime makes it too difficult to finance, strategy and construct projects domestically. This includes the American Petroleum Institute, the American Clean Power Association, the U.S. Chamber of Commerce and the National Association of Manufacturers.

    The White House expressed its support for the bill in a statement of administration policy this month.

    The bill now moves on to the House, where it seemingly has the votes to pass.

    Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., mentioned last week that the bill can pass in that chamber, while a number of Democrats including the centrist Blue Dog Coalition and Reps. Scott Peters, D-Calif., co-chair of the bipartisan Climate Solutions Caucus, and Nikki Budzinski, D-Ill., have expressed support.

    Budzinski was elected chair of the 112-member Upcoming Democrat Coalition last week for the next Congress, and that group issued a statement speaking favorably of permitting while stopping short of endorsing the bill as presently drafted.

    However, attendance on the House GOP side after Thanksgiving could be an concern: more than 30 lawmakers regularly skipped votes this week, the majority of them Republicans.

    And many Democrats have called on Heinrich and Whitehouse to punt consideration of the bill to the fresh Congress, when their party will have large majorities in both chambers.

    Merkley, who is in line to chair the Environment and Public Works Committee, and House Natural Resources ranking member Jared Huffman, D-Calif. — the expected chairman of that panel — both mentioned the bill included too many provisions Democrats opposed in order to garner Republican support.

    Industry observers note that some of the nation’s largest environmental groups including the Sierra Club and Natural Resources Defense Council oppose the bill. A coalition of 17 Democratic states also expressed their opposition. And some Native American tribes and organizations, including the National Congress of American Indians, also expressed their opposition.

    "I’m hoping to have a full opportunity to address the many legitimate concerns that stakeholders have raised with this bill," Merkley said before the vote Thursday night.

    Recent findings suggest that but Heinrich and Whitehouse resisted calls to delay the bill, arguing that President Donald Trump is in office for two more years and that any bill needs his support to be signed into law. They added that they will be able to address environmental issues under their majority, and that this bill would represent the “floor” of their ambitions.

    While Republicans have called for changes to the federal permitting system for decades, the effort gained steam with Democrats after the passage of their 2022 reconciliation law, which they dubbed the Inflation Reduction Act, or IRA.

    As part of the deal to get then-Senate Energy and Natural Resources Chairman Joe Manchin III, D-W.Va., on board with the IRA, the Biden administration agreed to support a bill overhauling the federal permitting system. Manchin introduced a bill that included changes to NEPA and transmission permitting, and would approve all remaining permits needed for the Mountain Valley Pipeline in his home state.

    However, his effort ultimately fell short on a 47-47 procedural vote to attach the bill to that year’s defense authorization measure.

    In the 118th Congress Manchin tried again, and in 2024 he and then-Energy and Natural Resources ranking member John Barrasso, R-Wyo., introduced what Manchin called a “perfectly crafted balance.” The committee approved that bill in July 2024, but it was never voted on by the full Senate.

    Capito, Whitehouse, Lee and Heinrich made a collective commitment to address permitting overhaul when they stepped into their current roles in January 2025, and spent nearly 21 months working on the legislation.

    Since Manchin’s first bill, the political calculus changed.

    After decades of stagnant energy demand, electricity prices began rising in part due to the expansion of data centers. Consumers also became increasingly frustrated with their local utilities over affordability concerns, which in turn spurred more lawmakers across the country, including on Capitol Hill, to critically examine their practices.

    Sources indicate that lee also pushed for language streamlining NHPA reviews, which had not been a focus of earlier permitting discussion. He's argued that the law has expanded beyond its originally intended scope and become a major barrier to infrastructure projects in Western states like Utah.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Every year, corporate shareholders have several hundred proposals to vote on at corporate annual meetings or, more often, via their proxy ballots.
    • Sources indicate that unlike many federal rule changes, which often include relatively minor tweaks to the existing bureaucracy, the SEC’s current proposal would repeal a major regulation known as Rule 14a-8 that’s been on the books for decades.
    • Richard Morrison is the host of the Free the Economy podcast and a senior fellow at the Competitive Enterprise Institute.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Every year, corporate shareholders have several hundred proposals to vote on at corporate annual meetings or, more often, via their proxy ballots. Those proposals have become more controversial and divisive over time. The last several years of battles over “woke capitalism” and its inevitable backlash were largely fought through the shareholder resolution process. Now the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) is about to rewrite the rules for what makes it onto those shareholder ballots, and that could mean a reset for how politics impacts corporate America — and vice versa.

    Sources indicate that unlike many federal rule changes, which often include relatively minor tweaks to the existing bureaucracy, the SEC’s current proposal would repeal a major regulation known as Rule 14a-8 that’s been on the books for decades. Originally implemented in 1942 and amended multiple times since, the rule gave the SEC the power to referee which ideas corporate boards need to put up for a vote and which ones they can safely ignore. But the SEC is now proposing to repeal the rule entirely, leaving those decisions up to state governments and individual companies.

    Richard Morrison is the host of the Free the Economy podcast and a senior fellow at the Competitive Enterprise Institute.

    Alec Mena is a research fellow at the Competitive Enterprise Institute.

    #225988. Breaking: Departing Senate spending kingpins angle for last earmark hurrah

    📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (825 w)
    📖 Baca
    Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Rollcall ↗ Open Full Page

    Breaking: Departing Senate spending kingpins angle for last earmark hurrah

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (825 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Susan Collins, R-Maine, left, and Mitch McConnell , R-Ky., won't be smiling as much if Democrats force a punt on spending bills to next year.
    • In a recent development, newly released Senate appropriations bills would distribute $8.7 billion in "congressionally directed spending" secured by 78 senators for their home states — earmarked dollars that could disappear if Congress resorts to a stopgap funding measure to avert a partial government shutdown after Dec.
    • Nearly 4,000 individual earmarks are contained in nine of the 12 draft fiscal 2027 spending bills, a CQ Roll Call tally found; the remaining three bills — Defense, State-Foreign Operations and Legislative Branch — don't have any.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that sens. Susan Collins, R-Maine, left, and Mitch McConnell , R-Ky., won't be smiling as much if Democrats force a punt on spending bills to next year. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call file photo).

    In a recent development, newly released Senate appropriations bills would distribute $8.7 billion in "congressionally directed spending" secured by 78 senators for their home states — earmarked dollars that could disappear if Congress resorts to a stopgap funding measure to avert a partial government shutdown after Dec. 11.

    Nearly 4,000 individual earmarks are contained in nine of the 12 draft fiscal 2027 spending bills, a CQ Roll Call tally found; the remaining three bills — Defense, State-Foreign Operations and Legislative Branch — don't have any.

    There's typically some overlap between House and Senate projects that would get weeded out in final negotiations to avoid duplication. But for comparison's sake, House Republicans included nearly 6,700 line items worth $8.2 billion in their earmarked spending bills.

    Democrats have signaled they'll push for a continuing resolution into the first quarter of next year enabling them to rewrite the full-year fiscal 2027 bills when they take the gavels in January, possibly upping the overall pot of earmarked funds — or at least divvying up the pie more favorably to blue states and districts.

    But that would mean the final attempt by departing lawmakers like Senate Appropriations Chair Susan Collins, R-Maine, and longtime Senate GOP leader and senior appropriator Mitch McConnell of Kentucky, to deliver for their states might be all for naught.

    And top Democrats with substantial earmarking success under GOP governance, such as Appropriations ranking member Patty Murray, D-Wash., will have to start from scratch.

    Here are some key stats on senators' earmarks in the latest batch of spending bills Collins is trying to get across the finish line.

    Naturally, much of the spoils go to Senate Appropriations Committee members, and that's no different this year. But with so many more Democrats requesting projects — often jointly with their fellow delegation member — individual contributions may appear diluted given they have to share the credit.

    That dilution demonstrates up in the rankings when allocating credit in a way that avoids double-counting — everyone gets an equal share of his or her joint projects, so $20 million sponsored jointly by two senators will appear as $10 million for each. Solo earmarkers in this scenario face no such dilution.

    Using the even-split methodology, the top 10 — all senior appropriators — look like this:.

    Another way to look at it is by simply adding up every instance of a senator affixing his or her name to a project, which leads to double-counting but gives them full credit for every earmark secured, even with jointly requested projects.

    Here's the top 10 in that scenario:.

    Finally, there's the solo earmarker leaderboard, only counting dollars secured without any co-sponsors:.

    McConnell and Collins hit the trifecta, ending up among the top three in all three scenarios.

    Related: Maine senators at odds over credit for earmarks.

    Unlike the House, where states with the largest populations receive the most funding by virtue of having more representatives securing earmarks, smaller states punch above their weight in the Senate — particularly when their delegations achieve exalted positions of seniority.

    Hence Washington state — with Murray and Cantwell, the Commerce Committee ranking member, representing it — is way out in front.

    It has been revealed that by contrast, the second- and third-most populous states — Texas and Florida — received a grand total of zero earmarked funds, because their GOP senators didn't request any. California, with the largest population, is No. 16 in the ranks; Latest York is 12th.

    Here are the top 10 states by earmarked funds procured in the Senate bills, clearly skewing toward smaller, typically reddish states:.

    The Transportation-HUD spending bill continues to be the go-to place for earmarks, accounting for 27 percent of all individual projects in the Senate bills and about one-third of all the earmarked dollars. The next-closest bill, Labor-HHS-Education, has half the earmarked amount that the "T-HUD" bill does.

    Top agencies and programs with earmarked funds are housed within, that's right, the departments of Transportation and Housing and Urban Development, with HUD leading the pack thanks to its ever-popular Community Development Fund accounting for all of that department's earmarks.

    Industry observers note that transportation isn't far behind, thanks largely to highway projects, followed by Health and Human Services and its Health Resources and Services Administration account, which funds community health centers. Defense Department military construction projects and the Army Corps of Engineers round out the group of $1 billion-plus agencies.

    Here are the top accounts for earmarked funds in this year's crop of bills:.

    The biggest individual earmarks are largely within Army Corps accounts funded in the draft Energy-Water bill, with some military construction and transportation projects and two mega NIST-based university construction earmarks thrown in on behalf of Collins and McConnell.

    📅 27 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 19m • 📚 Deep Dive (3794 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Viewfromthewing ↗ Open Full Page

    American Airlines And Citi Test A $695 Business Card That Could Earn 50% More Miles And Loyalty Points

    📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 19 min read (3794 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Viewfromthewing

    ⏱️ ~19 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, I receive compensation for content and many links on this blog.
    • American Airlines and Citi are working on a $695 AAdvantage Executive card for small businesses.
    • According to recent reports, doctor of Credit shares some card designs that Citi is surveying.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, I receive compensation for content and many links on this blog. Be aware that websites may earn compensation when a customer clicks on a link, when an application is approved, or when an account is opened. Citibank is an advertising partner of this site, as is American Express, Chase, Capital One, and others. Any opinions expressed in this post are my own, and have not been reviewed, approved, or endorsed by my advertising partners. I do not write about all offers that are available -- instead focusing on miles, points, and cash back (and currencies that can be converted into the same). Terms apply to the offers and benefits listed on this page.

    American Airlines and Citi are working on a $695 AAdvantage Executive card for small businesses. It’s been an odd omission. The $695 United Club Business Card already earns 1.5 miles per dollar on everyday spending. Delta Air Lines has its $650 SkyMiles Reserve Business card. American’s Admirals Club card has been a consumer product.

    According to recent reports, doctor of Credit shares some card designs that Citi is surveying. One looks a lot like the consumer Citi® / AAdvantage® Executive World Legend Mastercard® [See rates and fees] I’ve carried for a long time. However, the other would earn: 1.5 miles and 1.5 Loyalty Points per dollar on everyday purchases. Put $100,000 of bills on one employee’s card in a qualification year and the business would earn 150,000 redeemable miles. The employee would earn 150,000 Loyalty Points, enough for Platinum Pro, and the owner would earn 100,000 Loyalty Points, enough for Platinum. In January I wrote about Citi testing a $150 fee for the regular business card and the idea of replacing its $99 companion certificate with a flight discount. Citi went ahead with the fee and kept the certificate. So not everything being tested happens, and I’d put the strongest prediction on a card like this coming at a $695 annual fee with Admirals Club membership, realizing that the rest are potential options under consideration (and in some cases even controls that aren’t going to make the final product). Credit: Doctor of Credit What The Lounge Membership Gets A Business Both versions give the primary cardmember Admirals Club membership with up to two guests. The personal card also admits immediate family, which matters when there are four (or more) of you. Employee cards carry no additional annual fee. The company can buy lounge access for the people who travel, at $175 total for the first three and $175 apiece after that. So that’s basically the same as the consumer card, except that the annual fee plus lounge is optional rather. American charges $1,200 to $1,400 for full membership, depending on status. And the clubs are getting better. I prefer the newer American lounges to what United and Delta are building. My home club in Austin is slated to double in size and get an outdoor terrace. Someone who wants the lounge may already have gotten the Citi® / AAdvantage® Executive World Legend Mastercard®. But Citi’s going to want the smaller group of customers who want big company expenses on a business account. Some Ideas Being Surveyed For The Card Both versions shared from this survey would earn 4 miles per dollar on American Airlines and 12 on eligible hotel and car bookings through American. Both come with Group 4 boarding, priority check-in and screening, Omni Champion and Avis President’s Club status, up to $100 for inflight or club purchases, and $15 in Lyft credit after three eligible rides in a month. One largely copies the personal Executive card. It earns one mile and one Loyalty Point per dollar on ordinary spending, plus 10,000 Loyalty Points at each of four balances (50,000, 90,000, 165,000 and 240,000). The other awards 1.5 Loyalty Points on every eligible dollar the cardholder spends. It drops the four milestones, along with the two $250 American Airlines Vacations credits and two $100 inKind dining credits. Instead there’s $20 a month toward Melio or Xero and half off an annual Fox One and Wall Street Journal bundle (meh). It adds Sixt to the $120 Avis and Budget credit and covers a second domestic checked bag. But its two Omni free nights interest me. On the personal Executive card you enroll and complete a qualifying stay of at least two consecutive nights booked directly with Omni to earn one free night. If this didn’t require a stay to earn that would be exceptionally valuable (I’d probably redeem them in Fresh York or worst case if I didn’t otherwise use them, down the street at Barton Creek Resort in Austin). I like the potential add-on of rewards for $100,000 in spending, since the consumer version doesn’t really give a strong incentive to actually spend money on the card (it’s a great one to get and keep, but spending is really only incentivized by the Loyalty Points). Here they’re surveying a choice of 2,500 Loyalty Points, two Flagship Lounge passes or a $200 flight discount. American sells the passes for $150 apiece, though I’d value them as an upgrade from the Admirals Club I can already visit. It’s probably best to just take the flight discount unless the points pushed someone over a status or reward threshold. The $200 adds just 0.2% across $100,000. But for someone already at $96,000 spend it’s worthwhile for the next $4,000. Would I Keep Two $695 American Airlines Cards? I have the regular Citi® / AAdvantage BusinessTM World Elite Mastercard® [See rates and fees], and there’s a reason to spend on it even at one mile per dollar. Through December 31, 2028, eligible purchases on an employee’s card earn a Loyalty Point for the employee and another for the primary cardmember. Both survey designs call that a promotion. On the more interesting version of the premium business card, the extra half Loyalty Point goes to the person whose name is on the card. If employees pay the bills, the owner’s rate on those purchases stays at one. An owner who earns all four personal Executive bonuses from flying could give up 40,000 Loyalty Points by replacing the personal card with that one. The regular business card’s fee goes from $99 to $150 on January 24, 2027. At $100,000 of ordinary spending, E would cost $545 more and earn 50,000 more redeemable miles. That’s 1.09 cents per extra mile before valuing Omni nights or other benefits. If the alternative is a 2% cash back card with no annual fee, though, you’re giving up $2,000 and paying $695. You’d need nearly 1.8 cents apiece from the 150,000 miles to cover both with miles alone. Status remains the reason for spending on the card. A big initial bonus could make either version worth getting for a year. I’d keep my personal Executive and look at replacing my regular business card with this new one. On the personal Executive card you enroll and complete a qualifying stay of at least two consecutive nights booked directly with Omni to earn one free night. If this didn’t require a stay to earn that would be exceptionally valuable (I’d probably redeem them in Fresh York or worst case if I didn’t otherwise use them, down the street at Barton Creek Resort in Austin).

    I like the potential add-on of rewards for $100,000 in spending, since the consumer version doesn’t really give a strong incentive to actually spend money on the card (it’s a great one to get and keep, but spending is really only incentivized by the Loyalty Points). Here they’re surveying a choice of 2,500 Loyalty Points, two Flagship Lounge passes or a $200 flight discount. American sells the passes for $150 apiece, though I’d value them as an upgrade from the Admirals Club I can already visit. It’s probably best to just take the flight discount unless the points pushed someone over a status or reward threshold. The $200 adds just 0.2% across $100,000. But for someone already at $96,000 spend it’s worthwhile for the next $4,000.

    I have the regular Citi® / AAdvantage BusinessTM World Elite Mastercard® [See rates and fees], and there’s a reason to spend on it even at one mile per dollar. Through December 31, 2028, eligible purchases on an employee’s card earn a Loyalty Point for the employee and another for the primary cardmember. Both survey designs call that a promotion. On the more interesting version of the premium business card, the extra half Loyalty Point goes to the person whose name is on the card. If employees pay the bills, the owner’s rate on those purchases stays at one. An owner who earns all four personal Executive bonuses from flying could give up 40,000 Loyalty Points by replacing the personal card with that one. The regular business card’s fee goes from $99 to $150 on January 24, 2027. At $100,000 of ordinary spending, E would cost $545 more and earn 50,000 more redeemable miles. That’s 1.09 cents per extra mile before valuing Omni nights or other benefits. If the alternative is a 2% cash back card with no annual fee, though, you’re giving up $2,000 and paying $695. You’d need nearly 1.8 cents apiece from the 150,000 miles to cover both with miles alone. Status remains the reason for spending on the card. A big initial bonus could make either version worth getting for a year. I’d keep my personal Executive and look at replacing my regular business card with this new one.     📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that on the last day before the 2026 midterm elections, President Donald Trump gave a speech before the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, a site of considerable scandal in his second term. He joked it should be renamed after him and spent considerable time discussing Washington, D.C. construction projects and resurrecting conspiracy theories about monument vandals. When the president did turn to the elections, more than 23 minutes into an hour-long speech, he seemed to foreshadow major Republican losses in the House and Senate, describing it as “The most important midterm, I believe, in our lifetime.”.

    “When you vote, remember a party that hates America cannot be allowed to rule over the people who built our country,” Trump said, referring to Democrats, whom he said want to “blow all of this up by electing communist jihadists.”.

    “If the people that voted for me and voted in the last election where we had such a great victory, if they go out and vote, just a good portion of them, we will win in a landslide,” Trump said midway in his speech. “Now that doesn’t happen because usually whoever the sitting president is, Republican or Democrat, uh, good or bad, good president, great president, bad, for some reason the sitting president doesn’t win the midterms, but we gave this a very strong shot.”.

    Recent findings suggest that the last day of polling indicates that Democrats have odds that are better than good to flip control of the House and Senate. The final results from the Newly introduced York Times/Siena University polls report “The party is ahead in all seven states likeliest to decide control of the Senate: Michigan, Kansas, Texas, Maine, Ohio and, more narrowly, Alaska and Iowa.” The final predictions in the Cook Political Report included five additional shifts for Democrats in North Carolina, Florida, Tennessee and Virginia, projecting “that Democrats will win 15 to 25 seats, putting them at a 230- to 240-seat majority.” If a sweep happens in the toss up races, it’ll give Democrats their strongest majority since 2009.

    Industry observers note that meanwhile, early voting records have been smashed around the country, in places like South Carolina and Ohio. In Texas, more than 7.7 million voters did so early, surpassing the record turnout for a midterm election set in 2018. Across the nation, about 50 million ballots have already been cast so far, with the share of registered Democrats notably increased in several key state races. But according to the Upcoming York Times, around half the expected votes will come on Election Day itself, making it difficult at this point to determine how significant a role early votes will play in the outcome.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, in Abu Dhabi for peace talks, Russian negotiators revealed that Vladimir Putin is just like the rest of us, a nostalgist for the 1990s.
    • The Russian demand is chiefly about geography.
    • Michael Brendan Dougherty is a senior writer at National Review Online.

    According to recent reports, in Abu Dhabi for peace talks, Russian negotiators revealed that Vladimir Putin is just like the rest of us, a nostalgist for the 1990s. You and I might want to go back for the easeful sense of prosperity, the pre-9/11 sense of security, the pre-Instagram sense of contentment for the pleasures of your own life, or the still-unified popular culture that gave an entire diverse country something in common to talk about at work. Vladimir Putin’s men reiterated one of their primary pre-Ukraine war demands: Russia wants NATO to be back in its 1997 positions.

    Well, sort of. The Russian demand is chiefly about geography. If it were done, it would mean removing nine battlegroups in total: Sweden, in Finland; the U.K., in Estonia; Canada, in Latvia; Germany, in Lithuania; France, in Romania; Spain, in Slovakia; Italy, in Bulgaria; and the U.S., which has 10,000 men in Poland now but only 300 of them permanently there. The U.S. has Aegis Ashore weapons sites in Romania and Northern Poland, and there is a multinational, NATO division-level command center headquartered in northeastern Poland.

    Michael Brendan Dougherty is a senior writer at National Review Online.

    On “Even Putin Is a ’90s Nostalgist”.

    #225973. Sacha Baron Cohen reveals “Who Is America?” and the answer is terrifying

    📅 16 Jul 2018 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1870 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Salon ↗ Open Full Page

    Sacha Baron Cohen reveals “Who Is America?” and the answer is terrifying

    📅 16 Jul 2018 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1870 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Salon

    ⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that showtime debuted Sacha Baron Cohen’s latest series on Sunday, finally providing a partial to the question its title poses.
    • Baron Cohen bases his career on that knowledge, but watching it in action was much more entertaining two decades ago in the heyday of “Da Ali G Show.” His HBO prank show became a cultural phenomenon before the omnipresence of social media and its accelerated mainstreaming of conspiracy theory as news, before a sitting president began making the denigration of objective journalism into a sport and before the proliferation of junk science as fact.
    • Back then cameras were not so prevalent as to persuade everyone that they were only one turned corner away from stardom.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that showtime debuted Sacha Baron Cohen’s latest series on Sunday, finally providing a partial to the question its title poses. “Who Is America?” The answer, on its face, will not surprise you: we are a nation of easy marks. Not merely easy, but willing.

    Baron Cohen bases his career on that knowledge, but watching it in action was much more entertaining two decades ago in the heyday of “Da Ali G Show.” His HBO prank show became a cultural phenomenon before the omnipresence of social media and its accelerated mainstreaming of conspiracy theory as news, before a sitting president began making the denigration of objective journalism into a sport and before the proliferation of junk science as fact.

    Back then cameras were not so prevalent as to persuade everyone that they were only one turned corner away from stardom. But today, being on camera is so natural and desirable to most of us that we are willing to say or do just about anything for a few of the 15 minutes we believe to be our birthright.

    “Ali G” and the characters the show introduced, including Borat Sagdiyev and Brüno Gehard, also were born years before Project Veritas and InfoWars and other right-wing vehicles of disinformation made hidden camera hoaxing into something sinister.

    All of which is to say, “Who Is America?” is not, as Showtime would like you to believe, “the most dangerous show in history.” At best, it is an occasionally funny one.

    But to anyone who mourns the collective deterioration of our population’s capacity to engage in critical thought, but has no idea of how urgent of a crisis that happens to be, Baron Cohen’s upcoming endeavor is less of a comedy than a fright show. “Who Is America?” A nation of pliable dullards ripe for the hacking.

    Industry observers note that “Who Is America?” was produced in secret, and its pre-show marketing largely consisted of publicized declarations of outrage by such right-wing figures as Joe Walsh, Sarah Palin and Roy Moore. Each attempted to transform their extreme embarrassment at having been duped by a British clown hiding behind layers of latex and spirit gum into some approximation of righteous anger at noted comedian’s dishonesty.

    Showtime, meanwhile, maintained the aura of mystery surrounding the series almost to the brink of its debut, revealing the title only a little more than a week prior. The network released the briefest of clips featuring one famous interview subject, Dick Cheney.

    This in itself was a bit of flimflam Showtime’s part: “Hope you’ll tune in next week for an interview with me,” Cheney claims in the video, only to be a no-show in the premiere.

    You can’t blame “Who Is America?” for saving its biggest fish for later, because the famous politicians in the opener prove the problem of our collective gullibility just fine by themselves. In fact, although liberals may have gotten a hearty guffaw out of hearing Palin’s wailing about having been faked out by Baron Cohen, the very same character — Dr. Billy Wayne Ruddick Jr. PhD of Truthbrary.org — sat down for a conversation with none other than the honorable junior senator from Vermont, Bernie Sanders.

    Prior to the premiere Billy Wayne tweeted a response to Palin’s accusation that he made fun disabled veterans. “I did NOT say I was a War Vet,” Ruddick’s “official” response reads, going on to explain that the service was in was “not military, but United Parcel”.

    Sources indicate that nor does he make such assertions to Sanders, with whom he debates the merits of a universal healthcare strategy. And when I say debate, what I mean is that Sanders very calmly shares statistics with Billy Wayne long after the interviewer’s line of questioning stops making sense. And when Sanders asks Billy Wayne to confirm that he is disabled, given that he is conducting the interview while seated on a motorized scooter, Baron Cohen’s character replies that no, he is not. “This here scooter is to preserve my body’s finite energy,” Billy Wayne claims.

    READ MORE: That viral “strangers on a plane” Twitter story: Not a rom-com but a horror show.

    One may be tempted to qualify Sanders’ appearance by pointing out that he acquitted himself well in the face of a person best be described as a few coconuts short of a beach vacation in Binomo.

    According to recent reports, but this fails to answer the question of why Sanders signed a release, allowing this interview to be broadcast. Did anyone on Sanders’ team vet Truthbrary.org the moment Billy Wayne mentioned it? Even if they thought he was genuine, what is to be gained from being seen in a televised debate with a guy whose site includes a page titled  “Obamanoids — For Real!”?

    Sources indicate that (To be fair, reportedly Baron Cohen almost fooled veteran news anchor Ted Koppel as part of his project. Koppel told The Hollywood Reporter that he was contacted to appear in a Showtime project titled “Age of Reason,” said to feature “conversations with distinguished experts in science and public policy, highlighting the brightest and most reputable minds on today’s most important topics.” Koppel, perhaps receiving brainwaves from his colleague Sam Donaldson, wised up before Baron Cohen could pull him too deeply into his game.).

    A second character introduced in the premiere, an NPR shirt-wearing hyper-liberal named  Nira Cain-N’Degeocello, visits the opulent South Carolina home of wealthy Trump supporters he claims are  “afflicted with white privilege.” But it soon becomes clear that his marks’ problem isn’t close-mindedness but over-correcting in the acceptance department. When Baron Cohen’s interviewer waxes on about encouraging his daughter Malala to “free bleed” on the American flag as a lesson, they simply nod and listen; when he chats about his wife’s ongoing affair with a dolphin, they don’t have any questions like, say, whether what they’re hearing is real.

    This brings us to another answer to “Who Is America?”: we’re so aware of cameras, and desperate to have its focus upon us, that we will do and say anything without thinking of its possible permanence.

    Demonstrating this is Baron Cohen’s third character Rick Sherman, an ex-con turned TV host who visits a Laguna Beach, California gallery to show his work, which is a series of capable but otherwise unextraordinary portraits rendered in feces and ejaculate.

    Industry observers note that now, it’s entirely possible that the woman who runs the gallery might have been thinking she could have the next Andres Serrano on her hands. On the other hand, please.

    This is a subject entirely aware of being on view, so obsessed with appearing erudite that while Rick is off camera, having excused himself to the facilities to commit another brown-and-white vision to paper, she addresses the camera like the host she was born to be.

    It has been revealed that “Who knew the world was capable of such oxymoronic paradoxical juxtapositions?” she muses. And this is before the homemade pubic hair paintbrush comes out.

    Baron Cohen has pushed the limits of tolerant everyday people many times in the past, mostly in a way that makes them look reasonable or, at the very least, more intelligent than the put-ons he inflicts upon them. And this is perhaps one of the most depressing aspects about “Who Is America?”, its demonstration of how endemic our lack of analysis truly is. I’m not saying that gallery owner is a stupid woman, understand.

    In a recent development, but her interview is an example of prizing exposure over lasting consequence. By that I’m not merely referring to the fact that she placated a man who not only handed her pieces of cardboard purportedly smeared with his own dried excrement, or waited to receive a fresh sample of his work, but that she decided she needed to share her expert observation as to why she needed to do so by uttering a sentence full of five dollar words that add up to absolute nonsense.

    It has been revealed that (Either that or she’s a friend of Baron Cohen’s and in on the gag. I hope it’s option two, as opposed to her actually legitimizing the artistic relevance of number two.).

    A number of reviews of “Who Is America?” have pointed out that Baron Cohen’s sneaky deceit is no longer funny because the formerly insane viewpoints Baron Cohen’s tactics expose have been normalized.

    This has always been the danger, but it’s one every sort of parody or satire contends with in the current climate. It’s difficult to lampoon leaders seeking to legislate ludicrous patches to crises like gun violence instead of adopting common sense solutions like stricter regulation.

    Which brings us to the portion of “Who Is America?” guaranteed to dominate Monday’s gallery of crazy clips, fronted by Baron Cohen’s Col. Erran Morad, a self-styled Israeli anti-terrorism expert who calls himself “the terrorist terminator.”.

    The fake Mossad officer is there to promote his “Kinderguardians” program, a proposal that aims to train and arm toddlers in the classroom because, Moran notes, arming teachers is crazy.

    Sources indicate that and this is the portion that has Walsh’s boxers in a bunch, because he joins House representatives Dana Rohrabacher and Joe Wilson in lending on-camera endorsements. Walsh’s comments are interwoven with a series of fake testimonials from the likes of Larry Pratt, executive director emeritus of the lobbying group Gun Owners of America and rape joke enthusiast.

    According to recent reports, nobody forced Walsh to say, with gusto, “The way to stop a bad guy with is a good child with a gun. Happy shooting, kids!” If he didn’t want to say it, he wouldn’t have.

    What Walsh might be upset about is being upstaged by Pratt, who earns some of the episode’s biggest laughs by reading the “science” behind the effectiveness of the fake program, revealing he doesn’t know the difference between human anatomy and hitmakers who grace Billboard’s pop charts.

    It has been revealed that yes, “Who Is America?” gets mileage out of highlighting the callousness, sexism and extraordinary gullibility of conservatives, as Baron Cohen always has. But the things they say to him in disguise aren’t all that different than what they’d say on CNN, Fox, MSNBC or talk radio. Whatever power his comedy used to reveal is diminished by the fact that the charlatans no longer operate in secret.

    Next week’s episode introduces one or two upcoming characters, although I don’t imagine they do anything more “dangerous” than the four we met on Sunday. For a number of viewers who love Baron Cohen’s schtick, that won’t matter.

    To them “Who Is America?” is precisely on brand, showing Americans famous and everyday reacting to bizarre situations with varying degrees of what we consider to be normalcy in a time where the baseline version of normal is constantly morphing and shifting.

    According to recent reports, to other viewers, however, “Who Is America?” is a confirmation that Baron Cohen has run some tests and can confirm there is limited and ever decreasing brain activity in this worsening patient we know as America. It is something to behold, that’s for sure. But I’m not sure it’s the stuff of groundbreaking comedy. It’s not even really news.

    #225970. Breaking: “Borat 2” makes an America slathered in misogyny and disinformation reckon with itself

    📅 23 Oct 2020 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (1937 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Salon ↗ Open Full Page

    Breaking: “Borat 2” makes an America slathered in misogyny and disinformation reckon with itself

    📅 23 Oct 2020 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1937 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Salon

    ⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • On Wednesday multiple news outlets revealed the purported headliner of “Borat Subsequent Moviefilm” to be none other than Rudy Giuliani, President Donald Trump’s trusted lawyer and cable news’s favorite nutcase.
    • Industry observers note that compared with the mock attempted kidnapping Pamela Anderson, Borat’s ultimate get in 2006’s “Borat: Cultural Learnings of America for Make Benefit Glorious Nation of Kazakhstan,” the pranking of America’s mayor does not make for a grand climax or even an affectionate one.
    • In a recent development, all it took for the producers of “Borat Subsequent Moviefilm” to succeed in their mission was a simple honeytrap, presented in the form of Baron Cohen’s exceptional co-star Maria Bakalova dressed as a right-wing fake news Barbie.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    On Wednesday multiple news outlets revealed the purported headliner of “Borat Subsequent Moviefilm” to be none other than Rudy Giuliani, President Donald Trump’s trusted lawyer and cable news’s favorite nutcase.

    Industry observers note that compared with the mock attempted kidnapping Pamela Anderson, Borat’s ultimate get in 2006’s “Borat: Cultural Learnings of America for Make Benefit Glorious Nation of Kazakhstan,” the pranking of America’s mayor does not make for a grand climax or even an affectionate one. Instead, it more or less confirms what we already know about Rudy Giuliani: his corruptibility makes him shockingly easy to dupe.

    In a recent development, all it took for the producers of “Borat Subsequent Moviefilm” to succeed in their mission was a simple honeytrap, presented in the form of Baron Cohen’s exceptional co-star Maria Bakalova dressed as a right-wing fake news Barbie. By the time we get to that scene the Bulgarian actor has solidly established that she is the reason this feminist-themed sequel works as well as it does.

    According to recent reports, performance-wise, Bakalova fully commits and never breaks, keeping pace with Baron Cohen in every shared sequence and commanding every scene she pilots solo. If Baron Cohen were to ever greenlight an inheritor to his Borat franchise, she would more than do it justice.

    And this illustrates the subtextual call to action throughout “Subsequent Movefilm” for women of good conscience to reclaim their power, not only at the polls but in the realm of social equity. Baron Cohen and his writers cloak this in slapstick from the moment we’re introduced to Bakalova’s Tutar, the 15-year-old daughter Borat never realized he had.

    Recent findings suggest that tutar is filthy and coarse, raised in a pen and guided by a book given to her by the Kazakh government that insists that women cannot drive, own businesses or even touch their privates without causing great disaster on par with the sinking of the Titanic. Her highest aspiration is to live in a golden cage like Queen Melania, “the happiest wife in the world,” emboldening her to join Borat’s latest trip as a stowaway.

    Sources indicate that similarly life, and Borat’s government, have not been kind to him since “Cultural Learnings” conquered America with great success – high five! – 14 years ago.

    Recent findings suggest that america may have loved Borat but his countrymen, neighbors and family in his home village of Kuzcek felt great shame at how his documentary portrayed them (a nod, perhaps, at the Romanian villagers angered at being misrepresented in the 2006 film, who unsuccessfully sued its producers). In reaction he was sentenced to a life of hard labor in a gulag.

    When Kazakhstan’s current Premier Nazarbayev (Dani Popescu) realizes the regime has a use for Borat, he’s hauled out of prison, shaved into a familiar form – ill-fitting grey suit, walrus mustache, puffy hairstyle and all – and given a latest mission to smooth glorious leader’s entry into the world’s strongman club. How? By presenting to”Vice Premier Mikhail Pence” valuable offering: Johnny the Monkey, “Kazakhstan’s Minister of Culture and No.1 porno star.”.

    This is why the Giuliani spoiler leaking before the film’s release fails to ruin “Borat Subsequent Moviefilm” because, like old Johnny would do in a room full of bananas,  plunking Giuliani into a situation like the one announced in the film’s full title: “Borat Subsequent Moviefilm: Delivery of Prodigious Bribe to American Regime for Make Benefit Once Glorious Nation of Kazakhstan” merely yields the expected results. Giuliani was hoodwinked not by a monkey but old-fashioned monkey business. Wa-wa-wee-wa!

    Industry observers note that in the main, the humor driving “Borat Subsequent Moviefilm” is a continuation of what Baron Cohen does in his 2018 Showtime series “Who Is America?” – which is to say that he functions more as a prodding force these days than a hard crowbar. Long ago the Borat character functioned as a truth serum, the kind of amiable ignoramus people were inclined to countenance or forgive either out of politeness or a sense of superiority. Bigots would meet his bigotry with their own, perhaps, in a gesture of finding common ground, while others put up with him out of kindness.

    Now, as father and daughter embark travel through the good old U.S. of A, 2020 edition, they encounter a place where the rampant racism, anti-Semitism and Islamophobia Borat unearthed in 2006 is now on proud display across the land and slathered in misogyny.

    The sexism, though, is the road by which Borat and Tutar find their way into the psyche of the ugly American – enabling them to infiltrate a debutante ball where Borat gets a father to admit he’d pay $500 for Tutar within earshot of his own child, and another man, hopelessly drunk, slurs out unbidden that men love pretty girls in South. “They’re fun!”.

    Following a span of time in which Borat keeps Tutar in a cage while he sleeps in the relative luxury of a horse trailer he drags behind a jalopy, “Subsequent Moviefilm” makes Tutar’s empowerment the centerpiece of the movie’s second half. Baron Cohen’s signature obviousness and a style reminiscent of director Jason Woliner’s past TV work (which includes series such as “Nathan for You”) shapes how this transpires, and the audience either accepts this for what it is or may cringe at its clunkiness.

    Either way, the fact that “Borat Subsequent Moviefilm” and Baron Cohen need Bakalova is indisputable.

    There’s the practical matter that the character of Borat is famous, for one. Back in 2007 Baron Cohen announced that he was retiring two of his alter egos, Borat and Ali G, acknowledging to The Daily Telegraph that “the problem with success, although it’s fantastic, is that every fresh person who sees the Borat movie is one less person I ‘get’ with Borat again, so it’s a kind of self-defeating form, really.”.

    What he could not have predicted back then was how thoroughly the fabric of reality would be torn by the disinformation flood plaguing us today. However, he’s right about the problem of Borat’s fame. “Subsequent Moviefilm” confronts this early in the film when Borat sets down in America once again, only to be instantly recognized and pursued by crowds of thrilled Texans. This necessitates a trip to a local costume shop to purchase prosthetics and disguises.

    Nonetheless, Borat’s relevance in 2020 is debatable. Since the anti-Semitism and sexism at his heart are defining traits in a nation seized by white nationalism, that either makes him redundant or highly relevant — except for when he revealshis subjects’ prejudices.

    Recent findings suggest that but then, the laugh-until-you-cry parts of the original “Borat” don’t involve, say, the Islamophobic, homophobic rodeo organizer mouthing off or those Southern frat boys wishing aloud that slavery was still legal. The best antics involve Borat’s stupidity crashing against the patience and politeness of typical Americans, or ludicrous moments like the nude wrestling match between him and his producer Azamat (Ken Davilian) that spills out of their hotel room and well into public spaces.

    Fewer of those sight gags exist in “Subsequent Moviefilm.” Save for an extended segment in which he quarantines with a pair of right-wing QAnon adherents, they have been replaced instead by situational humor, such as when Tutar swallows a plastic baby cake decoration and Borat rushes her to what he believes to be a doctor’s office. Naturally they land in crisis pregnancy center where father and daughter are counseled, not by a doctor but by Pastor Jonathan Bright. This evolves precisely as one expects it would.

    Then there are the bits that have already made the news: Baron Cohen’s infiltrating the Conservative Political Action Conference in February dressed as Trump? They work their way to that, and a scene from a right-wing militia gathering in Washington state where Borat performed as Country Steve and got the audience to sing along to a racist ditty, starting with lyrics about injecting Obama “with the Wuhan flu.”.

    Gotcha moments like this and the Giuliani business don’t tell us anything we don’t already know. Instead, it’s what the context implies about America’s psychological state. The cringe comedy in the crisis center isn’t merely in the pastor’s misunderstanding about the nature of the baby inside Tutar’s stomach. It is his calm insistence in her keeping it there even after Tutar’s father tells him that he put it there. (He bought the cupcake, OK?).

    But this is part of an escalating series of moments that show us who America is: a nation of very fine people who live and let prejudice flourish so long as it doesn’t disturb the status quo.

    Sources indicate that there’s the Texas baker who uses icing to pipe the words “Jews Will Not Replace Us” on a chocolate cake without batting an eyelash. There’s the shop owner who guffaws along with Borat when he asks that Tutar be directed to the “no means yes” dress section. There’s the spray tanning salon technician who, in response to Borat asking, “What color is best for racist family?” says without pause or reaction, “I wouldn’t go any darker than a six or a seven.”.

    All of these are women, by the way.

    It has been revealed that this leads up to savior in this narrative: Jeanise Jones, a Black woman Borat hires to look after Tutar and who ends up talking some sense in to her, starting with waking her up to the fact that her father has been lying to her. (And how.) Jones is the level-headed figure in a vast land of fools; she’s also playing to the trope of the Black woman savior utilized in the first “Borat” and touted in this election cycle. Placed in the context of everyone else Borat and Tutar encounter, though, she’s a cool clarifying drink in a desert of dumb and therefore welcome.

    Evaluating the comedy value of “Subsequent Moviefilm” relative to the first “Borat” sets it up to lose, sad to say. It is enormously entertaining and, for the reasons listed above, a healthy treatment to whatever anxieties may be plaguing us a little more than a week leading up to the election. Whatever faults it has aren’t deadly, although it’s plain to see that the pandemic may have shifted the film’s ending in ways that don’t feel fully baked.

    Sources indicate that the most prominent difference between the “Borat” of 2006 and the 2020 “Subsequent Moviefilm” is in who America is now. Our inability to agree on basic facts has only worsened since Trump’s election in 2016, to say nothing of how decline and fall of basic critical thought has left us vulnerable to benevolent pranksters like Baron Cohen and outside forces who would mean us harm.

    Sources indicate that at the same time, there’s simply no getting around the fact that Kazakhstan receives little in the way of an image acquittal in this follow-up, an unavoidable and miserable result of alloying a problematic character to a place. If there’s a salvageable component to this, it is in how differently the sequel leaves us. When we first met Borat we comforted ourselves with the first-world notion that somehow we are better than people of so-called “lesser” nations.

    Now it doesn’t allow the audience to be so sure of itself, implying in the final scene that we aren’t merely ugly Americans. We’re a once glorious nation being led by goons who are sliding us backward into diminishment, and dangerously so. That is nothing to laugh about.

    “Borat Subsequent Moviefilm: Delivery of Prodigious Bribe to American Regime for Make Benefit Once Glorious Nation of Kazakhstan” is presently streaming on Amazon.

    What I’m Thankful For

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (241 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Nationalreview

    ⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that I’m thankful for one little moment on Monday this week, around 5:05 p.m.
    • I’m thankful for my older son’s soccer coach, who has known him for over three years now, moving my boy up from an in-house program, to a Sunday league, and this fall to the EDP (Elite Development Program), where this cheap-as-chips town team plays (and usually defeats) all the expensive “academy teams” in our area.
    • Michael Brendan Dougherty is a senior writer at National Review Online.

    It has been revealed that I’m thankful for one little moment on Monday this week, around 5:05 p.m. The dark of night was falling over most of the sky, except for a brilliant ring of purple just over the tree line to one side of us. We pulled the minivan into the parking lot of the karate studio, and my eight-year-old son hopped out of the car, grabbing my hand as we passed through the parking lot. I gave it a little squeeze, and he squeezed it back. Maybe just a few more years of that. He earned his first stripes on his white belt that night.

    I’m thankful for my older son’s soccer coach, who has known him for over three years now, moving my boy up from an in-house program, to a Sunday league, and this fall to the EDP (Elite Development Program), where this cheap-as-chips town team plays (and usually defeats) all the expensive “academy teams” in our area. My son was not, at first, a natural athlete — in fact, he was quite clumsy. But he had this enormous engine in him to run, and over the years developed patience for himself to work. His coach recognized him, coached his oversensitivity out of him, made him work — and enjoy working — harder than he ever would have done just by himself.

    Michael Brendan Dougherty is a senior writer at National Review Online.
