    House Democrats unveiled a 2027 legislative calendar Friday that includes 33 voting weeks, as the incoming majority party looks to pass an ambitious agenda following massive midterm election wins.

    Industry observers note that according to the calendar released by soon-to-be House Majority Leader Katherine M. Clark, the chamber would convene for the first session of the 120th Congress with a rare Sunday gathering on Jan. 3. The first votes of the year would take place that week.

    “House Democrats are hitting the ground running on January 3,” the Massachusetts Democrat said in a statement. “This calendar reflects the scale and urgency of our work ahead. Americans voted for a Majority that will move decisively to lower costs, protect healthcare, and hold the crooks accountable. Whether we’re working in DC or in our districts, that’s exactly what we’re going to do.”.

    Recent findings suggest that in most months, the House will be in session for three weeks, with the exception of the annual August recess. That will be followed by four consecutive weeks of voting in September.

    The calendar also includes a two-week break for Easter in March, while the Fourth of July falls on a Sunday.

    The 33-week schedule suggests a jam-packed year for the House, following a year in which the chamber saw dozens of canceled session days because of floor impasses and a record-long partial government shutdown. The struggles of the outgoing Republican majority has even bled into the lame-duck session, with absences by dozens of lawmakers forcing outgoing Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., to send a letter to members Friday urging them to “remain fully engaged” in the closing weeks of the 119th Congress.

    With the calendar released, House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries of New York has already outlined some of his top priorities for his presumptive speakership, including an ambitious health care agenda, immigration legislation and aggressive oversight of the Trump administration.

    But even after flipping both chambers of Congress, Democrats face the uphill battle of working with President Donald Trump if they want their agenda signed into law.

    Industry observers note that trump emphasized his “extreme” veto power during a news conference Friday, but he also said he thinks Jeffries and Senate Democratic leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y., are “smart.”.

    Sources indicate that “They're going to send things my way, and I'm going to veto them, and then they're going to send more things, and I'm going to veto them,” he noted. “I think after a month or so, they're going to send things, and I'm going to say, ‘I'm going to veto unless you want to do this and this and this.’".

    The Senate calendar for next year has not yet been released.

    Latest Update: Trump signs bill to halt penny production

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (382 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Rollcall

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • President Donald Trump conducts a news conference in the White House briefing room on Friday.
    • The penny is officially history under a bill President Donald Trump signed into law Friday that codifies the end of production of the one-cent piece.
    • The copper-plated coin is mostly composed of zinc and costs far more to produce than it's worth, prompting members of Congress at least since 1989 to consider killing it as an easy cost-saving measure for the federal government.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    President Donald Trump conducts a news conference in the White House briefing room on Friday. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

    The penny is officially history under a bill President Donald Trump signed into law Friday that codifies the end of production of the one-cent piece.

    The copper-plated coin is mostly composed of zinc and costs far more to produce than it's worth, prompting members of Congress at least since 1989 to consider killing it as an easy cost-saving measure for the federal government.

    Industry observers note that “Washington has a spending problem, and it reveals up in places big and small,” the bill's sponsor, Rep. Lisa McClain, R-Mich., stated Friday in a statement released by the office of House Financial Services Chairman French Hill, R-Ark. “If the federal government is spending nearly four cents to make a penny worth one cent, something is broken.”.

    Hill said in the statement that the bill also provides "clear legislative guidance for retailers, financial institutions, and consumers," referring to the measure's requirements that cash transactions not settled with exact change will be rounded to the nearest nickel.

    Recent findings suggest that the U.S. Mint stopped producing pennies a year ago under an executive order. Pennies already in circulation will still be legal tender, and the Mint may still problem special collectors editions. The legislation, named the Common Cents Act, also sets composition specifications for nickels.

    Like a well-traveled coin, the bill itself took a winding road to the White House. The House originally passed a similar bill in July and the Senate passed its version by unanimous consent on Aug. 7.

    But the Senate added a section that would require the Treasury secretary to notify Congress before discontinuing other coins. That sent the bill back to the House with a Senate number.

    Industry observers note that as the sponsor of the original measure, McClain insisted that the legislation have a House bill number. So, she reintroduced the revised Senate version, and the House voted on it on Sept. 14. The Senate passed it once again by unanimous consent on Sept. 28, sending it to the president's desk.

    Senate Banking Chairman Tim Scott, R-S.C., said the bill “modernizes our currency system and most importantly gives families and businesses clear rules for everyday cash transactions.”.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms defeated Republican billionaire Rick Jackson in Georgia‘s gubernatorial election Tuesday, becoming the first Black woman elected governor in American history and ending more than two decades of Republican control of the state’s highest office.

    Recent findings suggest that the contest pitted two sharply different candidates to succeed term-limited Republican Gov. Brian Kemp, whose departure opened the governor’s office for the first time in eight years.

    Bottoms, a former Atlanta mayor and adviser to President Joe Biden, campaigned on expanding access to health care, improving public education and addressing the rising cost of living. Jackson, a billionaire health care executive and political newcomer, emphasized cutting taxes, reducing government spending and bringing his private-sector experience to state government.

    We need your help to stay independent.

    Jackson invested more than $200 million of his own money into the campaign, making his bid one of the most expensive self-funded gubernatorial campaigns in American history.

    The election also ended Republicans’ decades-long control of Georgia’s governorship. The last Democrat elected governor was Roy Barnes in 1998. Barnes lost his reelection bid to Republican Sonny Perdue in 2002, and Republicans have held the office since Perdue took office in January 2003.

    Georgia’s changing political landscape added another dimension to the contest. Once a reliably Republican state in presidential elections, Georgia narrowly backed Democrat Joe Biden in 2020 before returning to President Donald Trump in 2024. Democrats also captured both U.S. Senate seats in 2021, with Raphael Warnock subsequently winning a full term in 2022.

    On Tuesday, Georgia voters also reelected Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff, demonstrating the state’s continued willingness to support Democrats in statewide contests.

    Bottoms is the first Black governor elected in Georgia, the first woman to hold the state’s highest office and the first Black woman elected governor anywhere in the United States. She is also the first Democrat to win Georgia’s governorship in 28 years, breaking a Republican winning streak dating back to 2002.

    James Talarico, the charismatic Texas state representative who campaigned by talking extensively about his Christian faith, has defeated state Attorney General Ken Paxton, who was Donald Trump’s hand-picked choice, in Tuesday’s most high-profile U.S. Senate race. Late on Tuesday evening, Talarico led by more than a million votes, and the Associated Press called the race just before 11 p.m. Eastern time.

    Recent findings suggest that this marks the first time a Democrat has won a statewide race in Texas since 1994, and another such result, perhaps even more surprising, followed almost immediately. Democrat Gina Hinojosa has won the Texas governor’s race, according to the AP, beating Republican incumbent Gov. Greg Abbott by more than 700,000 votes.

    Recent findings suggest that the substantial blue wave of 2026 has featured numerous surprising results, including the upset victory by Democrat Annie Andrews over Republican Sen. Darline Graham in South Carolina’s Senate race. But these dramatic and unexpected Democratic wins in Texas stand out. The Senate campaign between Talarico and Paxton became one of the most expensive state-level races in American history, and according to CNN analyst David Axelrod, Hinojosa was outspent 10 to one by Abbott. Talarico’s campaign also became a major target for Democratic donors and an opportunity to vent their frustration and anger with Trump’s second presidential term.

    Recent findings suggest that A combined $573 million were spent by Talarico and Paxton, as well as their defeated primary opponents, over the course of this campaign. Much of that spending was the result of Elon Musk, the world’s richest man. The CEO of SpaceX and Tesla pumped an estimated $474 million into this race, virtually all of it to support Paxton, setting a new record for a single donor in a political campaign. Most of that money was funneled through went to Musk’s personal super PAC, but around $168 million went to the Senate Leadership Fund. Another $10 million went to the pro-Paxton Lone Star Liberty PAC, which spammed voters with AI-generated robocalls attacking Talarico. Meanwhile, Talarico’s campaign and Democratic PACs raised about $133 million.

    Sources indicate that although Talarico, like other Democrats, focused on affordability and fighting corruption, he also sought to challenge the dominant view that only Republicans can be devout Christians. His campaign attracted various right-wing conspiracy theories, including claims that he was an emasculated “secret vegan” who suffered from mental illness. Democrats worried that this viral misinformation might overshadow numerous allegations about Paxton, including a Wall Street Journal report that he partied in Dubai with two fugitives from U.S. justice and a woman who wasn’t his wife.

    Although Talarico has led in recent public polls, the size of his victory was unexpected. At this writing, it appears almost certain that Democrats will win the Senate, having already flipped seats in both South Carolina and North Carolina, where former Gov. Roy Cooper easily won the open seat held by outgoing Republican Sen. Thom Tillis. Democrats also lead the Senate races in Iowa, Maine and Ohio, although those races remain undecided.

    • Klavan is the associate editor of the Claremont Review of Books and a professor of classical literature at the University of Austin.

    In a recent development, gratitude is like stretching, or deep breathing, or drinking water. It’s one of those miraculous things you can do for free, any time, with barely any effort, and it’s 100 percent certain to make you feel better — but somehow practicing it always feels like an exasperating chore. That’s how I experience it, anyway. There comes a moment at nearly all Thanksgiving tables when someone says, Now let’s all go around and say one thing we’re thankful for. And when this unimpeachably virtuous ritual is unveiled, my first thought is always, Oh God, when will it be over?

    But then of course — like drinking water, or breathing deeply — giving thanks is also something you’re always glad you did. Lo and behold, there really are people and things you love in this world, and to make a point of looking on them with appreciation is to see them lit up again in the living color of your own happiness. You might start out by dragging your feet; you are guaranteed to end up flush with joy. Maybe that’s part of the point: It changes you inside.

    In a recent development, spencer A. Klavan is the associate editor of the Claremont Review of Books and a professor of classical literature at the University of Austin. His latest book, A Way With Words: Why Language Makes Humans Irreplaceable, is available for preorder now.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that the signs were there from the outset. About 30 minutes after the polls in Kentucky’s 6th Congressional District closed at 6 p.m., the first numbers from rural counties began trickling in. It was no surprise that they favored Republican Ralph Alvarado over Democrat Zach Dembo. The district was reliably Democratic until 2012, when Andy Barr, a Republican who is now running to replace Mitch McConnell in the Senate, eked out a win. Since then, the GOP has gerrymandered the district to all but ensure it stayed in the fold.

    The real story, though, could be found in the margins. Alvarado was underperforming Barr’s 2024 results by around 20 percentage points — a staggering drop, indicating that a significant number of Republicans had either stayed home or decided to take a chance on Dembo. Off the Democratic map for the last 14 years, by 9:15 p.m., when it was reported that Alvarado had conceded, the district had become a microcosm of what was unfolding nationwide.

    The blue landslide, long predicted by pundits but mentioned with fingers crossed by Democrats, was becoming an avalanche.

    Further south in Georgia, an earlier-than-expected call for Jon Ossoff buoyed Democratic hopes, followed by a pickup in the North Carolina Senate race, which saw Gov. Roy Cooper projected to defeat former Republican National Committee Chairman Michael Whatley. Democrats even put up a fight in ruby-red Florida’s statewide races, with David Jolly, the nominee for governor, and Angie Nixon, the democratic socialist Senate candidate, running ahead of their opponents until the conservative Panhandle’s votes were counted.

    Recent findings suggest that then came South Carolina, where Darline Graham, who was foisted upon the state’s Republican Party by Donald Trump to succeed her brother, Sen. Lindsey Graham, after his death, went down to an historic defeat. The Palmetto State hasn’t seen a Democrat elected to the Senate since 1998.

    Amy Acton, Ohio’s Democratic nominee for governor, routed her opponent Vivek Ramaswamy after he released a widely condemned ad that weaponized a horrific part of her childhood. In Texas, James Talarico is projected for a stunning win over scandal-plagued Ken Paxton, and Gina Hinojosa ousted the incumbent Greg Abbott from the governor’s mansion.

    Other elections around the country — Senate races in Michigan, Kansas and Iowa; pivotal House contests and gubernatorial races — appear to be trending for Democrats.

    For a decade, the party has wondered when, or if, a reckoning would arrive for Trump and MAGA. That moment has arrived.

    Again and again, Republicans have followed the president over the cliff, no more so than during the past 22 months. In 2024, Trump expanded on the coalition that had carried him to success in 2016 by making inroads with Black men, Latinos and young voters. It was a success that, at least in part, led Republicans to launch a national gerrymandering scheme largely thwarted by Democrats, as well as an unfavorable economic climate of the president’s own making.

    But Trump also made the grievous error of attacking the very communities that helped return him to the White House. The combination of his assaults on voting rights and Black history, as well as the Supreme Court’s gutting of the Voting Rights Act, ensured that Black voters turned out overwhelmingly for Democrats. After more than a year of ICE raids, mass deportations and threats against naturalized citizens, Latinos have swung to the Democrats en masse, playing a decisive role in Talarico’s win. Trump’s attacks on civil rights, immigrants’ rights and the social safety net have cut across demographic groups, and have had a strong negative impact on young voters. Drunk on his own power, the president has spent the better part of two years splintering his own coalition — and giving Democrats an opening they were happy to exploit.

    The monumental defeat suffered by Republicans offers a sobering lesson for Democrats — to not forget what brought them to this night of victory.

    The message voters are sending is loud and clear: They want fighters, leaders who are willing to throw out conventional wisdom and do battle for working-class interests. That’s what Ossoff sensed last fall, when he was considered to be the nation’s most endangered Democrat. Instead of playing it safe, he staked his candidacy on affordability problems, particularly subsidies for the Affordable Care Act. In the midst of the longest government shutdown on record, Ossoff held firm: He would not vote to reopen the federal government unless the tax credits were restored.

    We need your help to stay independent.

    Other Democratic candidates got the message. Dr. Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan proved steadfast in linking the billions in federal funding that continue to subsidize Israel’s ongoing assault on Gaza to skyrocketing consumer prices on the homefront. Another physician, Dr. Annie Andrews, who defeated Graham, unabashedly campaigned on creating a healthcare public option and gun control measures in South Carolina — and won.

    Right now, Democrats are feeling the wind at their backs. But after the excitement fades from tonight’s successes, they will realize they are now facing an even bigger challenge: To stay true to the mandate they have been given by voters, grudgingly in some cases, and to not, as they have done so often in the past, slip on the proverbial banana peel that is always waiting for them around the corner.

    Throughout his campaign for the Senate, Paxton was fond of saying, “If we lose Texas, we lose America.” Tonight, Democrats put Texas solidly in their column — and America is still standing.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Virginia Foxx, R-N.C., presides over a House Rules Committee hearing in the Capitol on July 20.
    • After more than two decades in office and weeks of ballot counting, North Carolina Republican Virginia Foxx, chair of the powerful House Rules Committee, has conceded defeat in her reelection bid.
    • Retired journalist Chuck Hubbard bested Foxx in a nail-biter of a race — he was up by about 0.1 percentage point, or 330 votes out of nearly 300,000 ballots cast when the Associated Press called the race on Sunday.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Rep. Virginia Foxx, R-N.C., presides over a House Rules Committee hearing in the Capitol on July 20. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call).

    After more than two decades in office and weeks of ballot counting, North Carolina Republican Virginia Foxx, chair of the powerful House Rules Committee, has conceded defeat in her reelection bid.

    Retired journalist Chuck Hubbard bested Foxx in a nail-biter of a race — he was up by about 0.1 percentage point, or 330 votes out of nearly 300,000 ballots cast when the Associated Press called the race on Sunday.

    Foxx lost in a rematch against Hubbard, whom she beat by almost 20 points in their 2024 race.

    “Earlier today I spoke with Congresswoman Virginia Foxx who graciously conceded following the results of the recount process,” Hubbard wrote in a Facebook post Sunday. “Let me be the first to thank Congresswoman Foxx for her decades of service and countless sacrifices.”.

    Foxx was swept from office as part of a midterm surge that will put Democrats in charge of the House with the largest majority for either party since 1993 at 258 seats and counting; two other races where the Democrat is currently leading have yet to be called.

    A 260-seat majority would be the largest since 1989, according to the House historian's office.

    Until recently, Foxx's district was solidly Republican and had not elected a Democrat since 1992.

    It took nearly three weeks for the race to be called as provisional and mail-in ballots were added to the total. Three days after the election, as the final votes were tallied, Foxx requested the presence of nonpartisan election observers to monitor the counting process.

    “Election integrity is not a mere suggestion — it is the keystone of free and fair elections that have always guided the course of our nation throughout history,” she wrote in a Facebook post at the time. “The counting process for the 5th District election has not halted. The count is ongoing in accordance with North Carolina state law.”.

    On November 16, with the race still officially uncalled, Foxx requested a full recount; however the recount confirmed that Hubbard had won.

    “After a hard-fought and thorough election process, the voters of the Fifth Congressional District exercised their constitutional rights and made their voices heard,” Foxx remarked in a statement Sunday. “While I am saddened that I did not emerge victorious in this election, I continue to have great faith in our nation, our state and the people of North Carolina.”.

    As the recount was underway, Foxx filed for reelection in 2028, at which point she will be 85 years old.

    In her 11 terms in the House, Foxx built a reputation as a sharp-witted social conservative, unafraid to offer unfiltered views. She has also been a key ally of President Donald Trump and Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La.

    It has been revealed that foxx is the first Republican woman to serve as chair of the Rules Committee. The late Rep. Louise M. Slaughter, D-N.Y., who led the panel from 2007 to 2011, was the only other woman to hold the gavel.

    On the Rules panel, Foxx has been a workhorse for House Republicans’ agenda, often working late into the night and amending rules text on the fly in response to the high-stakes intraparty negotiations that have dominated Johnson’s speakership.

    According to recent reports, foxx’s acerbic wit is well matched on Rules by the panel’s ranking member Jim McGovern, D-Mass. The two often spar over policy and procedure alike.

    Foxx is the only woman chairing a House committee in the 119th Congress. According to the House historian's office, the last time the House had no female committee chairs was from 2005 to 2007, during the 109th Congress.

    Next in line in seniority to become the top Rules Republican is Minnesota Rep. Michelle Fischbach, who's expressed interest previously and got some practice sitting in for Foxx during committee hearings and managing rules on the floor when Foxx was away.

    Before her Rules role, Foxx was the top Republican on the House Education and Workforce panel from 2017 to the end of 2024.

    Industry observers note that she has been a vocal supporter of conservative efforts to abolish the Education Department and said she would do so “in a heartbeat." She points to the 10th Amendment, which states that the powers not delegated in the Constitution to the federal government are reserved for the states and individuals. Education, she asserts, is therefore not a federal responsibility.

    As a former school board member for 12 years, she notes that the government telling school boards how to work is “not the way this country should be operating.”.

    It has been revealed that A devout Catholic, Foxx is well known on Capitol Hill for her religious faith, attending weekly prayer meetings and Bible study sessions. She starts each day “with a prayer for wisdom and strength to do God’s will,” she told CQ Roll Call.

    In 2016, she published “God is in the House: Congressional Testimonies of Faith,” a book of essays on faith and legislative work by members of Congress.

    The Rules Committee has experienced relatively high turnover in recent years. Foxx’s predecessor, former-Rep. Michael Burgess, R-Texas, succeeded Chairman Tom Cole, R-Okla., in April 2024 after Cole departed to chair the Appropriations Committee. Cole himself only held the position for just over a year after taking over for McGovern, though he became the panel's top Republican in 2019.

    According to recent reports, she served in the state Senate from 1995 to 2004, and when Republican Richard M. Burr left his House seat to run for the Senate in 2004, Foxx entered the race to succeed him. She prevailed over seven other Republicans in the primary and went on to defeat her Democratic challenger in November. At 61, she was one of the oldest members of the freshman class of 2005.

    North Carolina’s 5th District encompasses much of northwestern North Carolina, including the Blue Ridge Mountains and the foothills of the Piedmont.

    • The astonishing results of the 2026 midterm elections do not just represent a rebuke or a political setback for Donald Trump.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, pretend I’m on the ballot, the president of the United States repeatedly told American voters over the last several weeks. Millions of voters did exactly that. Be careful what you wish for, my dude.

    The astonishing results of the 2026 midterm elections do not just represent a rebuke or a political setback for Donald Trump. Those neutral-sounding terms of art are not remotely adequate. This was a historic smackdown, a massive, crushing defeat on a scale suffered by no incumbent president in living memory. It represents this nation’s collective awakening — admittedly rather late in the game — to this individual’s uniquely poisonous effects on our public life and civil society.

    Many larger political questions will emerge from this epic defeat, which will see any and all surviving elected Republicans (not that there are many) scurrying for cover and trying to establish as much distance as possible from Trump. They will lose his number. They will profess that they were never convinced MAGA believers, or that they secretly disagreed with the ICE reign of terror, with the war in Iran, with the disastrous tariffs, with the ideological assault on liberal democracy.

    Is JD Vance still a plausible 2028 presidential contender, having hitched his wagon to this tyrant, who has now been thoroughly pantsed in public and exposed as a pathetic loser? Will Pete Hegseth get even one more opportunity for podcaster-style flexing before the defanged Pentagon press corps? Let’s give Marco Rubio an infinitesimal amount of credit for creeping quietly through the corridors of power and staying out of the headlines. Whether his neocon mouse act is enough to survive the Trumpocalypse moment remains to be seen.

    According to recent reports, in his inimitable style, Trump is already blaming others for this defeat. He has accused Texas Gov. Greg Abbott — who lost his seat to Democrat Gina Hinojosa in one of Tuesday night’s numerous shockers — of being a RINO sellout. As impossible as it is to talk about honor with these people, that is an act of dishonorable treachery, given how eagerly Abbott has crawled and begged and prostrated himself before the Trumpian throne.

    Recent findings suggest that then again, in an ass-backward way, Trump has a point. He didn’t do this all by himself; no one could have managed that. He loaded up the pipe with bigotry and xenophobia and fear and insane conspiracy theories, and adult Republican humans who used to believe in wrong-headed but somewhat sane political doctrines inhaled it all eagerly, persuading themselves that the resulting high would insulate them from the failure of their ideas. It only made the problem worse — all the problems, really — and they should have seen that coming.

    Industry observers note that the president corrupted and enslaved a historic American political party with a complicated but illustrious history, the party of Abraham Lincoln and Ulysses S. Grant and Dwight Eisenhower and Ronald Reagan. I’m not the biggest fan of that party either, but it has certainly had its moments, including the first woman to serve in both houses of Congress and the first Black man elected to the U.S. Senate. Trump insisted that it surrender everything to him — its principles, its history and its soul, if political parties have such a thing — and as in every fable about making a deal with the devil, now it has been destroyed.

    Sources indicate that we don’t know how this election would have turned out in the unimaginable alternate universe where Trump stayed out of it. But he didn’t. He forced Sen. John Cornyn out of the race in Texas, in favor of Ken Paxton. Look what happened. He picked Darline Graham to replace her late brother, Sen. Lindsey Graham, in South Carolina. Look what happened. He picked Mike Collins to run against Sen. Jon Ossoff in Georgia, and Michael Whatley to run against former Gov. Roy Cooper in North Carolina. Look what happened. He praised Ohio Sen. Jon Husted’s rear end and embraced gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy’s noxious campaign ad. Look what happened there, too.

    We need your help to stay independent.

    And that’s without considering the supposedly ingenious MAGA strategy of redistricting congressional seats in one state after another, with the objective of locking in a permanent Republican majority. How will that play out over the longer term? That’s impossible to say, but in 2026 it seems to have unleashed an extraordinary backlash. Forget all the hand-wringing about purple districts and swing districts; the congressional map is a nationwide wipeout. As I write this, the New York Times is predicting a Democratic majority in the House of Representatives of 256 seats. That may or may not hold up, but however this ends, it’s likely to be the biggest midterm swing in more than 30 years.

    In a recent development, are there still die-hard MAGA Republicans in deep-red exurbs or rural districts who will continue to profess fealty to Trump in the wake of this catastrophe, and perhaps even maintain that it’s all some kind of grand misunderstanding? Yeah, sure. Any cult movement has its true believers and willing sacrifices. Years after his resignation, the postmistress in the rural town where I spent summers as a kid never took down the portrait of Richard Nixon. Then she retired and moved away, someone else took the job and Nixon’s picture wound up out back, in the dumpster.

    That’s about where we are. Trump has always been poisonous. Republicans are finally learning that the hard way.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sen. Susan Collins, the five-term Republican from Maine, called her opponent Troy Jackson, a former logger and state senate president, to concede Tuesday night. The Associated Press called the election just after midnight, with Jackson leading by about six percentage points.

    In a recent development, despite nearly 30 years in the Senate, Collins has been seen as one of the most vulnerable Republican incumbents, a smaller pebble in the blue avalanche that wiped out MAGA candidates in the midterm elections. She was the lone Senate Republican to represent a state that former Democratic Vice President Kamala Harris carried in the 2024 election. She lost despite her efforts to distance herself from President Donald Trump. Her campaign claims she has never voted for the president and reportedly refused his help with her run.

    Recent findings suggest that that hasn’t stopped her from often playing a key role in Trump’s agenda, casting a critical vote in Brett Kavanaugh’s confirmation to the Supreme Court. Kavanaugh would later join the majority opinion in Dobbs v. Jackson Women’s Health Organization, which overturned Roe v. Wade and ended the constitutional right to an abortion. Indeed, Collins’ position on reproductive rights seems to have played a key role in her defeat. Collins received support from Trump despite her efforts, according to reporting from ProPublica earlier this year, which revealed how an FBI anti-corruption squad was investigating Collins before Trump killed the case.

    As for Jackson, he first ran for office in 2000 as a Republican for the Maine House of Representatives, but lost. He ran again as an independent two years later and won, becoming the first non-Democrat to represent the area since the late ‘70s.

    Before delegates at a state convention chose Jackson in July, Collins was originally running against oyster farmer Graham Platner, who won the Democratic primary with support from progressive leaders. But controversies surrounding Platner continued to pile up, and he finally withdrew from the race on July 10 following sexual assault allegations.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, photo Credit: Leonardo Hotel, Brighton, UK © José by Luiz Bernardes Ribeiro. Wikimedia Commons.

    Sources indicate that leonardo's UK hotels are making money from guests, but not enough to cover the rent. With costs rising and more rooms coming onto the market, the lease-heavy model that let hotel groups expand fast in the UK is starting to look like a liability.

    Rising wages and payroll taxes are squeezing Leonardo Hotels' UK business, but the bigger problem is the rent on its hotels, according to accounts filed with Companies House, the UK company register.

    It has been revealed that on paper, the drop is steep. The hotel chain swung to a £55.6 million ($74 million) pre-tax loss in 2025 from a £50.1 million ($67 million) profit. But the 2024 profit included an £89.8 million ($119 million) one-off gain from revaluing its leases. Without it, 2024 would have shown a loss of about £40 million ($53 million), so the loss widened by about £16 million ($21 million) rather than appearing from nowhere.

    The filing shows revenue at Leonardo Hotel Management (UK) Ltd was steady, rising 1.3% to £350.1 million ($466 million), with no upcoming hotels opened. Gross profit fell 12% to £37.6 million ($50 million), and the gross margin slipped to 10.7% from 12.4%. Staff costs rose 6% to £102.5 million ($136 million), and employer social security costs rose 34%.

    #225922. Industry News: Fascism mixed into cringey online content is easy to mock – but no less dangerous

    📅 04 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1082 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Salon ↗ Open Full Page

    Industry News: Fascism mixed into cringey online content is easy to mock – but no less dangerous

    📅 04 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1082 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Salon

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • This article was originally published on The Conversation.
    • Industry observers note that against the backdrop of an unpopular war in Iran, Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth announced on July 15, 2026, that the Pentagon would begin testing male service members 30 and older for low testosterone.
    • The combination of aggressive masculinity and militarism with the implications of testing for something like “spontaneous morning erections” as necessary for war fighting is emblematic of the administration’s tendency to combine fascist ideas and symbols with outright embarrassing messaging, or what I call “cringe fascism.”.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    This article was originally published on The Conversation.

    Industry observers note that against the backdrop of an unpopular war in Iran, Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth announced on July 15, 2026, that the Pentagon would begin testing male service members 30 and older for low testosterone. That, the department later stated, would include assessing symptoms of low testosterone such as “reduced libido, loss of spontaneous morning erections, erectile dysfunction, diminished energy and physical performance, impaired concentration, reduced muscle mass, and depressed mood.”.

    The combination of aggressive masculinity and militarism with the implications of testing for something like “spontaneous morning erections” as necessary for war fighting is emblematic of the administration’s tendency to combine fascist ideas and symbols with outright embarrassing messaging, or what I call “cringe fascism.”.

    For some time there’s been a contentious debate among writers, historians and public intellectuals over whether Donald Trump’s presidency could be considered “fascist.” Some have argued that such claims are hyperbolic or inaccurate, while others say it is a useful and accurate ideological label.

    Either way, it would be difficult to deny that the Trump administration frequently draws from the well of fascist imagery and symbolism in its official messaging.

    And that’s where the concept of cringe fascism fits in. In online parlance,“cringe” is a kind of embarrassment by proxy when someone posts something that should be embarrassing but which doesn’t seem to be to them.

    For their part, members of the Trump administration have relied on language and symbolism that borrows from the fascist or authoritarian playbook while doing so in a way that commenters often mock as patently ridiculous or embarrassing – or cringe.

    But the purported silliness of these ideas, as with Hegseth’s testosterone policy, hides a much more serious – and to some critics, fascist – reality. That, moreover, is why the deployment of cringe can be effective: It can generate enthusiasm among conservative voters by trolling the left while reducing deadly serious policy debates to the level of online memes.

    It has been revealed that as Americans prepare for the midterms and a surely contentious presidential election in 2028, such considerations of Trump’s authoritarian tendencies are being put to the test. That’s especially true as he consistently threatens the integrity of elections, deploys immigration and other federal law enforcement officers on American streets in a highly contested manner, and attempts to target the press and restrict its access.

    As a scholar of conspiracy theories, I have been amazed at some of the more blatant efforts to repurpose fascist imagery by members of Trump’s inner circle.

    Consider, for example, the use of ethnonationalist and fascist imagery of “blood and soil” in sloganeering by the Department of Homeland Security, or encouraging U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement recruits to “Defend the Homeland.”.

    And then there are the attacks on the press as the “enemy of the people,” echoing past totalitarian leaders, followed by Trump’s banning of mainstream media from the White House and the launch of Trump TV as the state channel. Critics view such moves to attack and restrict the press as hallmarks of fascist methods.

    Borrowing more obviously from fascist tropes was Trump posting on social media a mock-up of a potential new Space Force uniform. The post claimed to draw inspiration from Paul Verhoeven’s “Starship Troopers,” in which the soldiers are deliberately modeled on the fascist aesthetic and ideology of the Nazis.

    Alongside the authoritarian and fascist tropes, the Trump administration cannot seem to avoid “cringe.”.

    Recent examples include the White House tweeting images of Trump as a videogame character on a select screen with sleeveless blue suit and bulging muscles, or sharing an AI parody of the upcoming Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time game with an awkward video of a pixelated Trump running around the White House lawn. Or consider the post depicting Trump as Green Lantern, using his magic ring to raise a spectral border wall, launch a military attack and fix American industry.

    It has been revealed that on the one hand, the Trump administration seems determined to keep his party in power and enact a transformative MAGA policy agenda. On the other hand, Trump seems incapable of avoiding cringey riffs such as his digressions on men’s bodies in ways that seem strikingly at odds with his tough-guy persona. To see the commander in chief waxing poetic about Ohio Sen. Jon Husted’s rear feels deeply surreal.

    Trump’s seemingly incongruous comments occur at the same time that the secretary of defense is advocating hypermasculinity in the military through testosterone testing, reflecting a heady mix of masculinity and military supremacy that has long been a hallmark of fascism. Such a policy is also at odds with how the professional military has presented itself under previous administrations.

    The mixture of fascist aesthetics with cringe posting underscores the internal contradictions of the Trump administration.

    It is difficult to see critics’ view of Trump’s second term as “fascist” when observers get such awkward online displays of silliness. And when official communications from the White House and federal agencies are equal parts tough talk, trolling and cringe, the underlying policies can get lost in the shuffle.

    Is is hard to know whether this flood of cringe is always intentional, but it is certainly confusing and hilarious to both Trump’s supporters and his opponents. But that belies what many critics have decried as authoritarian actions by this administration, and these comparisons with fascism continue to animate public discourse.

    Masked ICE agents continue to operate with some legal protections from the White House in their sometimes-deadly efforts to pursue and round up people it broadly accuses of being in the country illegally.

    Likewise, the DHS announced that ICE agents could be deployed to polling locations, while the agency has reportedly attempted to get access to voter information to investigate alleged voter fraud through increased surveillance.

    The deployment of cringe might seems like a ridiculous, even unconscious, exercise by an administration that – as with the five-day tenure of former press secretary Katie Zacharia highlights – regularly exposes itself to derision and satire. Yet that’s why the use of such a concept can be so strategically effective: It turns potentially deadly serious policy consequences and ideological choices into a game of memes and online gamesmanship.

    Sources indicate that matthew N. Hannah, Associate Professor of Rhetoric, Politics and Culture, University of Wisconsin-Madison.

    #225921. Breaking: The petty joy of a blue election night

    📅 04 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1473 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Salon ↗ Open Full Page

    Breaking: The petty joy of a blue election night

    📅 04 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1473 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Salon

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that ten years ago, watching the dawning of the Trump era on Fox News felt appropriate somehow.
    • Still, once the phrase “President-elect Donald Trump” became as inevitable as Thanos, and Fox’s anchors giggled like ascendant supervillains, staring into that snarling maw seemed like the responsible thing to do.
    • Training my focus on CNN and MS NOW in time to catch 2026’s predicted blue wave promised to be just as illuminating.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that ten years ago, watching the dawning of the Trump era on Fox News felt appropriate somehow. Notice that I didn’t say it felt right; after all, we were sinking into an anti-Enlightenment Age propped up by Rupert Murdoch’s propaganda machine. Nothing about any of that felt right.

    Still, once the phrase “President-elect Donald Trump” became as inevitable as Thanos, and Fox’s anchors giggled like ascendant supervillains, staring into that snarling maw seemed like the responsible thing to do.

    Training my focus on CNN and MS NOW in time to catch 2026’s predicted blue wave promised to be just as illuminating. Back in 2016, while everyone else on CNN struggled to make sense of what was happening, commentator Van Jones somberly characterized the results as “whitelash against a changing country.”.

    It has been revealed that shortly after Trump was inaugurated, he turned against CNN full force, branding it and every other outlet denying favorable coverage as fake news. Trump’s 2024 victory further endangered any media outlets outside of the right-wing echo chamber, as he hit news organizations with obscenely ridiculous legal complaints to force them to bend the knee.

    In a recent development, so we’ll pardon Jones for his deliciously petty reaction to what Jake Tapper, the emcee of CNN’s “Election Night in America” telecast, awkwardly described as a “blue-nami.” By the time the Democrats took control of the House and Senate, the previously funereal Anderson Cooper was gleefully eager to hear what Jones had to say. And his colleague did not disappoint, delivering what may have been the night’s most satisfying monologue.

    Sources indicate that “If you join a cult, at some point the cult leader takes you to Jonestown and tries to get you to drink the Kool-Aid,” he observed as chastened GOP pundit Scott Jennings sat inches away. “This is Jonestown for the Republican Party. They drank the Kool-Aid, and they have candidates that are dropping like flies across the country because they did not stand up to this guy when he was doing things that were wrong . . .

    Sources indicate that “You join a cult, at some point, you go to Jonestown,” Jones repeated in closing. “That’s where you are tonight, Republicans.” Then he pretended to pass a cup to his Trumpian counterpart.

    Sources indicate that election night news coverage is a stressful affair in the best of times. In 2026, CNN and MS NOW, the channel formerly known as MSNBC, entered the fray as battered underdogs. MS NOW is now owned by Versant, a group of cable channels spun off from NBCUniversal. CNN, part of Warner Bros. Discovery, will soon be owned by Skydance and its Trump-allied owner David Ellison.

    Neither newsroom can claim relief over what’s on the horizon, which is why Cooper led CNN’s coverage with the air of an undertaker greeting democracy’s mourners. America’s major news outlets have been taking it on the chin with the rest of us — including Cooper, a former “60 Minutes” correspondent who fled Bari Weiss’ CBS takeover only for Ellison to come for his cable news shire anyway. Blue wave or not, CNN’s future is uncertain.

    So although MS NOW may be scrappier and looser these days, at least its reporters and pundits aren’t working through an institutional existential crisis. That fatigue showed up in how CNN’s Magic Wall wrangler, John King, lived cautiously from moment to moment, allowing only a mild display of wonder as he shifted between the largely scarlet 2024 map and the much bluer 2026 version.

    Recent findings suggest that “What’s happening right now?” King wondered. “What’s the right word? Is it a rebuke? Is it repudiation? Is it shellacking? Is it a spanking? I mean, at the moment, this is the collapse of the president’s party on live television as you watch it play out.”.

    And for the first time in a decade of watching election nights, it was a joy to experience — like learning how to hope again.

    Peddling optimism isn’t the job of any journalistic organization, of course. But knowing what CNN’s newsroom is contending with regardless of this election outcome makes their composure especially admirable. The CNN team had a 10-ton weight pressing down on them and still managed to convey the sense of celebration presumably gripping most of its viewers.

    It has been revealed that most people tune out election night noise regardless of whether the vote goes in their favor, perhaps gleaning what they can from the flashy graphics and chyrons. This gave MS NOW’s Ali Velshi an advantage at the network’s Massive Board now that his former co-worker Steve Kornacki has moved over to NBC. Both have earned fandoms by injecting levity into managing each election’s data flood. On Tuesday night, Kornacki inspired a meme simply by being captured on his new network’s Kornacki Cam as he walked down a hall.

    We need your help to stay independent.

    But Velshi kept his version of his predecessor’s two-step going, buzzing around on MS NOW’s Major Board with a hummingbird’s energy. “Annie Andrews is outperforming, and Darlene Graham is underperforming,” he rapidly blurted, breaking down the Democratic challenger’s road to her unexpected win in South Carolina over the late Republican Sen. Lindsey Graham’s sister, before turning to the camera with a delightfully bemused look to say, “This is a totally weird conversation that we are having. Right?” It’s true. After years of polls overstating the Democrats’ chances, it did feel strange to have underestimated how much they’d win.

    Sources indicate that still, Rachel Maddow‘s ebullience from the moment MS NOW’s coverage began was tough to beat. Before a single result came in, she cheerfully offered, “So far, the one thing we can definitively say is that Americans like our democracy, and they are enjoying using it in record numbers in this cycle.”.

    It has been revealed that once Democrats claimed majorities in the House and Senate a few hours later, she let loose. In calling the race for Pennsylvania’s 8th congressional district for Democratic Scranton Mayor Paige Cognetti, Maddow couldn’t resist calling her Republican opponent, Rob Bresnahan, a “sometime ghost hunter” as her colleagues snickered in the background.

    Industry observers note that this is an understandable reaction to voters’ referendum on the president’s unpopular and economically detrimental policies. Americans, regardless of partisan stance, are struggling to afford the basics. But as Chris Hayes pointed to the shock of so many Democratic upsets, he noted that high prices aren’t the only thing forcing this drastic change. “The rot that is coming from the top of the country is very, very, very clearly on voters’ minds,” he mentioned.

    So if Jones wants to indulge in a little grave dancing, so be it.

    Industry observers note that it was even better to see other correspondents take stock of all the history made on Tuesday night. Upcoming Hampshire voters chose a Democrat, Chris Pappas, to join the U.S. Senate, making him the first out gay man elected to the chamber.

    Voters turned Texas blue and elected four Black governors – including former Atlanta mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms, who became the first woman and the first Black person to be elected governor in Georgia, and the first female Black governor in our country’s history.

    According to recent reports, once that state’s contest for governor was called for Bottoms, MS NOW’s team tapped Symone Sanders-Townsend to contextualize what that meant for voters and Black women. Sanders-Townsend reminded us that when Trump calls Georgia to gripe, it will be Bottoms on the other end of the line. She’ll also be the one to ensure the 2028 election is certified for the rightful winner.

    But when Sanders-Townsend’s colleagues asked her to share how Bottoms’ victory made her feel, her reaction hit home. “After the 2024 presidential election, for myself and Black women all over this country, it felt like a repudiation of us,” she mentioned, holding back tears. “…There were Black women, myself included, that felt like, ‘Well, maybe America just does not want us.'”.

    So to Sanders-Townsend, and all the other Black women disappointed by their fellow citizens in 2024, Bottoms’ victory mentioned, “Georgia wanted Keisha.”.

    Recent findings suggest that that moment didn’t diminish Jones’ take on what this election night meant to him. “This is like Christmas and a birthday and an Easter bunny and Halloween!” he remarked. “This is the repudiation of Trumpism that people have been hoping for, seeing American democracy stand up.”.

    It has been revealed that but by allowing herself to cry on camera, Sanders-Townsend broadcast a different kind of signal. She let us know that on this night, and for the first time in a long time, it was OK to ease into some sense of relief. And that’s better than the fleeting pleasure of retaliatory pettiness, well-earned though it may be.

    #225920. Tech Report: Hail Mary effort on college sports bill could boost power conferences

    📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1115 w)
    📖 Baca
    General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Rollcall ↗ Open Full Page

    Tech Report: Hail Mary effort on college sports bill could boost power conferences

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1115 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Ted Cruz, R-Texas, pictured talking with reporters Nov.
    • President Donald Trump and GOP leaders are mounting a late push for a sweeping college sports bill that has stalled in the House, with new revisions that appear designed to appeal to several large state delegations by making it easier for high-profile schools to jump to the most lucrative conferences.
    • In a recent development, the Senate’s version of the bill known as the Protect College Sports Act, which passed in September, would cap collegiate athletic conference sizes at 20 schools.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sen. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, pictured talking with reporters Nov. 17, has expressed confidence the Protect College Sports Act can clear Congress before the end of session. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

    President Donald Trump and GOP leaders are mounting a late push for a sweeping college sports bill that has stalled in the House, with new revisions that appear designed to appeal to several large state delegations by making it easier for high-profile schools to jump to the most lucrative conferences.

    In a recent development, the Senate’s version of the bill known as the Protect College Sports Act, which passed in September, would cap collegiate athletic conference sizes at 20 schools. But a revised House version released Friday evening would raise that conference roster cap to 22 institutions after several Atlantic Coast Conference schools went public with their collective desire for the change.

    The change could clear the way for another round of conference realignment, including the Southeastern Conference and Major Ten expanding again after both did so in 2024.

    According to recent reports, college sports insiders have reported for some time that SEC and Big Ten officials have been eying a number of ACC schools to join their ranks — a list that includes the University of Florida, Florida State, the University of North Carolina and South Carolina’s Clemson University. All four recently sent letters to House lawmakers requesting the conference size change, according to the Charlotte Business Journal.

    The SEC and Substantial Ten presently have 16 members for revenue-generating sports.

    To reach the revised House bill’s 22-team ceiling, there has been speculation about other ACC schools also jumping ship, including North Carolina State University, Duke University, Wake Forest University, the University of Virginia and Virginia Tech. Because the bill, even with changes made by House Republican leaders, faces an uphill battle in the chamber, the 22-team cap change could assist its proponents.

    That’s because of factions that have opposed college sports legislation. The nearly 60-member Congressional Black Caucus still opposes the measure over GOP efforts to terminate majority-minority House districts and an assessment it would not do enough to help historically Black colleges and universities. And some House conservatives have raised concerns that it might hurt colleges and conferences by allowing student athletes to do things like unionize.

    In a recent development, the Sunshine, Tar Heel and Old Dominion states have 53 total House seats, making the conference cap change a potentially tactical weapon, should the amended measure hit the House floor. The House Rules Committee, in a Friday evening announcement, signaled the revised bill could get floor votes next week, after the chamber returns from a Thanksgiving recess.

    Recent findings suggest that the same Rules announcement informed members they have until midday Wednesday to submit further amendments ahead of a likely committee session on the legislation next week. If the panel signs off on a rule for the revised measure and some amendments, the next stop would be the chamber floor.

    The bill got a substantial boost from Trump during a Friday press conference at the White House.

    “If we don't pass that bill, you're not only going to not have sports, but you're going to have every college in the country go bankrupt,” Trump noted.

    According to recent reports, A White House official signaled the president was not concerned about the proposed House changes. “The president wants NIL reform to get done and for Congress to send him a bill that can reach his desk rapidly,” the official said in an email.

    House Republicans did not make any changes to the Senate-passed measure’s provisions meant to help safeguard women’s sports.

    In a recent development, house GOP leaders have proposed dropping the Senate’s threshold for when any conference merger would trigger antitrust violations. The House is proposing a breach of those laws if a conference that makes $600 million attempts to merge with or acquire another conference, down from the Senate’s $700 million level.

    Along with the proposed conference size and antitrust changes, the chamber’s revised bill would make a handful of targeted changes, including upcoming rules for how colleges and universities count name, image and likeness (NIL) agreements against a revenue-share cap.

    Industry observers note that it also proposes changing schools’ disclosure requirements for student athletic fees and a lower threshold for certain conference mergers. And it proposes changes to what would be a fresh congressional commission to oversee the college athletics landscape.

    The House has proposed altering the Senate-passed bill’s NIL accounting language with a provision stating that any institution with annual average media rights revenue of at least $50 million could no longer use student fees to help finance their sports teams. The change appears geared toward lawmakers hailing from districts with HBCUs, smaller “Group of Six” FBS conference members and schools that compete in Football Championship Subdivision.

    The revised measure would stipulate that all NIL agreements between a student athlete and an institution, an institution employee or volunteer, a conference, a conference employee or an associated entity would count against that institution’s revenue-share cap and player-retention funds.

    In another proposed alteration, institutions of higher learning would be required to report certain student athlete compensation data “individually by program and in the aggregate.” The Senate-approved bill would have required reporting “for personnel of each intercollegiate sports program.”.

    Instead of allowing “a person” to bring a civil action, as would the Senate-approved language, the rewritten House provision would grant such rights only to a “current or former student athlete.”.

    The House version also would make several changes to the Senate’s proposed 24-member Congressional Commission on the Future of College Athletics by shaking up which congressional committees would get to select its members. The changes also include adding representation from midsized conferences and would give one seat to “a student athlete or former student athlete.”.

    In a brief interview last week, Senate Commerce Committee Chair Ted Cruz noted he was confident the House would pass the bill “the week after Thanksgiving.”.

    “There’s plenty of time,” the Texas Republican, a co-author of the Senate bill, said when asked if the lame-duck session’s remaining planned three weeks would allow the House to finish its work on the measure and then give the Senate time to vote on an amended version. The House is slated to leave for a holiday season recess on Dec. 17; the Senate is scheduled to exit the next day.

    “I believe the House is going to take it up and pass the bill,” Cruz said, adding that he had talked to Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., about his plans. “I believe we will see in the House what we saw in the Senate: an overwhelming bipartisan vote.”.

    • On “Thanksgiving 1863 and the Changing Art Vibe in That Pivotal Year”.

    Sources indicate that this year, for my Thanksgiving story, I’m writing something experimental. I’ll treat the art of our country in 1863. That’s the year President Lincoln issued his proclamation designating the last Thursday in November as a national day of “Thanksgiving and Praise to our beneficent Father, who dwelleth in the Heavens.”.

    I’m an art historian and don’t believe that artists quaff a surfeit of blood-orange champagne mules, sing “Auld Lang Syne,” do a countdown if they’re sober enough to count backward, and decide — snap — to change styles or themes. That year — 1863 — was different, though, and that Thanksgiving was different. Eastman Johnson (1824–1906) was our savviest painter, tuned to the moment and its nuances.

    Brian T. Allen is National Review’s art critic.

    • The candidates were competing to replace retiring Democratic Sen.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that democrat Abdul El-Sayed is projected to defeat Republican Mike Rogers for Michigan‘s open U.S. Senate seat, a closely watched race that capped off a massive night for progressives.

    According to recent reports, the Associated Press called the race shortly after 2 a.m. Wednesday morning with El-Sayed leading by about seven points.

    The candidates were competing to replace retiring Democratic Sen. Gary Peters, whose departure created one of the most consequential open-seat contests of the midterm elections. El-Sayed, a former Detroit health director, campaigned on expanding access to health care and lowering costs, while Rogers, a former congressman and House Intelligence Committee chairman, emphasized manufacturing jobs, tax cuts and his alignment with President Donald Trump.

    Sources indicate that the race took an unexpected turn just two days before Election Day when Democratic Rep. Haley Stevens, who narrowly lost the party’s August primary to El-Sayed, endorsed Rogers during an appearance at a Detroit church.

    In a recent development, the endorsement stunned Michigan Democrats, prompting condemnation from party leaders and resignations among Stevens’ staff. Stevens cited disagreements with El-Sayed over Israel and his campaign’s direction, while Democrats accused her of undermining their nominee in a critical Senate contest.

    It has been revealed that el-Sayed sought to move past the controversy, urging supporters to focus on voting. His campaign reported raising $2.4 million on Sunday, while Michigan Democratic officials noted the endorsement had prompted an increase in volunteers. Rogers, meanwhile, highlighted Stevens’ support in the campaign’s final days.

    More than 2.3 million Michigan voters had already cast ballots by Monday, according to The Associated Press, raising questions about how much the late-breaking controversy could influence the outcome.

    Tech Report: Democrats better hope they don’t have another Manchin in their midst

    📅 04 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1192 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Salon

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that ever since the Covid-19 pandemic, America has been in a funk.
    • We finally woke up and shook it off.
    • According to recent reports, the historic landslide Democratic victory in Tuesday’s midterms elections is far more thorough than even the most positive polls had indicated.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that ever since the Covid-19 pandemic, America has been in a funk. The whole country has seemed to be in a sour mood, unhappy with everything, feeling as if the world has gone off its axis and life is out of balance. The trauma of that experience was probably far deeper and more injurious than we wanted to admit, so we just sort of sleepwalked as events cascaded around us, feeling emotionally distanced and impotent.

    We finally woke up and shook it off. For the first time in six years, the American people took back control of their own destiny and issued a stunning, overwhelming rebuke to the Republican Party, which had fallen back into power during that period of national somnolence and took a wrecking ball, figuratively and literally, to the country. America, it seems, decided to save itself.

    According to recent reports, the historic landslide Democratic victory in Tuesday’s midterms elections is far more thorough than even the most positive polls had indicated. Analysts assured us that while it looked likely the party would gain at least a House majority, the so-called real victory would be if Democrats reduced the margins in red states, which would serve as a warning to Republicans that they had gone too far. Nobody really expected that Democrats would actually win in places like South Carolina, Kansas, Iowa or perhaps even Mississippi, where, as I write this, Democrat Scott Colom has a 43-vote lead over GOP incumbent Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith.

    Political polarization was assumed to be set in stone; the GOP’s redistricting gambit and the Supreme Court’s gutting of the Voting Rights Act meant that Democrats could not expect to flip more than a handful of seats, and the party was facing one of the most inauspicious midterm Senate maps in recent memory. At this moment, they are expected to end up with 245 to 255 seats in the House and possibly 55 seats in the Senate, an unthinkable outcome as recently as yesterday morning.

    In a recent development, it will be a while before we see the final tally, but the results are so obviously decisive that even Donald Trump cannot fatuously claim that this election was stolen. All the threats against election workers and plans to contest the outcome are empty in the face of such a victory. It is finally, once and for all, clear that the country does not want the insanity and chaos that Trump has wrought.

    According to recent reports, according to voter polls — formerly known as exit polls — the top problem for voters was the cost of living, as expected. Reversing the tariffs and putting an end to the war with Iran would be the obvious ways to begin to alleviate some of the stress, followed by restoration of funding for healthcare and other vital safety net programs. Rolling back Trump’s tax cuts for the wealthy would go a long way as well. But the president Trump has already promised to be “Mr. Veto,” so the prospect for a latest era of bipartisan comity with the White House does not look good.

    It has been revealed that it’s always possible that congressional Republicans will feel chastised enough that they will work with Democrats to create veto-proof majorities on those issues, but I wouldn’t hold my breath. The best the Democrats can hope for is that Trump decides he needs to do something positive for his legacy besides building his ballroom and renaming the Atlantic Ocean, and he agrees to compromise on something. I wouldn’t hold my breath on that either. But that doesn’t mean Democrats shouldn’t pass the legislation — and make Trump and Republicans block it.

    Progress is hard to attain when, to maintain a majority, your coalition must include some who are opposed to it.

    It has been revealed that as great as it is that Democrats will decisively control both houses of Congress, that big tent brings with it some perennial problems that are likely to manifest themselves again. The red state-blue state divide represents a structural problem that has always been around, and it has been a specific problem for Democrats going back to at least the time of Franklin Roosevelt. Progress is hard to attain when, to maintain a majority, your coalition must include some who are opposed to it. During Roosevelt’s long presidency, the Democratic coalition included powerful southerners who controlled many congressional committees, and they would simply not pass anything that included civil rights or equitable federal programs. By the end of the 1930s, they had successfully joined with northern Republicans to block much of what remained of the Fresh Deal agenda.

    Eventually, as we know, most of that bloc migrated to the GOP, but until fairly recently it’s always been a somewhat fluid dynamic with a few conservative states in the heartland, the West, Southwest and even the South that would elect conservative Democrats. In the last Congress, we dealt with West Virginia’s Joe Manchin and Arizona’s Kyrsten Sinema in the Senate, and it was like pulling teeth to get legislation passed as they used their leverage to extract concessions and block progressive initiatives.

    Recent findings suggest that in the not too distant past, Sen. Zell Miller, D-Ga., cosponsored tax cuts, supported the Iraq War resolution and even delivered a keynote speech at the 2004 Republican National Convention. Centrist senators Ben Nelson of Nebraska and Joe Lieberman of Connecticut, along with the conservative Blue Dog Caucus in the House, successfully blocked progressive provisions of the Affordable Care Act. There were other so-called mavericks throughout the 1990s and 2000s who would join with the GOP or leverage their position to thwart liberal initiatives.

    We need your help to stay independent.

    Recent findings suggest that I only bring this up to remind people that with the addition of these red state legislators will come a whole set of problems. But given the alternative, they are good problems to have. While the pundits have already begun their ritual of handwringing over the possibility of progressives “overreading the mandate,” the reality is that everyone else understands that the most important priority for Democrats, as a now powerful force of opposition, is to put a check on Trump and begin the critically important process of oversight and accountability. One suspects that on this issue there will likely be unity among all the factions. MS NOW reports that their voter poll showed that 90% of voters said that government corruption was a crucial or major factor in their House vote. That also tracks with the findings of a recent Gallup poll. I would say that’s a pretty clear mandate and a good place to start.

    Whatever problems await the Democrats, and there will be many, this was the result we have needed ever since Trump first won the presidency 10 years ago. The damage he has caused in this decade of destruction is immeasurable, but maybe, just maybe, we have finally reached the beginning of the end of our long national nightmare, and we can begin the process of renewal and reformation.

    about the Democrats’ stunning win.

    #225912. Tech Giants Are Effectively Ungovernable. Here’s How to Change That.

    📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2344 w)

    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Foreignpolicy ↗ Open Full Page

    Tech Giants Are Effectively Ungovernable. Here’s How to Change That.

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2344 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foreignpolicy

    ⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
