    What Does the ICJ Ruling Mean for Myanmar?

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1897 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foreignpolicy

    ⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • The highlights this week: What the ICJ’s genocide ruling means for Myanmar, a flurry of trade deals in the region, and new U.S.
    • The highlights this week: What the ICJ’s genocide ruling means for Myanmar, a flurry of trade deals in the region, and latest U.S.
    • The state of Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya in 2017, the International Court of Justice (ICJ), the main judicial arm of the United Nations, ruled last Thursday.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Welcome to Foreign Policy’s Southeast Asia Brief.

    The highlights this week: What the ICJ’s genocide ruling means for Myanmar, a flurry of trade deals in the region, and new U.S. chip controls threatening Malaysian and Thai business.

    Welcome to Foreign Policy’s Southeast Asia Brief.

    The highlights this week: What the ICJ’s genocide ruling means for Myanmar, a flurry of trade deals in the region, and latest U.S. chip controls threatening Malaysian and Thai business.

    ICJ: Myanmar Committed Genocide.

    The state of Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya in 2017, the International Court of Justice (ICJ), the main judicial arm of the United Nations, ruled last Thursday.

    Industry observers note that the ruling documents how, following attacks by the Arakan Rohingya Salvation Army (ARSA), Myanmar carried out a campaign of genocidal violence against the Rohingya. It estimates that 10,000 Rohingya, about 1.2 percent of the total population, were killed.

    The court ruled 9-6 that the “only reasonable inference” was that this violence showed genocidal intent to destroy the Rohingya as a group—not just drive them out of Myanmar or exact collective punishment.

    The ruling orders Myanmar to cease violence against the group and prosecute those responsible, allow the safe return of Rohingya to their homes, and pay compensation.

    According to recent reports, sadly, none of this is likely. The junta has rejected the judgment as “unfair.”.

    Industry observers note that meanwhile, another armed group called the Arakan Army, which controls most of Rakhine province and mainly represents ethnic Rakhine Buddhists, has also committed large-scale violence against the Rohingya. Fighting between the Arakan Army and Rohingya militant groups—which has seen the Rohingya militants, including the ARSA, occasionally cooperate with the junta—has added to the hostility.

    The Arakan Army has made some overtures to Muslim communities in the province.

    For now, though, the Arakan Army is taking a wait-and-see attitude to the ICJ judgment. A spokesperson told local media, “We are constantly monitoring the current developments. We will stand firmly on truth and justice and take appropriate action for the benefit of the Arakan region.”.

    The country’s National Unity Government (NUG)—representing the civilian government overthrown by the junta in 2021 and associated with some of the main rebel forces—endorsed the judgment.

    It has been revealed that this was not a given. When Aung San Suu Kyi, an icon of the NUG, was acting as the country’s de facto leader, Myanmar consistently denied that the military’s actions against the Rohingya constituted a genocide.

    It has been revealed that in opposition, the NUG may now find its position easier. Its statement focused heavily on the junta’s culpability.

    It has been revealed that but it may find the whole judgment hard to accept. The ruling finds the state of Myanmar—not just the military—guilty of genocide. And at that time when the most severe offense took place, in 2016 and 2017, the paramount power in the state apparatus was Aung San Suu Kyi.

    In Southeast Asia, could this be a stumbling block for junta leader Min Aung Hlang’s push for diplomatic normalization with the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN)?

    In a recent development, thailand—the most vocal advocate for Myanmar’s full readmission to ASEAN—looks unmoved. “Thailand must take the position that best serves the country,” Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul told reporters.

    Thai Foreign Minister Sihasak Phuangketkeow argued that Thailand’s engagement did not contradict the ruling, as Thailand’s aim was to curb the current violence.

    Meanwhile, two other countries—Malaysia and the Philippines—have issued official statements on the matter.

    Malaysia’s brief statement said that it “respects the judgment.” The Philippines’ statement seemed a shade weaker, saying it “acknowledges the judgment” and, unlike Malaysia, does not mention the Rohingya by name.

    Other ASEAN countries have yet to make official statements.

    Still, for countries opposed to Myanmar’s full readmission to the bloc—most notably Singapore, which serves as the ASEAN chair next year—the judgment will reinforce this skepticism.

    On the global stage, China has objected. “China has concerns over concerns such as overreach of jurisdiction and expansive interpretation, and believes such practices are not conducive to dispute resolution,” a spokesperson noted.

    Industry observers note that regarding the United States, this judgment—plus the results of the country’s midterms—will likely impede the U.S. push toward normalization.

    Parts of the American right reject the judgment. While the U.S. government declared in 2022that the anti-Rohingya violence constituted a genocide, some on the right are concerned that the ICJ judgments lay the groundwork for a finding of genocide against Israel, linked to its war in Gaza.

    And the Myanmar junta clearly still thinks that it might find a sympathetic ear from the Trump administration.

    It has been revealed that when objecting to the ICJ ruling, a spokesperson for the Myanmar military cited a recent joint statement by U.S. President Donald Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping, and Russian President Vladimir Putin that the International Criminal Court “must not abuse” its jurisdiction.

    While the International Criminal Court is distinct from the ICJ, the spokesperson for Ming Aung Hlaing drew a parallel.

    Trump deals details. On Thursday evening, the White House disclosed the details of some of the various deals struck at last week’s ASEAN summit.

    The ASEAN deals, worth a total of $17 billion, include a $12 billion sale of Boeing aircraft to Philippine Airlines.

    The United States is also looking at providing $2 billion in loans for Philippine defense purchases and $400 million in military financing (though much of the funding was already committed).

    Thailand will also purchase $123 million of High Mobility Artillery Rocket Systems (HIMARS) from the United States.

    It has been revealed that the terms of the Thai deal, which are not yet final, are already provoking opposition there. Many in the agricultural powerhouse are unhappy with the prospect of more agricultural imports from the United States—in particular, pork. The government is on the defense, saying that it’s the best deal it could get.

    Amid controversy over the price tag, Thailand has also insisted that the HIMARS purchase is unrelated to the trade deal and was driven by national security considerations.

    Sources indicate that the Malaysian government also revealed that a U.S. consortium will help develop a sovereign artificial intelligence cloud for the Malaysian government, with the United States offering $50 million in support.

    EU-Indonesia trade deal. On Saturday, the European Union and Indonesia signed a trade deal that was 10 years in the making.

    Under the terms of the deal, both sides will remove import duties on about 90 percent of products, including EU automotives and most agricultural exports. The products not included will see their tariffs gradually reduced or receive tariff-free quotas.

    Indonesia expects that clothing, footwear, and palm oil will receive the biggest export boosts. It also hopes that the deal will boost European investment in Indonesia in sectors such as critical minerals, batteries, electric vehicles, pharmaceuticals, and electronics.

    The deal also addresses a substantial number of nontariff barriers that often bedevil foreign products entering Indonesia.

    The EU’s rules on deforestation, long a sticking point for Indonesia, have been finessed. While Indonesia did not secure an exemption, the EU left the door open to accepting Indonesia’s domestic standards.

    In a recent development, the deal comes as both the EU and Indonesia are looking to expand their global trade partnerships to offset U.S. tariffs.

    In a recent development, even more deals. The Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in China last week also saw a flurry of dealmaking.

    Singaporean Prime Minister Lawrence Wong and Xi met and announced negotiations to upgrade the two country’s free trade agreement.

    Indonesia and China said they will launch formal negotiations for a comprehensive economic partnership.

    They also confirmed strategic partnerships worth $71.8 billion, including the development of 10 “smart cities” by a partnership between Indonesian state-asset fund Danantara and a Chinese state-owned enterprise as well as deals involving a Chinese appliance maker and a consortium of other Chinese organizations investing $20 billion, also in partnership with Danantara.

    Meanwhile, Vietnam announced plans to deepen energy cooperation with Russia in both fossil fuels and nuclear energy.

    In a recent development, huang’s Return Is the Biggest National Security Scandal in U.S. History by James Palmer.

    In a recent development, the Middle East Is Finally on Its Own by Stephen M. Walt.

    Shenzhen Was No Yalta Conference by James Palmer.

    Elon Musk is quietly developing a couple of islands in the Philippines, reported by Gabryelle Dumalag in the Philippine Daily Inquirer.

    Malaysians turn to professional ticket concierges to secure seats at hot events, Norman Goh reports in Nikkei Asia.

    With the president’s popularity sinking, political parties are dodging the VP nomination in Indonesia, an editorial in Tempo.

    Last week, shortly before Trump jetted off to the Philippines and then China, the United States revealed new controls on chip exports following the Jensen Huang scandal.

    A license is now needed to export, reexport, or transfer advanced semiconductors to five countries: Brazil, Indonesia, Singapore, Malaysia, and Thailand.

    Additionally, data centers, foreign foundries, and chip exports are expected to perform due diligence to check if their customers are owned or controlled by U.S.-embargoed destinations—China, in this case.

    And the measures close the loophole of selling chips to data centers outside of China that provide processing power to companies in China.

    In a recent development, for countries that have been cashing in on the AI boom, this represents a major challenge. Southeast Asia has emerged as major data center hub. The new regulations will disrupt this.

    At least two partners of Nvidia that design equipment used in data centers powered by its chips have suspended shipments to Southeast Asia, according to reporting by Nikkei Asia.

    According to recent reports, nikkei Asia also reported that Taiwanese chipmaker Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Organization has already put several orders by Chinese and non-Chinese customers on hold. The regulations are so strict that they threaten to disrupt not just data centers but also smartphones, consumer electronics, and autonomous cars produced in Southeast Asia’s major electronics industry.

    In Malaysia, tech stocks sold off sharply in reaction to the news. Industry players also worried that it could seriously impact the country’s chip design industry.

    Thai business, meanwhile, is concerned that the regulations could put the brakes on the country’s booming data center industry.

    Sources indicate that reactions by governments have been mixed. Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim complained in an interview with the South China Morning Post that the United States was harder to work with than China, as the latter did not pick sides.

    Wong, the Singaporean prime minister, signaled a potential crackdown, saying that countries “abusing Singapore’s trusted position” to circumvent export controls was a “real concern.” However, he also made clear that Singapore expected to still work with both the United States and China.

    But hovering over all of this is this question: Will these rules last?

    Huang is now back at Nvidia, backed by Trump. The president, it seems—despite the best efforts of his administration’s hawks—remains unconvinced by chip controls.

    Sources indicate that joseph Rachman is the writer of Foreign Policy’s weekly Southeast Asia Brief. He is a freelance journalist based in Bangkok. X: @rachman_joseph.

    #225892. Trump reversed the Pied Piper’s bargain, and voters stiffed him

    📅 05 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1287 w)
    📖 Baca
    Business & Policy 📈 Bullish 🌐 Salon ↗ Open Full Page

    Trump reversed the Pied Piper’s bargain, and voters stiffed him

    📅 05 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1287 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Salon

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • When the pied piper loses his audience, we must ask whether the people have rediscovered their conscience or simply found a latest tune to follow.
    • On Tuesday night, Donald Trump and his MAGA movement saw what happens when political influence collides with the everyday realities of the people it seeks to lead.
    • It has been revealed that the 2026 midterm elections brought a dramatic shift in political power.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    When the pied piper loses his audience, we must ask whether the people have rediscovered their conscience or simply found a latest tune to follow.

    On Tuesday night, Donald Trump and his MAGA movement saw what happens when political influence collides with the everyday realities of the people it seeks to lead.

    It has been revealed that the 2026 midterm elections brought a dramatic shift in political power. Democrats won control of both the House and the Senate, flipping Senate seats in states such as Texas and Kansas, which were long thought to be out of reach, and winning House districts Trump easily carried just two years ago.Â.

    According to recent reports, voter polls placed the presidentâs approval at approximately 38%, with roughly six in 10 voters saying he was a factor in their vote. But beneath those numbers lies a more consequential story. Americans are confronting the cost of living, the economic consequences of tariffs, the uncertainty of war with Iran and diminishing confidence in American leadership abroad.

    Sources indicate that trump promised his voters he would drain the swamp, end foreign wars and bring prices down. Yet many Americans went to the polls questioning whether those promises had been kept. Unlike the Pied Piper of Hamelin, who rid the town of its rats, Trump now faces an electorate concerned that the problems he promised to eliminate have instead multiplied.Â.

    In the original story, the Piper fulfilled his bargain. He played his pipe, led the rats into the river and freed the town. But when the townspeople refused to pay him, he returned to exact revenge by leading away their children.Â.

    Over and over again throughout the midterm campaign, Trump urged supporters to vote as though he were personally on the ballot. In this telling, the Piper did not eliminate the rats. He added to them, and still he expected to be paid.

    Critics argue that Trump reversed that bargain. Rather than delivering the relief promised to ordinary Americans, the administration has left many struggling with economic uncertainty while continuing to demand political loyalty. Over and over again throughout the midterm campaign, Trump urged supporters to vote as though he were personally on the ballot. In this telling, the Piper did not eliminate the rats. He added to them, and still he expected to be paid.Â Â.

    Trumpâs supporters see a different story. They point to immigration raids and mass deportations, deregulation and challenges to established political institutions as evidence that the president delivered on important commitments. From their perspective, voters who rejected those policies after experiencing the consequences resemble townspeople who accepted the Piperâs services, but refused to honor their bargain.Â.

    Both interpretations expose a fundamental ethical question: When does political loyalty cease to be an expression of shared principles and become an abdication of independent judgment?Â.

    Sources indicate that in a democracy, voters are not obligated to follow the music indefinitely. They retain the right to question the destination, reconsider promises and withdraw their support. Political loyalty is not a debt citizens owe their leaders. It is a trust that leaders must continually earn.

    Albert Hirschman, an American economist and author of âExit, Voice, and Loyalty: Responses to Decline in Firms, Organizations, and States,â distinguished between voice (working to change an organization from within) and exit (abandoning it). A vote against an incumbent is often itself an act of a voice. But where voters withdrew their allegiance from a party or movement altogether, Tuesday looked more like an exit. Hirschman saw loyalty as what keeps members inside, speaking up rather than leaving. His framework suggests that when loyalty silences voice instead, exit becomes the only remaining option.Â.

    But elected officials carry a different and greater responsibility.Â.

    In a recent development, like the children of Hamelin, many Republican lawmakers followed the music toward an uncertain destination. Unlike those children, however, they had the authority â and the responsibility â to question where they were being led. Some embraced the presidentâs direction; others followed him despite reservations, knowing that dissent could invite a primary challenge. After all, they had seen others who challenged his leadership pay a considerable political cost. Kentucky Rep. Thomas Massie and Louisiana Sen. Bill Cassidy lost their Republican primaries to Trump-backed challengers.Â.

    Recent findings suggest that political cooperation is essential to governing. But cooperation becomes ethically troubling when loyalty to an individual displaces the obligation to question, deliberate and act independently. The oath of office is not a pledge of allegiance to a president, a party or a political movement. It is a commitment to uphold the Constitution. A president can command attention, share public debate and place enormous pressure on members of his own party. But the ability to demand loyalty does not create a moral entitlement to receive it.Â.

    Recent findings suggest that the children of Hamelinâs Pied Piper tale had no part in the broken bargain, yet they paid its price. In our democracy, ordinary Americans and future generations often inherit the consequences of political decisions, and today they are paying a price. Economic instability, weakened public trust and the costs of war do not disappear when an election ends. A leaderâs success cannot be measured solely by the number of people willing to follow along with them. It must also be measured by what happens to those who never chase the tune.Â.

    The election has shifted power in Washington. Democrats, after winning sizable, historic victories throughout the country, will soon have an opportunity to exercise congressional oversight and reinforce the institutional independence our constitutional system requires.Â.

    But changing who holds the instrument does not necessarily change the music.Â.

    Democrats now face their own ethical test. Will they exercise power with the transparency, accountability and respect for constitutional checks they demanded from their opponents? Will they welcome dissent within their own ranks? And will they resist the temptation to substitute partisan loyalty for independent judgment?Â Â.

    According to recent reports, an election can change the balance of power overnight. It cannot, by itself, restore public trust or guarantee ethical leadership. That requires leaders willing to place constitutional responsibility above political convenience, institutions prepared to exercise meaningful oversight, and citizens who refuse to surrender their judgment to the most compelling voice in the room. The first six months of the 120th Congress must be defined not merely by a change in political power, but by a demonstrable commitment to ethical reform, transparency, and accountability. The American people did not vote simply for a change in leadership. They voted for a government worthy of their trust.

    We need your help to stay independent.

    According to recent reports, the Pied Piperâs greatest power was not simply his ability to play a captivating tune. It was his ability to persuade others to follow without questioning where their journey would end.Â.

    In a recent development, political ethicist Dennis Thompson called this the problem of many hands: When many officials each contribute a small part to a collective outcome, responsibility seems to dissolve until no one bears it. So, when political loyalty becomes more crucial than independent judgment, who bears responsibility â the leader who plays the tune, or those who willingly follow? Thompsonâs framework does not allow individual lawmakers to hide behind presidential leadership, party discipline or collective decisions. Nor does it assign blame equally. Responsibility depends on each officialâs authority, knowledge, contribution and the alternatives available to them. By that measure, those who knew better and had the power to act cannot claim they were merely following the music from the leader in the red hat.

    When the music finally stops, the question is not simply who will lead next.Â.

    It is whether we have learned to listen differently.

    I’ll be the first to admit that I have a substantial problem—er, a bag problem. My closet is practically overflowing with thrifted purses, and my FP colleagues know that I come into the office carrying not one or two sensible totes, but three or four. So trust me when I say that I know bags, and this one stands above the rest.

    According to recent reports, baggu’s Medium Nylon Crescent Bag is a workhorse, ideal for a friend or loved one looking for a trusty companion for weekend errands, jet-setting adventures, and everything in between. I’ve previously recommended Baggu’s packing cubes for their durability and cute patterns. This product has those same qualities.

    Sleek and roomy, the crescent bag is available in a range of colors, materials (mine is leather), and sizes, although I’ve found that the medium-sized pouch is perfect for my needs.

    JisuLife Portable Handheld Fan Ultra2 ($72.67, presently on sale).

    I’ve traveled to a bunch of countries over the years, but my luggage tag collection is not the largest at FP—not by a long shot. Many of my colleagues have been to more destinations and stayed longer, just one of the things that makes working here so delightful. In the office, everyone has a travel tip.

    Recent findings suggest that mine: The gadgets you take with you should be multifunctional. The exemplar of an all-purpose gadget is this freakishly powerful fan that’s also a power bank, flashlight, and handy-dandy keyboard cleaner. I keep it in my carry-on, fan myself before takeoff, charge my phone over the Atlantic, and light up the seat pocket on arrival to make sure I didn’t leave my passport behind. As for my keyboard—it’s reliably crumb-free.

    Etnodim Ivory Wool Scarf “Zavii” ($122).

    Sources indicate that etnodim makes high-quality, gorgeous interpretations of classical Ukrainian clothes, from embroidered shirts and dresses to traditional kerchiefs. On a trip to Kyiv this fall, I got a traditional shirt, known as a vyshyvanka, for my daughter from their brand store in Podil, Kyiv’s equivalent of Brooklyn. Fortunately, you don’t have to travel 30-plus hours by plane and train to get their items, which are also sold online.

    While I’d heartily recommend Etnodim’s wildly colorful designs, their more basic items—like this merino wool scarf—go with anything. Best of all, you’ll be supporting a Ukrainian brand that celebrates the country’s unique identity, in opposition to Russia’s best efforts to stamp out such cultural expressions.

    Breville Milk Café milk frother ($199.95).

    In a recent development, after realizing just how much money I was spending per month on lattes at my local (international chain) coffee shop, I decided to look into making them at home. But I didn’t want to spend thousands of dollars on some behemoth machine that requires a specialist degree to operate, either.

    Industry observers note that enter the Breville Milk Café milk frother. It’s super easy to use and clean, it doesn’t take up much counter space, and it reliably makes the perfect steamed milk to my desired temperature and amount of foam. I’ve used it at least once—if not twice—a day for the last five months, and it hasn’t let me down yet.

    But that’s just the milk part of the equation. Now on to the coffee part….

    Breville Nespresso Original Essenza Mini Espresso Machine ($174.99).

    Industry observers note that the Nespresso Original Essenza Mini Espresso Machine is basically a Keurig for espresso. You don’t have to grind beans or fiddle with a million buttons and levers to make a single shot of espresso—just pop in a Nespresso pod; make sure the little, easily removable water tank in the back is full; and hit a button.

    According to recent reports, this machine is also compact, so it doesn’t monopolize your kitchen. Best of all, the espresso tastes just as rich and creamy as it would if you went to the corner coffee shop—and you don’t even have to put on pants to enjoy it.

    —Jennifer Williams, deputy editor.

    Ortlieb Vario Lite pannier backpack ($195).

    It has been revealed that FP recently moved offices to a space farther away from the D.C. Metro’s Red Line—and so I became a bike commuter.

    In a recent development, biking has long been my preferred mode of transportation on the weekends, when I shuttle between yoga and Trader Joe’s with the help of a storage basket. But I swiftly realized that commuting is an entirely different ball game. Laptop plus lunch is a heavy—and valuable—combo. I did not trust my basket, however adorable, to keep these items secure.

    Recent findings suggest that enter: a pannier backpack. Rather than settling either for a backpack (which would strain my back while biking and probably make me sweaty) or a pannier (which would be difficult to transport after parking my bike), I decided to invest in this brilliant product from Ortlieb, a German brand that happens to be—like me—Franconian. It has transformed my commute.

    The Vario Lite allows me to toggle seamlessly between pannier and backpack modes. It has an interior laptop pocket and outer compartment where I store my keys and phone for easy access. Its rolltop structure means that its size is flexible, and its backpack function is ergonomic. Did I mention that it’s waterproof, too?

    Recent findings suggest that the Vario Lite is the little brother of the Vario, a slightly larger pannier backpack from Ortlieb. I tried on both and found the Vario Lite to be a better fit on my 5’1” frame. But anyone can rest assured that there’s an entire line of high-quality pannier backpacks—in a range of colors—to choose from.

    Brick Phone Distraction Blocker ($56.80, right now on sale).

    The Brick—a magnetic square you can use to curtail access to your phone—is an invention I resisted for a long time. Its very existence was proof that we were living at capitalism’s nadir: You’re telling me I need to buy a little plastic brick to blunt the pernicious effects of this other little plastic brick?

    Recent findings suggest that and yet. The Brick has made my life better, and here are the numbers to back up that claim. Before acquiring the device, I was averaging 10 hours and 40 minutes on my phone per day. Now that number is down to just under eight hours. Sometimes, when there isn’t an international spy scandal all over the news, it has been known to hit seven.

    According to recent reports, that I have been wasting this much of my life scrolling is mortifying enough. What’s worse is how easy it was to break the habit. The minor inconvenience the Brick depends on is that once you block certain apps you can only unblock them by tapping your phone to the cube. Tapping the cube is very easy. But most of the time, it’s simply too much of a bother. So instead of doomscrolling, you put down the phone and do something else instead, such as engaging with your children or animals.

    Turns out you can throw money at seemingly intractable problems. Capitalism, you win this round.

    Scotch Precision Ultra Edge Scissors ($11.39).

    Sources indicate that I, too, initially recommended the Brick (above) but voluntarily scrapped my write-up lest attention spans wane while reading too many words about a plastic square. Instead, I’d like to recommend something analogue to fill your newfound free time: paper collage.

    Industry observers note that I recently turned to physical collaging as a cathartic supplement to the digital work I sometimes do for FP. It’s the perfect hobby for the world traveler with piles of ephemera or magazine readers with a backlog of vintage Foreign Policy and National Geographic. Pull together a gift collage kit with paper bits of your choice and these sharp, precise scissors.

    It has been revealed that these superior snips come recommended secondhand by Ray Orr, a collage artist and former visual journalist and co-founder of Living Room DC, a creative space in D.C.’s Mount Pleasant neighborhood. Consider gifting a workshop or drop-in session for collage or artmaking in the cozy spot.

    —Lori Kelley, executive creative director.

    Cocinare FLOW B9 Gooseneck Electric Kettle ($55.99, at the moment on sale).

    You know what they say: A warm cup of tea a day keeps the geopolitical crises away. Or maybe two cups, given the present outlook. Actually, scratch that—might be best to have three.

    World leaders may have decided to shirk responsibility for confronting our warming planet, but you can still control the temperature of water at home with this luxurious electric kettle. No software required; this baby does not run on Outlook. Just plug the kettle in, set it to the optimal steeping temperature for your beverage of choice, and hit the button. A quiet moment with a perfectly warmed cup of tea is just minutes away. (For a slightly less precise but more budget-friendly option, consider this alternative.).

    Everyman’s Library Pocket Classics ($16-$28).

    It has been revealed that if you’re like me, packing for a trip is a calculation of how much reading material you can bring to fill time spent in transit without losing precious real estate in your bag. “They’ll have bookstores there,” a wise friend once reminded me. But a smart traveler comes prepared!

    Short story collections from Penguin Random House’s Everyman’s Library Pocket Classics Series are a compact travel companion and a great gift for someone you know who’s getting excited for an upcoming trip (or still reminiscing about their last one).

    Industry observers note that from India to Russia to Ireland, these anthologies compile literary short stories and book excerpts related to the featured country, continent, or city. Their contents can introduce you to a newly introduced destination, deepen your appreciation for a place you already love, or even inspire a change of itinerary.

    In a recent development, I’ve found the anthology format to be ideal for the random stretches of time to kill when traveling between destinations. The stories are just the right length to digest on a plane, bus, or train ride, and can even make the inevitable delay more enjoyable.

    Zeedog Ruff Leash ($15.20, currently on sale).

    It has been revealed that this year, I became the owner of a young dog—and also the continued owner of pair of aging arms. After having my shoulder wrenched by my puppy’s eagerness to chase D.C.’s rats a few too many times, I switched to this leash from Zeedog.

    Industry observers note that through a simple shock-absorbing design, which looks like a stretchy wave at the end of the leash, the Ruff Leash absorbs the force when your dog yanks. It also comes, like puppies, in a stylish variety of colors. Strongly recommended for anyone foolish enough, like me, to get one.

    Sony WH-1000XM6 Noise-Canceling Headphones ($348, currently on sale).

    Sources indicate that living in a loud city like New York, I’ve long been a believer in a good pair of headphones. Even before advances in noise-canceling technology, hearing the Talking Heads instead of the roar of an oncoming subway was an amazing way to mitigate the sounds of crowded urban life.

    It has been revealed that recently, I upgraded from my older Sony headphones to the upcoming WH-1000XM6s. What they lack in catchy brand naming, they make up for in incredible sound quality and call clarity. From Zoom calls to catching background noise in video edits, they sound incredible while blocking out everything I don’t want to hear.

    —Connor Curfman, staff designer.

    Hebe Studio Paint By Numbers Kit ($57).

    In a recent development, I’ve long admired the bold colors and vibrant, travel-inspired scenes painted by Rhi James, the U.K. artist behind Hebe Studio. Her paint-by-numbers kits offer a delightfully nostalgic way to slow down and create beautiful artwork of your own. With these kits—which are designed to be beginner-friendly and include high-quality paints, brushes, and canvas—it’s easy to feel confident as you bring your masterpiece to life. James’s enchanting landscapes are a unique gift that will add a personal touch to someone’s home while also giving them a creative escape.

    —Sara Stewart, senior creative director, product.

    Quince Mongolian Cashmere Pullover Hoodie ($99.90).

    Whether or not you’re comfortable thinking of yourself as the kind of person who wears a cashmere pullover hoodie, you will feel comfortable wearing a cashmere pullover hoodie. Quince cashmere is responsibly and sustainably sourced, so you can also feel comfortable about the conditions of the goat whose soft, soft hair you are wearing. This makes a great gift for anyone whose head gets jealous when they put on a sweater.

    Schoolhouse x Pendleton Abington Hall Throw ($139.99-$238.99, currently on sale).

    In a recent development, as winter approaches, there’s nowhere I want to be but snuggled under a blanket and sitting by a crackling fire. I grew up in the woods of the Pacific Northwest and, to me, Pendleton is the height of luxury. Since 1909, this Oregon-based mill has been producing wool blankets and textiles to outfit lumberjacks and the Beach Boys alike. Pendleton’s collaboration with home goods brand Schoolhouse marries its heritage product with modern style. This 100 percent wool, “Made in USA” blanket is sure to elevate any cozy space and keep you warm all winter long.

    —Rylie Munn, social media editor.

    It has been revealed that A confession: I have long known what the perfect holiday gift is, but I’ve kept it to myself. No more! It’s a puzzle from Liberty Puzzles, a wooden jigsaw puzzle made in Boulder, Colorado. (Full disclosure: I worked at Liberty Puzzles long ago, but unlike my friends at fast-food joints, who came away swearing off the menu, I left charmed having seen how the product gets made.).

    What sets a Liberty Puzzle apart from the typical cardboard variety? For starters, the shapes. Each one is unusual, and thick, laser-cut pieces fall into place with a satisfying click. They also have a faint smell of burnt maple. Best of all, if you ever lose a piece—say, in the stomach of a mischievous furry friend—the organization will replace it for free.

    The catalog is quite global, including landscapes, art, maps, and vintage posters, so there’s something for everyone. I’ll make it easy for you: A gastronomical map of Italy for the couple fresh back from their honeymoon! A woodblock print of Japan’s snow-dusted Mount Haruna for the burgeoning snowboarder! A painting of Diana and her nymphs for the Roman history buff in your life! They even make kids’ puzzles.

    Torres Selecta Iberian Ham Gourmet Potato Chips ($49).

    Give the candy canes a break this year and stuff your stockings with chips!

    Industry observers note that I first encountered these pork-flavored potato chips at my neighborhood wine bar years ago, and they swiftly became a cult favorite. They’ve been on my mind again, having recently returned from Andalusia, Spain, where jamón ibérico seemed to show up at every meal.

    Recent findings suggest that salty, savory, and downright decadent, these chips would pair great with a dollop of creme fraiche; a dab of fig jam, pickled shallots, or salmon roe; and a glass of cava. They’re the perfect treat for the adventurous eater on your list, or anyone who’s still dreaming of their last trip.

    —Megan DuBois, associate editor.

    Mens Soft Fleece Drawstring Elastic Waist Cargo Pants ($16.97).

    Yes, you read that right: I’m recommending sweatpants.

    My travel frequency has gone up a lot this year (not a complaint!), and I’ve put a lot of thought into what I wear on long flights. Cargo sweatpants have been a game-changer for comfort and convenience. The additional pockets are useful for carrying chargers, chewing gum, and other paraphernalia without constantly having to open the overhead bin. And the pockets have buttons to close them, so I avoid the constant fear of losing my passport. The sweatpants are also possibly the most comfortable item of clothing I own.

    While I purchased my pair at a brick-and-mortar store in India (shout-out to Marks & Spencer), I’m sure this equivalent on Amazon is just as good. Having closed pockets is the key. And these sweatpants cost less than some Manhattan cocktails, so you can pick up a few to keep in rotation.

    Bic 4-Color Original Retractable Ballpoint Pen ($4.38, currently on sale).

    One of the dangers of having kids is the constant temptation to indulge in nostalgia for the objects of one’s own youth. But sometimes nostalgia can be an invitation to genuine rediscovery.

    Such was my experience with the classic Bic four-color pen. I bought one for my fifth-grade son during this year’s back-to-school run-up and watched as his newfound power dawned. You’re writing in blue, and with a flick of the thumb: Boom! Green. If the mood strikes: Boom! Back to blue—or red?

    I soon bought a four-color pen for myself and promptly came to a renewed appreciation for its simple design and small daily offer of variety. But reading about the pen’s history also gave me a deeper understanding of its geopolitical significance. I hadn’t known that Bic is a French company, and that the iconic four-color pen has always—since its original release in 1970—been a product proudly made in France. The factory in the town of Montévrain still closely guards its manufacturing secrets.

    It has been revealed that the Bic four-color pen isn’t just a writing implement—it’s a precisely engineered machine, an enduring symbol of Francofuturism. All of which makes it the perfect stocking stuffer for the status-conscious middle schooler in your life—or the wonky Europhilic aesthete.

    The Oregon Trail Card Game ($18.50).

    Recent findings suggest that although I have never been much of a video gamer, I would be lying if I noted that the 1990s classic Oregon Trail did not eat up hours of my childhood. Fighting to survive bandits, broken axels, and (of course) dysentery was a favorite activity of mine when the days were cold, the nights were long, and I needed an escape from our chaotic world.

    In a recent development, so when I was gifted a physical version of the iconic game, I was hooked. The story is the same: Make your way from Independence, Missouri, to Willamette Valley, Oregon, without succumbing to drowning, starvation, or a host of other calamities. My friends and I have spent hours around my coffee table attempting to cross the treacherous 2,000-plus-mile passage without incident. There have been screaming matches, thrown cards, and more typhoid outbreaks than we can count.

    And, of course, we have died every time.

    —Alexandra Sharp, World Brief writer.

    An FP Insider Gift Subscription and Limited-Edition Tote Bag ($124.50 with code HOLIDAY50).

    Recent findings suggest that the best gift for an independent thinker in your life is one year of Foreign Policy. This holiday season, an annual FP Insider gift subscription includes a limited-edition FOREIGN POLICY tote, made from durable heavyweight cotton canvas with an external side pocket. Plus: ad-free reading and behind-the-scenes dispatches from FP’s stable of geopolitical experts. Visit our gift subscriptions page for more information. Want this tote for yourself? Join or upgrade to Insider to unlock VIP membership perks.

    Sources indicate that products are independently selected by FP staff. FP earns an affiliate commission on anything purchased through links to Amazon.com on this page.

    Commenting is a benefit of a Foreign Policy subscription.

    Please follow our comment guidelines, stay on topic, and be civil, courteous, and respectful of others’ beliefs.

    Tech Report: Gay candidates won where it was supposed to be impossible

    📅 05 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1146 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Salon

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • On Tuesday night, two things happened at once, and the country will be tempted to remember only one of them.
    • Sources indicate that the first made me go quiet at my kitchen table.
    • And on Long Island, in a district Donald Trump carried, a gay Democrat named Chris Gallant, whose private photographs were leaked against him precisely because someone believed that seeing him would be enough to end him, came within about two points of flipping a seat the forecasters had rated safely Republican.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    On Tuesday night, two things happened at once, and the country will be tempted to remember only one of them.

    Sources indicate that the first made me go quiet at my kitchen table. Chris Pappas won election to the U.S. Senate in New Hampshire, becoming the first openly gay man ever sent to that chamber, and part of the margin that handed Democrats the Senate. In Indiana, J.D. Ford, the first openly gay person ever elected to that stateâs legislature, unseated a Republican incumbent and is headed to the House. In Texas, of all places, James Talarico beat Ken Paxton to become the first Democrat to win statewide in more than thirty years, after a campaign in which anti-LGBTQ+ messaging was reportedly Paxtonâs single largest category of advertising, and in which the vice president of the United States stood on a stage and used âgayâ as a punchline against him. Talarico is straight, and he won anyway.

    And on Long Island, in a district Donald Trump carried, a gay Democrat named Chris Gallant, whose private photographs were leaked against him precisely because someone believed that seeing him would be enough to end him, came within about two points of flipping a seat the forecasters had rated safely Republican. He conceded the election on Wednesday, down by roughly 6,700 votes in the closest race of the incumbent Republican Nick LaLotaâs career. In the same breath, Gallant called LaLota a brother in arms and told the district he was still their neighbor, which is to say he refused the shame he was supposed to feel from the photo leak to the very end. Whatever that is, it is not the story of a man sunk by leather. It is the story of a man who nearly won the unwinnable while carrying the exact weight that was supposed to be disqualifying.

    In 2026, you cannot reliably win an American election by making a manâs gayness, real or invented, the center of your campaign. Republicans tried it in Texas and lost the whole state. They tried it on Long Island and watched a red seat nearly flip.

    In a recent development, put those results next to one another and a sentence forms that would have been unimaginable a decade ago: In 2026, you cannot reliably win an American election by making a manâs gayness, real or invented, the center of your campaign. Republicans tried it in Texas and lost the whole state. They tried it on Long Island and watched a red seat nearly flip. The oldest weapon in the drawer â the one that raised me, the one that could empty a lunch table in the 1990s â is losing its edge at the ballot box. Voters keep looking at the openly gay candidate and sending him to Washington.

    That is the headline, and it is real, and I am not going to let anyone talk me out of being moved by it.

    In a recent development, but here is the second thing that happened Tuesday night. In the same hours, often on the same ballots, and it is the part the rainbow-wave coverage is already rushing past. In Arizona and Nebraska, voters approved measures to bar transgender girls from girlsâ sports. In Colorado, two measures aimed at transgender young people, one on sports and one restricting certain surgical care for minors, are narrowly passing. In Washington State, an initiative to keep transgender girls out of girlsâ sports passed comfortably. The same electorate that refused to punish a Senate candidate for being gay reached down the ballot and punished trans kids for existing.

    In a recent development, this is the thing I need people to see before the celebration hardens into a story we tell ourselves. The contempt did not disappear on Tuesday. It relocated. A political movement that has learned it can no longer win by hating gay men has not given up the strategy. It has updated the target. The MAGA machine that aired the Paxton ads and laughed at Vanceâs joke is the same one now writing ballot measures about 11-year-olds, because cruelty still tests well when it is aimed at the group with the least power to answer back. Gays are simply the part of the community that got powerful enough to be left alone.

    Sources indicate that I know this pattern in my body, because I have watched it my whole life. The fear moves. First it was the plague, then it was the gay man as predator, then it was marriage as the end of the world, and each time the broader culture eventually got bored or ashamed and the fear went looking for a upcoming address. Right now the address is a trans child in a locker room. The people who found that child did not arrive by accident. They are the same people, running the same play, because it is the only play they have ever had.

    Recent findings suggest that so I want to be careful about the victory lap, even as I take one. It is a genuine and hard-won thing that Chris Pappas will be a senator and J.D. Ford will be a congressman, and that a straight man in Texas could not be destroyed by being called gay. Those wins are not small, and the people who did the work to make them real earned every bit of the joy.Â.

    In a recent development, but a movement does not get to accept its own seats at the table while the youngest and most defenseless members of its own community are voted off the field in four states on the same night. This is not a win we get to keep cleanly. It is a split screen, and if we only look at our half of it, we become exactly the kind of people who could be bought off with a little representation while someone else pays the bill.

    We need your help to stay independent.

    According to recent reports, the refusal to be ashamed won some rooms on Tuesday. I felt it. The task now is to extend that refusal to the people the machine has decided to hunt next, to say as loudly for trans kids what the voters of Newly introduced Hampshire and Indiana and Texas just stated for us: that you do not get to make a personâs existence a punchline, or a wedge, or a ballot measure. We learned that lesson about gay men the slow and brutal way. The whole point of learning it is to spare the next group from learning it alone.

    Chris Gallant did not quite win. But he came close enough to prove the old weapon is dulling. The question Tuesday really asked is whether we will hand the people wielding it a latest one, or finally take the thing out of their hands.

    Don’t Let China Hawks Exploit the Nvidia Scandal

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1278 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foreignpolicy

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Amid the flurry of commentary over Nvidia and Jensen Huang’s “gone today, here tomorrow” act, there is one question that remains undiscussed: Has U.S.
    • According to recent reports, the overwhelming reaction to Huang’s reinstatement has been bipartisan outrage at U.S.
    • Industry observers note that amid the flurry of commentary over Nvidia and Jensen Huang’s “gone today, here tomorrow” act, there is one question that remains undiscussed: Has U.S.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Get audio access with any FP subscription.

    Amid the flurry of commentary over Nvidia and Jensen Huang’s “gone today, here tomorrow” act, there is one question that remains undiscussed: Has U.S. policy toward China succeeded in its aims of maintaining American preeminence and security?

    According to recent reports, the overwhelming reaction to Huang’s reinstatement has been bipartisan outrage at U.S. President Donald Trump’s interference in a private firm, coupled with demands for stricter enforcement of U.S. export controls on the sale of Nvidia’s chips to China. As Sen. Tom Cotton mentioned, “I have warned the administration from the start about Communist China obtaining our most advanced chips through both smuggling and remote access.”.

    Industry observers note that amid the flurry of commentary over Nvidia and Jensen Huang’s “gone today, here tomorrow” act, there is one question that remains undiscussed: Has U.S. policy toward China succeeded in its aims of maintaining American preeminence and security?

    In a recent development, the overwhelming reaction to Huang’s reinstatement has been bipartisan outrage at U.S. President Donald Trump’s interference in a private organization, coupled with demands for stricter enforcement of U.S. export controls on the sale of Nvidia’s chips to China. As Sen. Tom Cotton said, “I have warned the administration from the start about Communist China obtaining our most advanced chips through both smuggling and remote access.”.

    That sentiment is widely shared. But should it be?

    Recent findings suggest that there was a point sometime in the mid-2010s when U.S. policy shifted decisively from engaging China to containing it. This began during U.S. President Barack Obama’s second term, and then it accelerated with the first tariff war and the campaign against Huawei during the first season of the Trump show. It was cemented as consensus policy during the U.S. President Joe Biden’s interregnum and has been maintained during the second season of Trump.

    According to recent reports, this shift was driven by a growing consensus that engagement had failed. China’s entry into the World Trade Organization in 2001 was supposed to make it more democratic and open. It did not. China under President Xi Jinping instead turned away from political reforms, silencing any hint of opposition to the Chinese Communist Party (CCP). Internationally, Beijing adopted a more confrontational stance toward the United States while continuing to steal American intellectual property.

    In this context, Washington embraced export controls on high-end technology that could enhance the Chinese military or give Chinese companies an edge in the race for preeminence in artificial intelligence. But instead of meaningfully containing or slowing China, these export controls have only succeeded in raising tensions and increasing the potential of a future war.

    According to recent reports, by most informed accounts, the restrictions in place since 2022 have delayed or impaired the ability of Chinese companies to build AI frontier models on the scale, scope, and speed of Anthropic or OpenAI. The restrictions on semiconductor manufacturing equipment sales to China have also created supply constraints that have pressured the Chinese military.

    As a result, however, China has become far more self-reliant and aggressively built out its own domestic chip design and manufacturing. Though these domestic efforts lag behind the United States, Nvidia, and Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company by months or even a few years, this has not prevented dramatic breakthroughs such as the unveiling of China’s AI model DeepSeek.

    Recent findings suggest that what’s more, China has managed to evade export controls and obtain high-end chips, either through third parties and other countries in Southeast Asia or through good old-fashioned theft and copying. If Nvidia knowingly and purposely evaded those controls with the acquiescence of some in the Trump administration, that remains a profound scandal. But the reality is that even without this kind of corruption, sanctions have consistently failed to prevent countries from accessing things that are available worldwide, even highly controlled military equipment. A country as large and as intertwined with the global economy as China simply cannot be cut off for long.

    In a recent development, by trying to control China’s chip access and only partly succeeding, Washington has pushed Beijing into a more unequivocally hostile stance. The CCP and Xi perceived, rightly, that the United States had no intention of allowing its peaceful rise and concluded that confrontation was inevitable.

    Industry observers note that especially in the past two years, Washington also began to cut off China’s access to aspects of the domestic U.S. market. The Trump administration has blocked Chinese attempts to purchase U.S. companies and prevented thousands of Chinese students from studying at American universities. Students and investments both made China more dependent on and integrated with the United States.

    It has been revealed that but many Americans, drawing the wrong lessons from the brief period of Japanese ascendency in the late 1980s, saw these developments as a sign of American weakness, not strength. Japan’s investment in Rockefeller Center and Pebble Beach actually bound the country more closely to the United States and in the process demonstrated how attractive and singular U.S. properties and capital markets were (and are). Instead of recognizing this, policymakers simply carried their aversion to foreign investment over to China.

    Industry observers note that in the past year, both the Trump administration and Xi seem to have established what was termed “mutually assured disruption.” China can withhold rare-earth exports that are vital to tech companies everywhere, while Washington can use trade restrictions to squeeze the China export machine. The result has been a period of relative calm in U.S.-China tensions.

    According to recent reports, now, with the Nvidia drama, that modus vivendi is in question on Capitol Hill. Congress sees the complicity of the White House as a political opening that it can exploit to double down on its preferred strategy of strangling Chinese technological growth.

    Sources indicate that but the calls for greater export controls and more scrutiny of trade will not make the United States economically or militarily more secure. They will instead push China ever deeper into its adversarial stance. In this latest climate, any vestiges of bilateral engagement will be harder to sustain, aggravating the relationship that will determine the stability of the global system over the next decades.

    There is still time to pursue a better policy. From the outset, Washington should have loosened controls on high-end chip exports, which could have helped ease Xi and the CCP’s iron grip on China and soothe bilateral tensions over time. The refrain that the United States can’t afford to let China win the race for artificial general intelligence is grounded in the same fallacy that any country could contain such a technology and that there is some magical first-mover advantage. There certainly wasn’t with any prior technology, nuclear weapons included.

    A more sensible and open policy on chip exports remains the best path going forward. Congress can still pursue it, even as it seeks to hold Trump accountable for any corrupt acts—and Huang for any mistakes he may have made. Nvidia’s scandals do not prove that engagement was wrong and should not preclude the United States and China from developing a more cooperative relationship. Global peace should not be sacrificed on account of Huang’s actions, or Trump’s.

    Zachary Karabell is the author of the Edgy Optimist Substack and an opinion contributor at the Washington Post.

    • According to recent reports, itâs difficult to find the right words for the end of something that has meant so much to so many people.
    • When Salon debuted in November 1995, the web was a very different place.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Today, after 31 years, we are saddened to announce that Salon is ceasing publication.

    According to recent reports, itâs difficult to find the right words for the end of something that has meant so much to so many people. Salon was never just a website. It was an idea about what journalism could be, born at a moment when the internet was still a largely unexplored frontier.

    When Salon debuted in November 1995, the web was a very different place. A small group of journalists set out to create something original: a publication with a strong voice, a curiosity about the world and a belief that the internet could bring journalism and readers together in new ways. They helped pioneer a form of journalism that would come to define an entirely new era of publishing.

    Sources indicate that over three decades, Salon has brought together politics, culture, criticism and ideas in a way that was distinctly our own. Our journalism examined power and politics, questioned assumptions, surfaced stories that deserved attention and made room for perspectives that were too often overlooked. Our writers and editors helped shape conversations about the forces changing our lives. The work was never simply about keeping up with the news. It was about making sense of it.

    Recent findings suggest that the history of Salon is also the history of the people who made it. We are profoundly grateful to the journalists, editors, photographers, producers, designers, business teams and countless other colleagues who brought this publication to life across its many chapters. To the founders who imagined it, the staff members who built it, the contributors who gave it their voices and the alumni who carried its spirit into the world: Thank you. Salon’s legacy belongs to all of you.

    Recent findings suggest that the business realities of independent digital journalism have changed profoundly over the years. After careful consideration, we have reached the difficult decision that our publishing model is no longer sustainable. We know this news will be deeply disappointing to many of you, and we share that sadness.

    Thirty-one years is a remarkable run, but what matters most is what happened during those years: the journalism, the ideas, the voices, the conversations and the community that grew around them. Salon helped demonstrate what digital journalism could be and could become. We hope that legacy will continue to matter long after today.

    In a recent development, thank you for being part of our story. It has been an extraordinary privilege.

    The Party Shaping Spain’s Election Isn’t Even on the Ballot

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2140 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foreignpolicy

    ⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways

    • Recent findings suggest that catalonia’s independence movement is moving to the right, and Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez might pay the price in snap parliamentary elections on Nov.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Get audio access with any FP subscription.

    Sources indicate that catalonia’s independence movement is moving to the right, and Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez might pay the price in snap parliamentary elections on Nov. 29. Junts per Catalunya, the separatist party that supported Sánchez to form a minority government in 2023, turned against him last year to fend off a fresh far-right rival—ultimately forcing the early vote.

    According to recent reports, sánchez called elections after failing to get emergency legislation aimed at tackling Spain’s housing crisis through parliament in October. The conservative People’s Party (PP), the far-right Vox party, and the center-right Junts all voted against the package.

    Recent findings suggest that catalonia’s independence movement is moving to the right, and Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez might pay the price in snap parliamentary elections on Nov. 29. Junts per Catalunya, the separatist party that supported Sánchez to form a minority government in 2023, turned against him last year to fend off a latest far-right rival—ultimately forcing the early vote.

    In a recent development, sánchez called elections after failing to get emergency legislation aimed at tackling Spain’s housing crisis through parliament in October. The conservative People’s Party (PP), the far-right Vox party, and the center-right Junts all voted against the package.

    It was the latest example of Junts going against the minority government’s initiatives. When party head Carles Puigdemont declared that Junts would revoke its backing and move into the opposition last year, he blamed Sánchez’s Socialist Workers’ Party for broken promises. But the pro-independence party is also facing a growing threat at home in Catalonia.

    According to recent reports, that threat is Aliança Catalana—a far-right, separatist party led by Sílvia Orriols, the mayor of the small town of Ripoll. Orriols founded Aliança in 2020 after breaking with another separatist party; its platform combines a demand for Catalan independence with hard-line hostility toward immigration and Islam. She pushed for a tougher approach to immigration after the 2017 Barcelona attacks, carried out by a terror cell based in Ripoll.

    Unlike Junts, Aliança has elected not to stand in the Nov. 29 national elections, refusing to take part based on its Catalonian separatism. “We are not thinking about influencing Madrid, and that’s part of the foundation of Aliança,” said the party’s press chief, Eduard Berraondo.

    Sources indicate that polling at the moment points to a right-wing majority. The PP leads with 31.2 percent of the vote, with the Socialists at 29.3 percent, and Vox at 18 percent as of Nov. 24, according to newspaper Ara’s polling average. Together, the PP and Vox are projected to win around 190 seats, above the 176 needed for a majority in the 350-seat Congress of Deputies. Only the state-run Center for Sociological Studies pollster, which critics say favors the government, puts the Socialists ahead.

    So, although Aliança isn’t on the ballot, its rapid rise is reshaping Spanish politics.

    The party’s hard line on immigration and Islam has pushed Junts to the right, making the party ever less likely to partner with the Socialists. Aliança’s voters could help decide where Catalonia’s right-wing vote goes: back to Junts, across to Vox, or nowhere at all. Finally, the party’s growing popularity suggests a deeper shift among Catalan independence supporters, away from progressivism and toward a more exclusionary view of who counts as Catalan.

    Aliança has risen rapidly in Catalonia. The far-right party won just two of 135 seats in the Catalan parliamentary elections in 2024, but the latest survey from the Catalan government’s polling agency, the Centre d’Estudis d’Opinió (CEO), projects that the party would capture between 23 and 25 seats if regional elections were held now. Junts, which holds 35 seats, would fall to between 18 and 20.

    According to recent reports, catalonia’s next regional elections must be held by late June 2028. Almost 1 in 5 people who voted for Junts in 2024 now say they would back Aliança—but a majority of those wavering respondents still ranked Junts as their second choice.

    Aliança’s message lands with voters anxious about rapid population growth, crime, and stretched public services. Around 18 percent of its supporters say they would vote for Vox on Nov. 29, according to the CEO. This matters in Madrid, where each seat that Junts loses weakens the leverage that once made it a kingmaker.

    Recent findings suggest that junts is responding to Aliança’s rise by shifting to the right. The party has demanded that Madrid hand Catalonia control over immigration, backed bans on the burqa and niqab in public spaces, and pushed for tougher rules on repeat criminal offenders. The party has also proposed making immigrants wait 10 years after registering as residents before they can apply for subsidized housing, more than three times the current maximum.

    Industry observers note that catalonia elects 48 members of Spain’s national parliament; Junts holds seven of those seats. In return for the party’s support after the 2023 election, the Socialists pushed through an amnesty law covering those involved in the 2017 Catalan independence push, including Puigdemont, who at the time served as Catalonia’s president and fled to Belgium to avoid arrest. The Supreme Court lifted his arrest warrant in October, clearing the way for his return.

    In a recent development, junts has ruled out backing either Sánchez or the PP’s party leader for prime minister, though it has left the door open to supporting a different Socialist candidate. Competing with Aliança for allegiance in Catalonia, it has little room to prop up a left-wing government. With a PP-Vox majority, that might not matter. But if the right-wing vote falls short, Spain’s government could once again hang on a handful of Catalan votes.

    It has been revealed that the CEO expects Junts to win just four or five parliamentary seats in the snap elections, while Vox could more than double its share of Catalonia’s seats—from two seats to five or six. Some of those votes might come from Aliança supporters.

    “From Nov. 29, a dual voter will emerge: someone who votes Aliança in municipal and Catalan elections, and Vox in Spanish ones,” noted Xavier Torrens, a professor of political science at the University of Barcelona.

    Vox and Aliança are opposed when it comes to the question of Catalonia’s independence, but on immigration, they speak the same language.

    Sources indicate that “Many people vote Vox because they reject immigration, feel unsafe, or believe immigrants take a large share of public benefits. Aliança notes the same,” said Xavier Rius, a Catalan journalist and the author of a book on Aliança.

    Berraondo rejected a direct comparison between his party and Vox, insisting that their positions overlap only on immigration and law and order and that Aliança does not share Vox’s opposition to abortion and gay rights.

    Still, Aliança might see a PP-Vox victory as good news for its future. “Imagine you think that if the PP and Vox win the elections in November, they could start the dirty job of changing the immigration rules,” Berraondo mentioned. “Then you can take advantage of it if you are in government in Catalonia in 2028.”.

    This political convergence would once have been unthinkable. The Catalan independence movement defined itself against the Spanish nationalism that Vox represents and long prided itself on being progressive, inclusive, and pro-European. Center-right parties joined the independence push in the 2010s, but Aliança is the first far-right separatist party to gain traction in Catalonia.

    So, how did a far-right party emerge from the movement, and why now? Part of the answer lies in 2017. That October, Catalonia’s pro-independence government held a referendum that Spain’s Constitutional Court had declared illegal. Puigdemont signed a declaration of independence and then days later confirmed that he asked parliament to suspended it. Weeks later, Madrid suspended Catalonia’s autonomy, and the movement’s leaders were jailed or fled abroad.

    For many Junts supporters, the promise that independence was within reach proved hollow. Puigdemont’s about-face and rush to negotiate with Madrid seemed to reveal that the party prioritized its political leverage over independence—a perception later reinforced when Junts backed Sanchez’s government and demanded amnesty for its leaders rather than any move toward independence.

    Orriols, the Aliança leader, has built her appeal on that sense of betrayal, casting the referendum moment as a deception and Puigdemont as a leader who lost his nerve. Voters who have switched allegiance from Junts to Aliança are, on average, around 56 years old, with nearly 89 percent supporting independence, according to the CEO. Their top concerns are immigration and insecurity. These are disappointed separatists—not newcomers to the cause.

    “Part of Junts’s electorate realized that the whole narrative about independence was just fluff, that they weren’t serious about it,” remarked Massimo Maoret, a professor at IESE Business School in Barcelona and a longtime observer of Catalan politics. Aliança, he added, has tapped into that feeling “together with anti-immigrant, and especially anti-Islamic, sentiment.”.

    Further, as the cost of living rises, the concerns over affordable housing that brought down Sánchez’s government have also boosted the far-right party. Aliança “is winning an anti-system, anti-establishment vote, driven by people being fed up with the rising cost of living, the high cost of housing, and the poor functioning of public services such as rail transport,” Torrens mentioned.

    Aliança has drawn a connection between those issues and immigration, from pushing a debate over who counts as Catalan. For decades, the independence movement embraced a slogan popularized by Jordi Pujol, a former Catalan president: “Anyone who lives and works in Catalonia is Catalan.”.

    Aliança takes a different line. “Aliança considers that only some of Catalonia’s inhabitants are Catalan, while the rest are immigrants settled in Catalonia but not Catalan,” Torrens said. Orriols has said that Muslims could not be Catalan because “they don’t integrate with the country’s culture and values.”.

    Recent findings suggest that vox could unseat Pedro Sánchez in snap elections. How do you beat such an unusual party?

    Why Spain’s Sánchez has succeeded while Britain’s Starmer floundered.

    According to recent reports, the question is the extent to which Aliança is shaping the independence movement. Junts has already shifted toward some of Aliança’s positions on immigration—but Jordi Turull, Junts’s secretary-general, has warned that the far right “will do nothing but take us further from our goal of a prosperous and complete Catalan republic.”.

    Recent findings suggest that josep Vila, the president of the Catalan National Assembly, a grassroots pro-independence organization, declined to say whether Aliança belonged to the movement. The group was “not concerned by the diversity of political options,” Vila wrote in an email, as long as they shared a strategy for independence.

    Meanwhile, Aliança’s base is broadening beyond the independence movement. According to the CEO, only 53 percent of its supporters now back independence, down from 62 percent late last year. Taken together, the data suggest a shift in priorities. For disillusioned separatists and newcomers alike, concerns about immigration, security, and the cost of living increasingly outweigh the question of independence.

    Sources indicate that in some ways, Catalonia seems to be following a familiar European script of an emergent far right—this time from within a separatist movement. Torrens makes a distinction between national-populist parties that took decades to break through, such as France’s National Rally, and those that do so within a few years, such as Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni’s Brothers of Italy, Portugal’s Chega, and Vox itself.

    Aliança, he stated, is on the fast track. The party’s first test comes in this week’s snap elections, when its supporters could shape the outcome. The bigger tests come later: municipal elections in May 2027 and the regional election by 2028. For now, Aliança seems to have shifted the Catalan independence movement’s center of gravity, as a movement that prided itself on building a Catalonia for all has absorbed an us-versus-them view of who belongs.

    Industry observers note that the Nov. 29 vote will offer the first signs of how far that shift reaches beyond Catalonia. If Junts loses seats in Madrid, and especially if the PP and Vox win a majority on their own, then Catalan separatists could lose their leverage over Spain’s government for the first time in years. The irony is that some of Aliança’s own supporters might help sweep the nationalists in.
