    Latest Update: Trump’s ‘Unprecedented Intervention’ in Nvidia

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1804 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foreignpolicy

    ⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that prefer to listen?
    • Jensen Huang was reinstated this week as CEO of Nvidia, a semiconductor manufacturer that’s a linchpin of the global artificial intelligence economy.
    • Was Huang’s reinstatement initiated by Silicon Valley or D.C.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that prefer to listen? To hear this entire conversation, and more episodes in the weeks ahead, follow Ones and Tooze wherever you get your podcasts.

    Jensen Huang was reinstated this week as CEO of Nvidia, a semiconductor manufacturer that’s a linchpin of the global artificial intelligence economy. That occurred only after U.S. President Donald Trump personally intervened to persuade Nvidia’s board—despite allegations that Huang’s affair with an alleged Chinese spy, and his efforts to sell Nvidia’s chips to China in contravention of U.S. policy, may have undermined U.S. national security.

    Was Huang’s reinstatement initiated by Silicon Valley or D.C. elites? What levers did Trump use to pressure Nvidia’s board? Does Huang, or Nvidia more generally, qualify as “too major to fail”?

    Jensen Huang was reinstated this week as CEO of Nvidia, a semiconductor manufacturer that’s a linchpin of the global artificial intelligence economy. That occurred only after U.S. President Donald Trump personally intervened to persuade Nvidia’s board—despite allegations that Huang’s affair with an alleged Chinese spy, and his efforts to sell Nvidia’s chips to China in contravention of U.S. policy, may have undermined U.S. national security.

    In a recent development, was Huang’s reinstatement initiated by Silicon Valley or D.C. elites? What levers did Trump use to pressure Nvidia’s board? Does Huang, or Nvidia more generally, qualify as “too big to fail”?

    Sources indicate that those are just a few of the questions that came up in my recent conversation with FP economics columnist Adam Tooze on the podcast we co-host, Ones and Tooze. What follows is an excerpt, edited for length and clarity. For the full conversation, look for Ones and Tooze wherever you get your podcasts. And check out Adam’s Substack newsletter.

    Cameron Abadi: Was Huang’s reinstatement initiated by Silicon Valley tech elites or by D.C. political elites—or an entwinement between the two?

    Adam Tooze: Some reporting suggests that the rally around Huang really began in Silicon Valley itself. So it was a key group of people who were close to him: Uber founder Travis Kalanick, a bunch of venture capitalists like Gavin Baker, who’s been tweeting very effusively about this, Brad Gerstner and Marc Andreessen, who we’ve discussed on the show before. Heavy hitters. Apparently, there’s some Goldman Sachs interest as well. None of those people have really been willing to comment. But there was a rallying around Jensen Huang and the need to bring him back in. I think, basically, it was a combination of their influence plus a sell-off in the market that really prompted Trump to act. The venture capitalists have good connections to [Vice President] J.D. Vance, because he had that little foray in Silicon Valley finance by way of Peter Thiel. And they seem to then have been able to act on figures inside the Trump administration. Jensen Huang is, after all, very well known to Trump. The two have been seen together a lot in public.

    In a recent development, and then there was some last-minute fig leaf-style conversations with the attorney general just to confirm that they’re not actually supporting a figure that is currently under investigation by the American judicial authorities. So apparently the attorney general, Todd Blanche, signed off on this. And that was really then the decisive moment when Trump then intervened with the board, which seems to be a remarkably weak institution. For a firm of Nvidia’s size and significance, its corporate governance is schoolyard. It comes out of the era when it was a scrappy manufacturer of accelerator chips for video games rather than the biggest company in the world and the backstop to AI. So it seems to just be this incredible kind of jury-rigged, duct tape—you know, people refer to duct-tape empire—kind of setup that we’re dealing with here. And truly dramatic in its impact then on the market, though questions are being asked, I think, about how long the rebound can really last given the underlying questions about AI and the broader economy.

    CA: What are the mechanics by which a leader of the U.S. government overrides a corporate board? And are there any precedents for a U.S. president personally intervening in a boardroom decision like this?

    According to recent reports, AT: I don’t think he has very many direct levers, other than his public sway. As corporate America has demonstrated across the board during his second term, no one wants to be on his wrong side. So if he told this weak corporate governance body at Nvidia that, you know, this is the way to go, and there really were no legal objections, at least at the level of espionage, then presumably they felt it was in the shareholders’ best interest to just do as they were told. It’s not entirely without precedent.

    Recent findings suggest that the most recent instance would be the Obama administration’s move against the leadership of General Motors in the spring of 2009 when the federal government did a bailout for General Motors. And they removed Rick Wagoner, who they didn’t feel that they could work with. Then beyond that, you have to go further back in history to the Cold War-era presidencies. So there’s action by the [Franklin] Roosevelt administration against the Ford Motor Company leadership when they were deeply worried during the wartime about the succession of Henry Ford and deaths within the Ford family. There’s Truman intervening in the steel industry in the early 1950s. There’s a moment when Kennedy also intervenes at U.S. Steel in ’62.

    But, you know, the fundamental difference here is that we’re not in a state of war. This is not a matter of urgent national security or of macroeconomic pressure like in the early 1950s during the Korean War. This isn’t the aftermath of the 2008 financial crisis. Nvidia is not on the receiving end of a federal government bailout. You know, the analogies quite rapidly break down and leave one feeling that in some senses, this truly is an unprecedented intervention. This is the most valuable organization in the world at various points. And it just basically doesn’t appear to have any serious corporate governance whatsoever.

    Jensen Huang and the broader AI sector represent an enormous risk for the entire public.

    The return of Nvidia’s Jensen Huang exposes a dangerous gap in corporate oversight.

    CA: The intervention on behalf of Jensen Huang seemed to be motivated by a sense that he was somehow essential, not only to the success of the company, but through the company, to the success of the American economy overall. In what sense could Huang be considered to be “too big to fail”?

    AT: Well, that term comes out of banking. And within the banking sector, since the Dodd-Frank reforms and other global financial stability reforms in the aftermath of 2008, designations as GSIB, so globally systemically significant banks and financial institutions, are formalized and have been formalized. And they do actually have a relatively formal or quantitative definition. I mean, you can look at bank balance sheets and just trace networks of interconnection and risks that arise from those. And there’s a quite serious study of those kinds of risks. And one could do the same for Nvidia. And there has been a great deal of speculation along these lines, or not just speculation, but investigation. And it’s quite clear that the circular financing mechanisms that we’ve also discussed on the show going back awhile now all center on Nvidia. And so questions have been asked about the stability of the Nvidia financing structure.

    It has been revealed that but I think the question was always, should they not be subject to some kind of oversight? Right now, there is no risk of failure, right? In some senses this invocation of failure in the worst-case scenario—you know, she’s a spy and Nvidia is going to fail and therefore, you know, we must do x or y, or not do x or y, or bring him back or shove him out or whatever—the whole discourse is massively exaggerated. I mean, they’re a very successful tech business, which right now is in the middle of a boom in AI, which does have some bubble characteristics. But the financing of this is extended and ramified, but it’s the cloud providers, not necessarily Nvidia, that anyone thought of as being immediately in trouble. And even those are some way away from outright failure. And so this, you know, this language of exigency and this language of crisis, you know, it has a historical root and there are some structural reasons why one might worry about Nvidia, but it doesn’t justify the current action one way or the other. And the fact that the company is as poorly structured as it is such that so much revolves around one man is prima-facie reason for, you know, some serious rethinking and some serious structural governance.

    But that would require market pressure. And you know, the financial markets right now are bonkers. That they would reprice the manufacturer by 30 percent of a trillion dollars on the basis of this kind of news is, in itself, you know, profoundly delegitimizing. So to my mind, like, it’s an absolute disaster of American public discourse, because the allegations appear to be hugely exaggerated, the damage done to the market suggests that the corporate governance is terrible, the reporting by the American media has been shambolic, the president’s intervention is unprecedented and bonkers, and now the markets vindicate the whole thing by raising the value of Nvidia by 30 percent. I mean, it feels like everyone’s kind of lost their minds in some ways. And yet, as someone famously said, whilst the music plays, you dance. Because if you’re not on the Nvidia train, you’re not doing as well as other people. And all of these boosters are saying this is a vindication of the American success story and Jensen Huang is the latest character in that ongoing narrative. It all feels a bit delirious, to be honest.

    Cameron Abadi is a deputy editor at Foreign Policy. X: @CameronAbadi.

    Recent findings suggest that adam Tooze is a columnist at Foreign Policy and a history professor and the director of the European Institute at Columbia University. He is the author of Chartbook, a newsletter on economics, geopolitics, and history. X: @adam_tooze.

    Latest Update: Why deep pockets weren’t enough to save the GOP in 2026: 'Money is not magic'

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1550 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foxnews

    ⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Brendan Glavin, director of insights at the campaign finance research group OpenSecrets, explains why the GOP's cash advantage didn't translate to victories on Election Day.
    • Before polling began to show dire warning signs for the GOP ahead of the midterm elections, some in conservative circles felt they had a not-so-secret weapon that would give them an edge over their Democratic rivals — a massive amount of cash.
    • Across the Republican National Committee, Senate Leadership Fund, Congressional Leadership Fund, National Republican Congressional Committee and the National Republican Senatorial Committee, the GOP brought in roughly $1.7 billion in funds to fuel its ill-fated midterm campaigns.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Brendan Glavin, director of insights at the campaign finance research group OpenSecrets, explains why the GOP's cash advantage didn't translate to victories on Election Day.

    Before polling began to show dire warning signs for the GOP ahead of the midterm elections, some in conservative circles felt they had a not-so-secret weapon that would give them an edge over their Democratic rivals — a massive amount of cash.

    Across the Republican National Committee, Senate Leadership Fund, Congressional Leadership Fund, National Republican Congressional Committee and the National Republican Senatorial Committee, the GOP brought in roughly $1.7 billion in funds to fuel its ill-fated midterm campaigns.

    The five equivalent Democratic committees, meanwhile, raised well over $300 million less than that total but walked away with massive pickups in even traditionally deep red strongholds like Texas, South Carolina, Kansas and Mississippi.

    Experts from across the political spectrum explained this result to Fox News Digital by arguing that the impact of money on politics is less than what many in the public may assume and that massive fundraising hauls can only take a party so far when it faces political headwinds as strong as those weathered by the GOP in the run-up to election night.

    MUSK PICKS HIS FIRST GOP WARRIORS AS A 2026 MONEY SURGE TAKES SHAPE.

    GOP electoral efforts were buoyed by a duo of PACs — President Donald Trump’s MAGA Inc. and Elon Musk’s America PAC. (Getty Images).

    On top of their already significant nine-figure lead, GOP electoral efforts were also buoyed by a duo of PACs — President Donald Trump’s MAGA Inc. and Elon Musk’s America PAC — which themselves collected an additional $665.4 million for Republicans to burn through. Despite such a massive financial edge, the GOP suffered one of its worst midterm performances in history, losing Senate seats even in deep red jurisdictions like South Carolina and Mississippi.

    Still, Capital Research Center President Scott Walter, argues: "Money is not magic.".

    "Democrats should remember that when tempted to curtail political speech with donation limits, and Republicans should remember that when tempted to think more money automatically means more votes," the leader of the right-of-center group told Fox News Digital. "That will be news to those like Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse, D-R.I., who thinks billionaires and ‘dark money’ control the cosmos.".

    Walter pointed out, citing data aggregated by OpenSecrets, that the biggest donor in any given election cycle rarely ends up getting what they want out of the American political system.

    Brendan Glavin, the director of insights at OpenSecrets, a nonprofit dedicated to tracking money in politics, told Fox News Digital that, while money certainly moves the needle in elections, its actual impact can be blunted by a variety of factors — many of which were at play during the recent midterms.

    According to recent reports, AI IS SUPERCHARGING POLITICAL AD WARS. BUT VIRAL DOESN’T MEAN VICTORIOUS.

    Elon Musk presents a $1 million check during an America PAC town hall ahead of the Wisconsin Supreme Court election, in Green Bay, Wisconsin, on March 30, 2025. (Jamie Kelter Davis/Bloomberg via Getty Images).

    "​​Certainly, you know, the money makes a difference," stated Glavin.

    "When both sides are engaging in a sort of arms race, right, and they're both spending almost equivalently, then really the effect is lost," he explained. "If you're somebody [who] sees an ad for one candidate, and then it's immediately followed by an ad for another candidate… essentially, you're not moving the needle.".

    In many of the marquee races of Election Day, such as the Senate races in Texas and Michigan, both parties had enough money to saturate the airwaves with their messaging, potentially creating the environment described by Glavin.

    It has been revealed that "This election was very unique," he told Fox News Digital. "What people probably really didn’t see until afterward is there was this significant headwind and voters were feeling a certain way and more ads were not going to change that.".

    SCHUMER WARNS OF REPUBLICAN ADVANTAGE THAT COULD CHANGE THE BATTLE FOR SENATE CONTROL.

    It has been revealed that "I am inclined to believe that almost every dollar spent by the big SuperPAC funded by Elon Musk was worthless," one expert remarked. (Brandon Bell/Getty Images).

    Glavin, to support his argument, pointed to the fact that self-funding candidates running in elections often fail to make much headway, serving as evidence for the claim that ludicrous amounts of money don’t automatically equate to political success.

    One of the most obvious recent examples is former New York City Mayor Michael Bloomberg, who spent roughly $1.1 billion of his own money on his 2020 presidential campaign. He won only 55 delegates in the Democratic primaries at an approximate cost of $18 million per delegate.

    Academics who spoke to Fox News Digital were divided on the impact money has on elections.

    "Money has diminishing returns," Ray La Raja, a professor of political science at the University of Massachusetts, Amherst, told Fox News Digital. "And in [an] election wave environment where the president and his party is overwhelmingly disliked or distrusted, money can do little to save them.".

    JASON CHAFFETZ: FIVE TIMELESS POLITICAL LESSONS THAT GOT LOST IN 2026.

    Industry observers note that michael Bloomberg discusses his presidential run on Nov. 25, 2019, in Norfolk, Virginia. (Drew Angerer/Getty Images).

    John Sides, a political science professor at Vanderbilt University, meanwhile, pointed Fox News Digital to a 2022 study he and two other academics conducted studying the impact of television advertising on election outcomes.

    According to their study, there is a relatively direct relationship between ad spending and voter share and, while there is a degree of diminishing returns in elections with very high spending, there is still a marginal impact.

    Joe Arlinghaus, a Texas-based conservative political strategist, told Fox News Digital that how money is spent matters more than how much of it is spent, an assertion he mentioned could explain why the GOP did so poorly despite its hefty cash advantage.

    Industry observers note that "Most people understand that newly introduced technologies get better and better and better as time goes on," he stated. "Bugs get worked out. Inferior practitioners get pushed aside. Trial and error leads to better and better practices. This is what has been happening in the Democratic election world.".

    He noted that Republicans have failed to keep up on that front.

    "I am inclined to believe that almost every dollar spent by the massive SuperPAC funded by Elon Musk was worthless," Arlinghaus added.

    Glavin shared that perspective, noting how "Musk just recently commented about how he may be regretting a little bit all the money he spent.".

    "It's hard to tell how serious he is about that and whether or not he'll just come back again for the next election," he added, speculating that the massive flood of money seemingly doing very little for the GOP on Election Day could cause some megadonors to reconsider their future giving.

    THE SOROS POLITICAL MACHINE IS PUTTING MILLIONS TO WORK BEFORE ELECTION DAY — AND ZEROING IN ON KEY RACES.

    Industry observers note that democratic National Committee chair Ken Martin addresses party members at the DNC's summer meeting, on Aug. 25, 2025, in Minneapolis, Minnesota. (Paul Steinhauser - Fox News).

    In a recent development, one source familiar with Republican politics told Fox News Digital that "advertisements pay for mortgages in Great Falls," a reference to claims that political consultants spend money in ways that make them wealthier, not necessarily in ways that help candidates win. Great Falls is a wealthy suburb of Washington, D.C.

    According to recent reports, while Republicans enjoyed an overall fundraising advantage, largely driven by wealthy large-dollar donors, individual Democratic candidates in high-priority races generally raised more money than their Republican rivals, as was the case in Georgia, Michigan and Texas’s Senate elections, among other contests. Some say this should have been an early warning sign for the GOP that grassroots support was wavering, though others are skeptical of such an assertion.

    Colin Seeberger, the chief strategy officer at the Center for American Progress Action Fund, a liberal advocacy group, told Fox News Digital that the fundraising advantages enjoyed by individual Democrats were a "reflection of voters' enthusiasm for those individual campaigns.".

    He also stated voters had an "overwhelming frustration with the direction of the country and how the president and majorities in Congress … were disconnected from what voters said that they wanted [from] the people of their government.".

    BLUE WAVE NEARLY SWALLOWED SOME OF AMERICA'S REDDEST STATES AS ELECTION DATA EXPOSES GOP'S CLOSE CALLS.

    The massive flood of money seemingly doing very little for the GOP on Election Day could cause some megadonors to reconsider their future giving, one expert remarked. (Brendan Smialowski/AFP via Getty Images).

    "I'm not sure that the party that raises more definitively has an enthusiasm advantage," Sides, the Vanderbilt professor, remarked, pointing to past elections where Democrats have secured more donations than the GOP but lost anyway.

    CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP.

    Seeberger echoed Arlinghaus’ claim that Republicans may have squandered some of their financial advantage by making poor spending decisions, saying, "When you're spending the majority of those sums to talk about issues that register low on the rankings of what voters say are their priorities, there's going to be limited returns on the impact.".

    #225859. Tech Report: The Fantasy of a Turkish Middle East

    📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2277 w)

    Tech Report: The Fantasy of a Turkish Middle East

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2277 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foreignaffairs

    ⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • MELIHA BENLI ALTUNISIK is Professor of International Relations at Middle East Technical University.
    • Since Hamas’s October 7, 2023, attack on Israel, the future of the Middle East has been fiercely contested.
    • In a recent development, turkey, like every major power in the Middle East, has tried to fill the vacuum.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    MELIHA BENLI ALTUNISIK is Professor of International Relations at Middle East Technical University.

    Ankara’s Risky Bid to Impose Regional Order.

    Since Hamas’s October 7, 2023, attack on Israel, the future of the Middle East has been fiercely contested. The previous Gulf-centered order had Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates (UAE) trying to stabilize and shape the region using economic statecraft and the normalization of relations with former foes in Iran, Israel, Turkey, and Syria. Three years of war in Gaza, and more recently in Iran and the Gulf, have severely disrupted that order-building project and generated a deep sense of uncertainty about what comes next.

    In a recent development, turkey, like every major power in the Middle East, has tried to fill the vacuum. Before 2023, Ankara’s influence had been in decline; after years of diplomatic isolation following the Arab uprisings, it had just begun repairing its ties with major regional actors. But in the past few years, Turkey has earned American backing for its policies in Syria and its regional diplomacy, and it has made an effort to secure the home front by pursuing a peace process with the Kurdistan Workers’ Party (PKK), a militant group that has fought a decades-long insurgency against the Turkish state. Most recently, in August, Pakistan, Saudi Arabia, and Turkey signed the Mecca Defense Alliance, a collective security agreement that institutionalizes Turkey’s regional positioning and pulls the country directly into Saudi Arabia’s war with the Houthis.

    Turkey’s post–October 7 strategy has restored the country’s position as a regional heavyweight. But it is not capable of meeting its larger objective: establishing order on its own terms. Turkey, like the region’s other aspiring leaders, lacks the power to impose a new security framework on its own. Its nascent efforts to build one, such as the new Mecca pact, merely make countries outside the bloc feel unsafe, feeding instability. Turkey’s most ambitious plays for regional leadership are therefore likely to prove ineffective or even counterproductive. As long as the Middle East’s highly militarized, zero-sum security dynamics remain, Ankara would be better off concentrating on interests closer to home that it has the power to protect.

    This is not the first time that Turkey has tried to shape the broader Middle Eastern order. Ankara saw the Arab uprisings in the early 2010s as a historic window of opportunity. The ruling Justice and Development Party (AKP) described the political transformation sweeping the region as “the people’s coming to power,” and the Turkish government expected that eventual elections in the Arab countries rocked by protest would bring into office parties aligned with the Muslim Brotherhood, which was ideologically sympathetic and had practical links to the AKP. The emergence of friendly governments, the thinking went, would increase Turkey’s influence in the region.

    According to recent reports, yet these hopes soon receded. Egypt’s Muslim Brotherhood–affiliated president, Mohamed Morsi, was overthrown in 2013, and Turkey’s bet on the opposition movement in Syria failed as Bashar al-Assad clung to power. Turkey was left isolated. A rival axis composed of Egypt, Saudi Arabia, and the UAE objected to Turkey’s Muslim Brotherhood ties and sought to limit Ankara’s influence. This group contested Turkey’s positions across the Middle East, North Africa, the eastern Mediterranean, and the Horn of Africa, effectively fighting proxy battles with Turkey in conflicts in Libya, Somalia, and Syria.

    It has been revealed that then, the attacks on October 7, 2023, ushered in another period of upheaval. Some changes since have played in Turkey’s favor. Chief among them is the collapse of the Assad regime in Syria in December 2024 at the hands of opposition groups led by Hayat Tahrir al-Sham. Turkey had arguably invested more than any other country in pursuit of regime change in Damascus; it assisted opposition groups for years. Yet as the years went by, that objective seemed increasingly out of reach. The region’s other major powers made their peace with the regime’s survival, and even Ankara began considering rapprochement with Assad to avoid being left out in the cold. Assad’s fall changed Turkey’s fortunes overnight, handing it a level of influence in Syria it had not held in more than a decade.

    Industry observers note that other developments proved more dangerous for Ankara. Israel’s foreign policy became more assertive and revisionist after October 7, and its expansive security objectives began to clash with Turkey’s own. Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan’s sharp criticism of Israeli policies in Gaza strained the relationship, and it deteriorated further when Turkey expanded its foothold in post-Assad Syria and Israel came to view Ankara’s military presence there as a direct threat. As Israel continues to strike sites in Syria—attacks Ankara has condemned—the risk of escalation is only growing. A miscalculation on either side could lead to a direct clash between Israeli and Turkish forces.

    The U.S.-Israeli war with Iran, meanwhile, has cut both ways for Turkey. While Tehran’s attention has been focused elsewhere, Ankara has welcomed Iran’s retreat from Syria and the chance to push back against its remaining influence in Iraq. Turkey also has no interest in seeing a nuclear-armed Iran upend the regional balance of power. Yet the prospect of chaos across Turkey’s eastern border, should the Iranian regime fall, has bred real anxiety in Ankara, as has the possibility that Iran could become emboldened if the regime emerges from the war intact.

    Recent findings suggest that in this complex environment, Ankara has pursued a three-pronged strategy to protect its security interests and, it hopes, capitalize on opportunities the upheaval has created. Since U.S. President Donald Trump’s return to power, Erdogan has drawn Turkey closer to the United States and tried to use his relationship with Washington to advance Ankara’s regional policies. Turkey has also pressed ahead with regional normalization, building on efforts to repair ties with Saudi Arabia, Egypt, and other key Arab countries in the early 2020s, with the aim to forge a broader regional bloc. And, domestically, Ankara launched the “Turkey Without Terror” process, an attempt to resolve the conflict with the PKK inside and outside Turkey, which Turkey’s adversaries have long exploited by arming Kurdish groups or backing them politically.

    Industry observers note that some of Ankara’s policies have borne fruit. Consider, for instance, the outreach to Washington. Erdogan’s close relations with Trump helped bring the United States on board with Turkey’s expanded role in Syria. Turkey was one of the four countries Washington brought in to help negotiate the U.S.-proposed October 2025 cease-fire agreement between Israel and Hamas, and as a result, Trump offered and Erdogan accepted a seat on the U.S. president’s so-called Board of Peace for Gaza’s reconstruction. Turkey has played an active part mediating between the United States and Iran during the latest war. And Trump publicly endorsed the Mecca Defense Alliance, calling it “substantial, bold, and notable.” All of this points to a recognition in Washington of Turkey’s regional importance, the U.S. administration’s willingness to support some of Ankara’s priorities, and Turkey’s determination to elevate its own position.

    Yet there are undeniable limits to Turkey’s quest for influence. At a February 2026 Board of Peace summit, for instance, Turkey was excluded from participating in a planned international troop deployment and police training in Gaza—a sign that warming relations with Washington were not enough to override Israeli objections to having a Turkish military footprint in the Palestinian territory. In Syria, similarly, the support Turkey has secured from the Trump administration has not stopped Israel from launching military strikes at Syrian targets near Turkish positions. Simply put, Turkey has not been able to use its relationship with the Trump administration to overcome the limit Israeli opposition places on the scope of Turkey’s regional role.

    Recent findings suggest that turkey’s regional normalization efforts have yielded mixed results, too. Restoring diplomatic ties with significant players such as Saudi Arabia is in Turkey’s interest, to be sure. But the alliances Ankara is entering with these countries risk making Turkey and the region less secure, not more. The Mecca pact with Pakistan and Saudi Arabia could end up hardening rival blocs and elevating regional tensions. Turkey insists that the alliance is directed against no country in particular and has suggested that Egypt, Syria, or even Iran could eventually join. But in the meantime, Iran, Israel, and the Houthis could see it as a threat and try to test or weaken its members’ commitment.

    Furthermore, the pact could pull Turkey into other countries’ wars. That possibility is already on the table now that the Turkish parliament has ratified the agreement and the Houthis are escalating their attacks on Saudi Arabia. The Turkish government has insisted that any military support it provided would be confined to deterrence, intelligence sharing, and defense-industrial cooperation. Yet Saudi Arabia is now seeking Pakistan’s and Turkey’s help with air defense and territorial protection, and the three states have agreed to prepare forces for rapid deployment. Sending Turkish troops to Saudi Arabia would still require separate parliamentary approval. If parliament allowed it, even a limited deployment would risk drawing Turkey into a wider regional conflict.

    It has been revealed that some kind of regional security framework is necessary. The problem is that no country in the region, including Turkey, has the power to impose a security order on the rest, so whenever someone tries, other countries feel threatened. An informal cooperation framework that is open to all countries in the region—and that asks its members to commit to nonaggression instead of making mutual-defense pledges—might work better. But the assembly and functioning of such a coalition require trust that governments in the region do not have. Breaking the impasse would likely require the United States to play a more constructive role than it has in recent years—not simply endorsing whatever regional arrangement emerges, as Trump did with the Mecca pact, or pressuring countries to normalize relations with Israel without expecting Israel to change its policies in return, as Trump has also done. Instead, Washington, perhaps with the help of Beijing, would need to compel regional rivals such as Iran and Saudi Arabia to take confidence-building measures that would make an inclusive security framework viable in the long run. Without this external push, the narrower security blocs that emerge in the region will only lead to further instability.

    Ankara’s strongest cards lie closer to home. The Kurdish peace process has moved slowly since February 2025, when Abdullah Ocalan, the imprisoned leader of the PKK, called on the militant group to disarm. But it has yielded tangible progress. In May 2025, the PKK announced that it would dissolve. In Syria, Kurdish forces are being integrated into the Syrian army, and Mazloum Abdi, the commander of the People’s Defense Units, a Kurdish armed group affiliated with the PKK, was appointed as a presidential adviser in August. Syria’s postconflict transition remains fragile, and the reconciliation between Damascus and Kurdish militants in the northeast may owe as much to American pressure as it does to Turkey’s domestic efforts to make peace with the PKK. But for Turkey, the eventual integration of Syrian Kurdish forces into the Syrian state removes the risk Ankara saw in having an autonomous, armed Kurdish entity on its southern border. And, given the close security and economic ties Ankara has developed with Damascus, as well as the political and legal steps the government can take at home to complete the disbanding of the PKK and to deepen democratic reforms, Turkey has the ability to keep these encouraging developments on track.

    In a recent development, turkey’s regional policies are most successful when the country plays to its strengths—not when it is trying to throw its weight around the region. In the first decade of the twenty-first century, Ankara built real influence by mediating between Syria and Israel and between Palestinian factions, expanding its economic engagement in the Levant, and proposing projects to connect the region’s energy and transportation infrastructure. Military power, meanwhile, has proved most effective when applied for specific purposes, such as to secure the border with Syria. This combination is Turkey’s winning formula: diplomacy and economic outreach to extend its influence, and limited force to protect its core interests. Broad, open-ended commitments, by contrast, risk drawing Turkey into regional conflicts without making it safer.

    In a recent development, today, sticking to a more effective formula does not mean retreating from regional politics. It means setting priorities and planning long-term. Consolidating the Kurdish peace process, keeping Washington invested in Syria’s stabilization, managing the risk of confrontation with Israel in Syria, and maintaining constructive relations with the Kurdistan Regional Government in northern Iraq and the Iraqi government in Baghdad are key to keeping Turkey’s borders secure and are within Turkey’s ability to achieve. Ankara can continue to use its experience in mediation when opportunities to advance peace processes present themselves. It can also promote economic connectivity, both by expanding trade ties and by supporting regional infrastructure projects such as the Iraq-Europe Development Road and a proposed pipeline network connecting the Gulf to Jordan, Syria, and Turkey. It need not shy away from security cooperation with the Gulf, either, if it can engage without making formal commitments. Yet in all these endeavors, Ankara should remember that it has the most clout when it stays out of the region’s conflicts.

    According to recent reports, the Middle East’s escalating wars and rival blocs could make a narrower Turkish security policy more difficult to sustain today than it was in the past. Defending Ankara’s interests and playing a constructive role in a volatile neighborhood will require a careful balance. The best way Turkey can contribute to regional stability may be to avoid trying to do too much.

    Evidence sought by government spanned decades in Omar probe, new records show

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., attends a news conference with members of the Congressional Progressive Caucus in the Capitol in January.
    • A federal judge Monday released more than 160 pages related to the search of Rep.
    • District Court for the District of Columbia ordered the documents unsealed Monday as part of a lawsuit brought by news organizations and an advocacy group seeking to unseal the records related to the search.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., attends a news conference with members of the Congressional Progressive Caucus in the Capitol in January. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

    A federal judge Monday released more than 160 pages related to the search of Rep. Ilhan Omar’s home last month, detailing a week-long court effort from the federal government to secure the documents.

    Judge James Boasberg for the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia ordered the documents unsealed Monday as part of a lawsuit brought by news organizations and an advocacy group seeking to unseal the records related to the search.

    The records unsealed Monday show the government first sought a search warrant in the case on Oct. 2, 10 days before the Trump administration eventually secured the warrant. Dozens of the 169 pages released Monday were redacted entirely. Others contained significant redactions which made much of them unreadable.

    According to recent reports, the records show that the presiding judge in the case, U.S. Magistrate Judge Matthew J. Sharbaugh, questioned the government about how it would handle the “Speech or Debate implications” of the search.

    The Speech or Debate Clause is a provision of the Constitution which gives sitting members of Congress immunity from being charged or even having to testify about anything dealing with “speech or debate” in Congress.

    The unsealed document says the government does not think the investigation touches on Omar’s work as a member of Congress at all, and engaged in a weeklong back-and-forth with Sharbaugh about what, if any, alterations to make to the search warrant.

    “The United States believes that ILHAN has committed [REDACTED] crimes over decades — beginning long before she was ever in Congress,” one government motion included in the documents notes.

    According to recent reports, eventually, Sharbaugh granted the search warrant on Oct. 9, seeking records, electronics and a cell phone related to the undisclosed charges. But the warrant also contained an order allowing Omar to assert her speech or debate immunity before the government could search what it seized in the warrant, according to the documents disclosed Monday.

    “But the concern that remains and the issue this Court independently raised with the government after its initial review of the warrant application is whether the search of a sitting Member of Congress’ residence implicates the Speech or Debate Clause. The government says no. This Court sees it differently,” Sharbaugh says in an Oct. 9 order.

    The documents also noted that the government notified the office of the House Counsel, which mentioned there could be no Speech or Debate protection for a member’s private residence.

    According to recent reports, the government’s filings in the case suggested that they are looking for evidence of crimes that may have occurred as early as 1980, around the time Omar was born. The documents unsealed Monday do not include the nature of the crimes the government is investigating.

    Separately Monday,  the DOJ opposed releasing information from a second suit filed by Omar seeking return of items taken by agents during the search without further briefing.

    “Ultimately, if the Press Applicants want access to the Separate Docket, the Court should require them to file papers showing why they’re entitled to it,” the filing says.

    According to recent reports, the administration executed the search warrant last month ahead of the elections, drawing criticism from Democrats and outside experts that the decision was made for political reasons. Since the search, administration officials have said there is a criminal investigation into Omar, tied to her immigration into the United States as a child.

    After ruling last week that some records could be unsealed, Boasberg said the press organizations and advocacy group could still seek to unseal more records.

    De Gaulle and the Art of European Defiance

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2618 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foreignpolicy

    ⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read

    • According to recent reports, with year-end best-of lists about to arrive, one strong contender for film of the year might seem unlikely at first: a five-hour, two-part, largely French-language biopic of French general and statesman Charles de Gaulle that only recently reached U.S.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Get audio access with any FP subscription.

    Recent findings suggest that with year-end best-of lists about to arrive, one strong contender for film of the year might seem unlikely at first: a five-hour, two-part, largely French-language biopic of French general and statesman Charles de Gaulle that only recently reached U.S. screens. Directed by Antonin Baudry and starring a strikingly de Gaulle-like Simon Abkarian, this French blockbuster comes with an almost-American budget of 74 million euros, one of the largest in the history of francophone cinema. Perhaps unsurprisingly given its subject, it became the hit of the French summer, offering audiences a nostalgic vision of national greatness at a moment of paralysis and division.

    According to recent reports, more surprisingly, the de Gaulle diptych has won praise outside of France as well, helped by the fact that it works superbly as both action and entertainment. Epic in scale, beautifully shot, both wryly amusing and often touching, its twin installments pass far more swiftly than their daunting runtime might suggest. There are clear contemporary echoes, too, in de Gaulle’s personal struggles and story of dogged European defiance. Indeed, it is not hard to see why viewers in France and elsewhere have warmed to this tale of an embattled European leader fighting to re-build sovereignty in the face of pressure from the United States as the moorings of a crumbling old order give way to something frightening and new.

    According to recent reports, with year-end best-of lists about to arrive, one strong contender for film of the year might seem unlikely at first: a five-hour, two-part, largely French-language biopic of French general and statesman Charles de Gaulle that only recently reached U.S. screens. Directed by Antonin Baudry and starring a strikingly de Gaulle-like Simon Abkarian, this French blockbuster comes with an almost-American budget of 74 million euros, one of the largest in the history of francophone cinema. Perhaps unsurprisingly given its subject, it became the hit of the French summer, offering audiences a nostalgic vision of national greatness at a moment of paralysis and division.

    It has been revealed that more surprisingly, the de Gaulle diptych has won praise outside of France as well, helped by the fact that it works superbly as both action and entertainment. Epic in scale, beautifully shot, both wryly amusing and often touching, its twin installments pass far more quickly than their daunting runtime might suggest. There are clear contemporary echoes, too, in de Gaulle’s personal struggles and story of dogged European defiance. Indeed, it is not hard to see why viewers in France and elsewhere have warmed to this tale of an embattled European leader fighting to re-build sovereignty in the face of pressure from the United States as the moorings of a crumbling old order give way to something frightening and fresh.

    Industry observers note that each of the film’s two parts is just over two and a half hours long. The first, De Gaulle: Résistance (158 minutes; released in France as L’Age de fer), opens with the humiliation of the French collapse in June 1940. Refusing to accept the armistice, de Gaulle flees to England in a tiny plane. From there, he presses British Prime Minister Winston Churchill for greater support and builds a shaky government-in-exile from scratch, operating from a tiny office in central London.

    According to recent reports, the second, De Gaulle: Liberté (159 minutes; J’écris ton nom in France), covers 1943 to the end of 1944, following both the actions of the Resistance and de Gaulle’s power struggles with rival claimants to French leadership, before moving on to D-Day and the liberation of Paris. The epic closes movingly on Armistice Day, when Churchill visits the freed capital as de Gaulle’s guest.

    For audiences outside France, some of this will be familiar, from de Gaulle’s defiant broadcasts on the BBC to his haughty and stubborn personal affect. Undeniably imperious and quite unable to forget a slight, Abkarian’s de Gaulle is both a model of determination in the face adversity and, to the Allied leaders who bankrolled him, a quintessentially French pain in the ass.

    A still from De Gaulle: Résistance.Pathe Films.

    Recent findings suggest that other episodes are less well known in the English-speaking world, however, even as they remain central to France’s own story of the war, from the British destruction of the French fleet at Mers-el-Kébir in July 1940 (to keep its warships out of German hands) to the epic battle at Bir Hakeim in mid-1942. Perhaps now more familiar to tourists as the name of a Paris metro station, Bir Hakeim saw 3,700 Free French soldiers and their African colonial troops hold an isolated desert fort in Libya against German Gen. Erwin Rommel’s Afrika Korps for more than two weeks. Fighting against overwhelming odds, their bravery allowed Britain’s Eighth Army to fall back to El Alamein and regroup, marking an eventual turning point in the wider war. Providing the first film with a dramatic 15-minute denouement, the battle proved that de Gaulle’s ragtag movement could fight as a real army, provided a much-needed fillip to Free French morale, and strengthened the general’s position as a legitimate and potentially successful French leader.

    Although this is very much a big-budget war movie, much of its power lies, paradoxically, in its intimate portrayal of the quiet complexities of leadership. In the public mind, de Gaulle can often come across as a cartoonish figure, all stubborn resolve, frosty self-regard, and Gallic hauteur. Abkarian’s ramrod-stiff performance is magnetic and provides plenty of evidence of this. But it also offers something more human, portraying with affection de Gaulle’s strange mix of grandeur and loneliness. The first film dwells in particular on his isolation and frequent despair. Arriving in London as a defeated tank division commander and former undersecretary of war, de Gaulle has no army, no money, barely any staff, and little claim to legitimate leadership. His situation is often tragi-comic, as when he tries unsuccessfully to win over members of the French expatriate community at a drinks party, or when he attempts to address a British audience in a packed theater, only to walk off ashamed without saying a word. In one especially memorable scene, he weeps alone in the bath of his small, dingy flat. In many others he is disconsolate, close to losing hope, and tempted to give up.

    This most Gallic of films is in fact based on an equally epic book by a British academic: A Certain Idea of France, Julian Jackson’s 900-page biography, published in 2018. Reviewing it in the New Yorker, Adam Gopnik dwelt on the crippling weakness de Gaulle faced in 1940, and how he ultimately managed to think his way out of it via a mixture of imagination, self-belief, and obstinacy. De Gaulle depended “more on theatrical élan than did pretty much any other public man of his century,” as Gopnik put it. “No one has ever played a weaker hand more compellingly. His life was one long brilliant bluff.”.

    Recent findings suggest that it is this vulnerability, rather than the more familiar image of pigheaded strength, that likely appealed to French audiences, prompting a reassessment of his traditionally unbending image and the controversial Gaullist legacy it inspired. For all that, the film is also huge fun. Its action sequences are slickly executed and, unusually for a European production, come with plenty of exuberant, Hollywood-style explosions. But it works as entertainment above all because at its center is the double act of de Gaulle and Churchill, played by Simon Russell Beale, easily the best of the many actors who have attempted the role.

    A still from De Gaulle: Liberté.Pathe Films.

    Recent findings suggest that the two men are endlessly frustrated by one another and an obvious study in contrasts: one reserved, austere, and abstemious, the other impulsive, theatrical, and alcoholic. Yet each recognizes in the other a wartime leader fighting to save his nation against massive odds, creating a certain fondness and clear mutual regard. Among their many fine scenes is a comic row involving translation. De Gaulle speaks poor English; Churchill’s French is comical but serviceable. As they argue, both men hear their respective interpreters diplomatically softening their words. Each leader throws his man out of the room in turn, preferring to fight out their differences in broken language. The grudging but sincere warmth between the two both humanizes the complexities of wartime leadership and provides the film’s emotional heart.

    Recent findings suggest that some critics have accused director Baudry of playing fast and loose with history, mixing invented characters with historical leaders, among other sins against accuracy. Jackson, who acted as a consultant on the production, has written warmly in its defense: “My pavlovian historical pedantry – ‘no that is wrong, it didn’t happen like that’, ‘you have these events in the wrong order’, etc – was quickly slapped down with the reminder that this was a film not a documentary.”.

    In a recent development, the film’s very French portrayal of the United States, with a Machiavellian President Franklin D. Roosevelt cast as a chief villain, is one obvious area of potential historical dispute. But it also provides the film with its drama. Curiously, Adolf Hitler is never seen and barely even mentioned, while few German soldiers even appear. Instead, the real antagonist is Roosevelt’s Washington, and the U.S. president’s mounting frustration with an upstart French exile who contributes little manpower to the war effort yet irritatingly demands to be treated as an equal and a great power. In this sense it has something in common with zombie movies, where the greatest danger often comes less from the outside menace and more from potential betrayal within the group of humans struggling to survive.

    A still from De Gaulle: Liberté.Pathe Films.

    In Roosevelt’s eyes, France had forfeited any claim to great-power status, while de Gaulle himself was merely an arrogant annoyance and obstacle to his plans. This broader threat to French survival is embodied in a plan to create the Allied Military Government of Occupied Territories (AMGOT), which the film presents as a U.S. scheme to permanently dismantle and divide the country. In this vision, a liberated France would be run by U.S. and British administrators, much as occupied Germany later was. That AMGOT was never the fully formed plan for France the film suggests is almost beside the point. In one memorable scene, Churchill is shown a future map of Europe in which France has vanished, carved up into a “Fresh Wallonia” and other invented entities. In an act of covert friendship, he leaks it to de Gaulle; a rare act of British solidarity with the French over the Americans.

    Industry observers note that as exaggerated as the film’s version of the AMGOT proposal may be—and Jackson concedes it is somewhat overplayed—the question of how to deal with a powerful United States runs throughout the film, giving it its most obvious modern resonance. In part this reflects a traditional and enduring Franco-British divide, with France seeking self-sufficiency and sovereignty while Britain prefers proximity and access to Washington.

    To distract from runaway protests, the French president is making a show of independence on the world stage.

    The film’s ideas have poisoned military thinking for centuries.

    On the eve of D-Day in June 1944, for instance, de Gaulle’s demands over his forces’ role in the coming liberation of France prompt another giant bust-up with Churchill, and one especially memorable exchange, recounted in de Gaulle’s own highly readable memoirs. “”Every time we have to choose between Europe and the open seas, we shall always choose the open seas,”” he recalls Churchill declaring. “”Every time I have to choose between you and Roosevelt, I shall always choose Roosevelt.”” From Churchill’s point of view, this was entirely sensible; Britain had no obvious alternative to a superpower’s existential support, and it would have been foolish to side with an exile liberation army possessing no resources of its own. Nonetheless, it was a line de Gaulle would go on to quote throughout his life: an emblem of British perfidy and deference to Washington.

    Late in the second film, in a scene set in November 1944, de Gaulle sounds out Churchill on a deeper Anglo-French alliance. Churchill declines because Britain must stay close to Washington. The portrayal feels both enduring but also clearly modern, depicting two exhausted European powers facing common adversity but still quite unable to choose to be full partners with one another.

    Recent findings suggest that more than anything, the film brings to mind the modern predicament of embattled and weakened middle powers, trying to find their way in a world dominated by far larger and more chaotic forces. During World War II, Britain and France both still thought of themselves as great powers—in de Gaulle’s case almost absurdly so, given his limited circumstances. Yet both clearly lived at the mercy of others, be they Hitler’s marauding armies or the caprice of an indispensable but overbearing U.S. ally.

    Today European nations face a version of the same bind, struggling to rebuild sovereignty in a world dominated by superpowers increasingly willing to coerce and threaten them. The message of the film is clearly a comfortable one for French audiences: France was right all along about untrustworthy Americans, and about the need for strength and independence rather than reliance on potentially unreliable U.S.-led institutions like NATO. Nonetheless, here de Gaulle offers modern Europeans clear lessons on how to counteract weakness, via a mixture of political imagination, risk-taking, and—above all—a willingness to stand up to U.S. power from time to time.

    What most people understand as “Gaullist” policies are increasingly common far beyond France as our geopolitical order frays, not least intrusive industrial policies aimed at technological self-sufficiency. Ben Judah, a British author and former political advisor, has gone further, proposing a new agenda of “Anglo-Gaullism” inspired by the French leader’s mixture of interventionism and political élan. “[T]he genius of de Gaulle was to re-enchant through storytelling a nation that had utterly lost confidence in itself,” he writes. Europe could clearly use a little more of that Gaullist enchantment today.

    According to recent reports, it is almost a cliche to contrast the giants of World War II with the slighter figures of our own generation. Yet watching de Gaulle’s struggles, it is hard not to think of the supplication of modern leaders like Mark Rutte, NATO’s secretary-general, whose approach to U.S. President Donald Trump was memorably described by Susan Glasser of the New Yorker as “strategic self-abasement.” De Gaulle is often fairly criticized for a grandiose vision of French leadership that far outstripped France’s actual power, leading to unhelpful delusions of national grandeur fed by the vision of its grandest of leaders. Nonetheless, de Gaulle’s obdurate refusal to accept decline—and his determination that France should stand, as he put it, as a nation “in the front rank”—should serve as an inspiration to Europe’s leaders today. This, too, is the lesson of the two excellent films that bear his name: to hold a vision of national power and to will it obstinately into existence, even if only by learning how to play a bad hand well.

    James Crabtree is a columnist at Foreign Policy, a distinguished visiting fellow at the European Council on Foreign Relations, and the author of The Perimeter: America's Struggle for Primacy in the Pacific (forthcoming in January) and The Billionaire Raj: A Journey Through India’s Fresh Gilded Age. X: @jamescrabtree.

    According to recent reports, one X user noted how Trump "just told the DOJ to fast-track the death penalty for child killers and predators. [Gavin Newsom], on the other hand, is proudly defending his decision to spare 548 of the worst of the worst.

    "Tells you everything you need to know.".

    In a recent development, another user posted, "Are you f---ing kidding me? His arrogance and hypocrisy are immeasurable.".

    "After pardoning everyone on death row in California, Newsom calls for reform of the president’s pardon powers," another wrote on X. "You can’t make this stuff up.".

    Trump called out Newsom at the DOJ alongside Attorney General Todd Blanche, FBI Director Kash Patel and family members of victims of the 548 death row inmates. He referred to the inmates as "the most evil monsters on the face of the Earth," and accused Newsom of stealing closure for the victims' families.

    Some of the crimes committed by inmates who will no longer face the death sentence include slaughtering entire families, torturing and murdering children and killing police officers.

    In Newsom’s video, he defended his decision to commute the death sentences to life without parole, accusing Trump of abusing his pardon powers.

    In a recent development, "Donald Trump doesn’t oppose mercy. He sells it," Newsom remarked in the video. "If you’re poor, Black or Brown, you get the needle. If you’re rich and know Donald Trump, you get a pardon and a personal phone call.".

    SLAIN FIREFIGHTER'S MOTHER PLEADS WITH TRUMP TO INTERVENE AFTER NEWSOM STOPS KILLER'S DEATH SENTENCE.

    It has been revealed that trump issued 220 total pardons in his second term as president and 143 during his first term. While Trump has granted pardons to wealthy individuals and political allies, he has also pardoned Black Americans, most notably Alice Marie Johnson, who was serving a life sentence for drug trafficking and money laundering offenses before he commuted her sentence in 2018 and pardoned her in 2020.

    Trump has been criticized for his comments Tuesday that a pardon for Jensen Huang was "always an option" ahead of the Nvidia CEO's scheduled appearances before Congress next week following his re-instatement after claims he had an affair with a suspected Chinese spy.

    "I don't think he needs a pardon at all," Vice President JD Vance told reporters Wednesday when asked about the potential.

    Part of the blowback against Newsom also stems from his decision to override California voters' rejection to abolish the death penalty, defending his clemency authority as an example of "when law as applied cannot be squared with justice.".

    It has been revealed that "And the Governor of CA should not be able to sell out crime victims and prosecutors by overriding juries, judges and the WILL of CA voters," a former Sacramento District Attorney posted to X. "Worst Governor in history.".

    Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier stated Monday he led 14 attorneys general in condemning Newsom’s plan, arguing Newsom had overridden juries, courts and California voters.

    Recent findings suggest that some critics have speculated Newsom's move to revoke California inmates death sentences is a tactic gearing up for his bid as the Democratic nominee for the 2028 presidential election. He is seen as one of the top candidates for the party.

    JAMES CARVILLE WARNS GAVIN NEWSOM FACES CALIFORNIA BAGGAGE IN POTENTIAL 2028 RUN.

    Industry observers note that gov. Gavin Newsom speaks March 26, 2025, in Los Angeles. (Frazer Harrison/WireImage).

    It has been revealed that "You should think twice about this decision," a user stated. "You may personally end up needing a Presidential pardon one day.".

    A coalition of California prosecutors and victims’ relatives asked the state Supreme Court last week to halt Newsom’s blueprint, arguing that he failed to give families a chance to be heard before pursuing the commutations. Newsom asked the justices to act before his term ends in January.

    California voters rejected measures to abolish the death penalty in 2012 and 2016. The state last carried out an execution in 2006, and Newsom imposed a moratorium shortly after taking office in 2019.

    #225854. Is China Misreading the Moment?

    📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 16m • 📚 Deep Dive (3252 w)
