    Is China Misreading the Moment?

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 16 min read (3252 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foreignaffairs

    ⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that RUSH DOSHI is an Assistant Professor at Georgetown University and Director of the China Strategy Initiative at the Council on Foreign Relations.
    • Beijing’s Overreach Threatens the Détente With America.
    • President Donald Trump lands in Shenzhen later this week for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit, he will sit down with Chinese leader Xi Jinping for the fourth time amid an unexpected détente between Washington and Beijing.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that RUSH DOSHI is an Assistant Professor at Georgetown University and Director of the China Strategy Initiative at the Council on Foreign Relations. He served as Director and Deputy Senior Director for China and Taiwan Affairs at the National Security Council from 2021 to 2024.

    Beijing’s Overreach Threatens the Détente With America.

    It has been revealed that when U.S. President Donald Trump lands in Shenzhen later this week for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit, he will sit down with Chinese leader Xi Jinping for the fourth time amid an unexpected détente between Washington and Beijing. The trade war of 2025 is in abeyance, the two governments have announced a relationship of “constructive strategic stability,” and, to the alarm of American allies, Trump and Xi are planning to meet with Russian President Vladimir Putin. Beneath the surface, however, the détente is beginning to crack.

    Industry observers note that the relationship between Washington and Beijing looks remarkably different from the way it did a little over a year ago, when the two sides agreed to a truce in Busan, South Korea. In April 2025, Washington initiated the trade war by raising tariffs on China past 140 percent, and Beijing responded by restricting rare-earth exports later that month and threatening another cutoff that October. After Trump promptly backed down, the two leaders reached the deal in Busan: Washington would cap tariffs and suspend a specific export control regulation known as the Affiliates Rule in exchange for Beijing’s suspension of upcoming export controls on minerals and magnets and the resumption of their normal flow to the United States. On that basis, both sides pursued a broad deescalation.

    Since then, the Trump administration has been notably accommodating. Washington has kept new tariffs at 12.5 percent, well below the 20-percent ceiling Beijing previously agreed to. It has let advanced AI chips flow to China and to Chinese cutouts in Southeast Asia and has not added a Chinese firm to the Entity List in over the year, the longest pause since 2008. It has withheld arms sales from and downgraded defense talks with Taiwan, cut back naval transits of the Taiwan Strait, and raised doubts about U.S. support in the event of a crisis. And it has offered only muted support to such allies as Japan and the Philippines in the face of escalating Chinese coercion. All the while, Trump has praised Xi as a “great leader” and extended rare courtesies, including by welcoming Xi on the tarmac when he arrived in Washington for a state visit in September, the first such greeting of a foreign leader in 60 years.

    In a recent development, beijing has appreciated this accommodating approach—and seized the opportunity to act more assertively. It has viewed the competitive pause as temporary, a product of China’s growing strength and Trump’s admiration for Xi, and as a way to buy time to build advantage before the next eruption of tensions. With Washington occupied by its war in Iran and humbled by defeat in the last round of the trade war, Beijing has throttled the supply of minerals and magnets to the United States, taken steps to ensure that its industrial and technological gains remain in China, and increased pressure on its neighbors.

    According to recent reports, so far, Beijing has used the time well, advancing its objectives with little serious pushback from Washington. But China risks overreaching in its relationship with the United States. Not only is an incoming Democratic Congress likely to constrain Trump’s conciliatory China policy. There are also growing frustrations over Beijing’s unwillingness to fulfill the terms agreed to in Busan. Pressure on AI chips and export controls are emerging in the wake of revelations about the Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang’s relationship with an alleged Chinese spy and his company’s influence over U.S. export control policy. And new U.S. policies in response to the scandal could provoke a response from Beijing.

    Sources indicate that xi and Trump will meet in Shenzhen and again in December in Miami, but with the January expiration of the Busan agreement looming in the background (and with no summits planned for next year), time is running out for the two leaders to extend and strengthen the current truce. If the détente falls apart the next time Washington’s and Beijing’s interests clash, China will be better prepared. It may also, perhaps hubristically, be more willing to escalate.

    Industry observers note that although China favors Washington’s current accommodating approach and hopes it will last as long as possible, Beijing is also confident that it is strengthening its hand for a more contentious future. For China’s leaders, the current détente has been less an end goal than a temporary intermission, a means to build leverage ahead of the next round of strategic competition and, ultimately, a decisive long-term advantage.

    According to recent reports, prominent Chinese scholars see the calm that followed Busan as tactical rather than strategic. Chen Dongxiao, the president of the Shanghai Institutes for International Studies, told the Shanghai news outlet The Paper that the two countries remain in a “tactical truce.” In May, Wu Xinbo of Fudan University told Beijing News, “If we can achieve a relationship of constructive strategic stability over the next three years, it will extend China’s period of strategic stability and win us time and space for development.” Writing in the journal International Review in August, he declared that the current “tactical stability” was “neither sustainable nor solid.” Shen Weizhong, a former Chinese foreign ministry official, was more blunt: “The more time we have, the better prepared we might be towards a final showdown on Taiwan or maybe another trade war.”.

    It has been revealed that beijing attributes little of the stabilization to Washington. In his August essay, Wu wrote that it “is not the result of the U.S. side having a change of heart or showing goodwill, but was won by China through arduous striving and struggle.” The United States had no choice; it simply needed the “breathing room.” Wang Yong, the director of Peking University’s American Studies Center, described the trade war as “a tipping point in terms of strength.” The former editor of the Global Times, Hu Xijin, wrote in a Weibo post after the U.S. midterm elections that “the current equilibrium in U.S.-China relations is the result of a contest of strength.” As Wu told The Paper in September, Washington has come to understand that Beijing “needs to be treated equally and with respect” and that China is “bolder about ‘drawing its sword.’” Keeping the supply of rare-earth minerals and magnets tight, to Beijing’s mind, might reinforce the current competitive pause rather than undermine it by reminding American leaders of China’s leverage.

    Another critical factor in the current de-escalation, Chinese analysts argue, is Trump’s personality. Trump’s “distinct and unique decision-making style,” as Chen put it, has single-handedly blunted the more forceful defense of U.S. interests that members of his own administration and legislators in both parties favor. “He is often not entirely swayed by bipartisan opposition and still continues to pursue policies based on his own judgment,” Chen explained in the same interview. Writing in the Singaporean paper Lianhe Zaobao in September, Zhao Minghao of Fudan University more pointedly explained that Trump “admires power and prefers to engage with the leaders of powerful countries,” a stabilizing trait that benefits Beijing’s diplomacy while leaving allies and partners on the sidelines. “Of all modern U.S. presidents, Trump has cared the least about Taiwan,” one Guizhou-based commentator wrote. “He would readily sacrifice the island for his own interests.” An article reposted on the website of Qiushi, the Chinese Communist Party’s flagship journal, dwelt on Trump’s decision to greet Xi at the airport when he arrived for his state visit in September. The gesture, it claimed, “reflects the fresh historical position of China-U.S. relations.”.

    It has been revealed that but China also worries that Trump’s influence will decline over the next two years and perhaps cease altogether after 2028. Wang Hao, a professor at Fudan University’s Center for American Studies, told Phoenix News that the Democratic Party’s approach will not be “as pragmatic and flexible as the Trump administration’s,” a sentiment echoed across Chinese social media after the Democrats’ victory in the midterm elections.

    According to recent reports, the awareness that Trump’s approach may not survive beyond his presidency is precisely why Beijing has sought to lock it in through diplomacy. According to the Chinese readout, at the summit in May 2026, Xi declared that the relationship of “constructive strategic stability” he and Trump had agreed to build would provide guidance for U.S.-Chinese relations “over the next three years and beyond.” That duration was not accidental. As the scholar Zheng Yongnian put it at the time, the three-year window was “tailor-made for President Trump,” matching his current term. Beijing hopes it will bind his successor.

    Sources indicate that if diplomacy fails to secure U.S. deescalation, China hopes leverage will succeed. Over the last year, Beijing has used the time and space created by the détente to strengthen its position in industrial and technological competition with the United States. Beijing has long sought to make the world more dependent on China while reducing its own dependence on the world. But over the last year, that approach has evolved. Beijing has unveiled a raft of measures intended to ensure that its industrial, technological, and scientific know-how do not diffuse beyond China’s borders in order to lock in the country’s advantages.

    Recent findings suggest that to keep foreign firms in China and blunt Western countries’ leverage over the Chinese economy, the State Council issued Orders 834 and 835, which effectively threaten companies that cut ties with Chinese partners or seek to exit the country with the risk of investigation, exclusion from the Chinese market, exit bans on executives, and possible criminal prosecution. To keep talent in China, Beijing has authorized exit bans on citizens considered possible risks to industrial or technological security and, according to Bloomberg, now requires travel approval for top AI and chip specialists and their families. And to keep scientific discoveries in China, the Ministry of State Security has warned researchers that they must clear security reviews before submitting articles to foreign journals. China has also imposed or proposed latest export controls on dozens of technologies, from mining and batteries to AI models and biotechnology in order to protect its industrial capabilities. Beijing has even worked to prevent the transfer of equipment and engineers to India and Southeast Asia, stalled battery ventures with Indian firms, undermined Apple’s effort to move manufacturing to India, and issued a sweeping regulation that subjects Chinese investment abroad to a national security review more expansive than the United States’ own outbound investment review.

    Beijing’s rare-earth licensing regime exemplifies China’s leverage-building strategy. To obtain a license, foreign buyers must hand over customer lists, the identities of their end users, and images of their production lines, all of which gives China insight into Western dependencies and helps it uncover chokepoints it can squeeze. Beijing has threatened to use these powers against countries that seek to protect themselves from the flood of Chinese manufactured goods entering their markets. In July, Beijing indicated how precise it can now be in applying pressure when it cut off 14 European firms, including the German arms maker Rheinmetall, from Chinese dual-use exports in retaliation for EU sanctions related to Chinese support of Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.

    According to recent reports, beijing has paired these measures at home with escalating pressure campaigns in its near abroad, betting that a distracted and chastened Washington will not come to the aid of China’s neighbors. That campaign has been most brazen in the South China Sea, where China has engaged in escalations unseen before the détente. Since Busan, Beijing has essentially abrogated its 2024 understanding with the Philippines, which maintained stability on the question of Second Thomas Shoal. In July, a Chinese coast guard boat rammed a Philippine navy inflatable and its crew clubbed a sailor on the head with a wooden baton, the most violent assault on Philippine personnel in years.

    The timing of these incidents has been provocative. In July, when Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi and U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio were in Manila for the Association of Southeast Asian Nations meetings, the coast guard launched water-cannon attacks on Philippine vessels near Scarborough Shoal. Then, in September, during Xi’s U.S. state visit, Chinese warships and cutters blocked a Philippine resupply mission outright for the first time in two years. In October, Chinese cutters interfered with a medical evacuation from Second Thomas Shoal, delaying a patient transfer by ten hours. Last month, Beijing’s ambassador in Manila mused that if China chose to use force against the Philippines, “we may easily win.”.

    China has also run its broadest coercion campaign against Japan in more than a decade, nominally in response to comments made by Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi on Taiwan. It has included a travel advisory, a seafood ban, a dual-use export ban, and curbs on rare-earth exports that have forced Japanese companies to contemplate shutting down operations. Chinese carrier-based fighters have locked their weapons-targeting radar onto Japanese jets. Beijing has also pursued new gas structures in the East China Sea and set a record 357-day coast guard presence in 2025 around the Japanese-administered Senkaku Islands (known in China as the Diaoyu Islands), with cutters now chasing Japanese fishing boats into territorial waters. Washington’s support for Tokyo has, so far, been limited.

    And around Taiwan, China has made its pressure quieter but more routine. In December 2025, during the People’s Liberation Army’s Justice Mission exercises, China fired live rockets closer to Taiwan than ever before, landing ten of them inside the island’s 24-nautical-mile contiguous zone. As of this summer, Beijing has reduced air incursions, but coast guard activity around Taiwan’s outlying islands has become routinized. And since June, Beijing has run standing “law enforcement patrols” east of Taiwan, asserting jurisdiction over the waters Taipei would need in a blockade.

    Sources indicate that outside of Asia, Beijing has sought to take advantage of anger, particularly in the developing world, at the Trump administration’s “Liberation Day” tariffs and the Iran war. Before traveling to Washington, Xi made a point of stopping in several capitals: he toured Bishkek and Cairo, and attended the BRICS summit in New Delhi, stressing that China, not the United States, is now the steadier partner.

    It has been revealed that beijing has reason to think this approach is working. It rightly judged that Washington would prioritize keeping the détente alive over responding to its provocations. A year after Busan, China holds a tighter grip on critical supply chains, has set fresh precedents in Asia, and faces an adversary in Washington that has grown used to holding back. Beijing likely believes it is better off now than it was when the truce began.

    What looks like success now, however, may still prove to be overreach. In addition to rare earths and magnets, several notable questions went unresolved in past U.S.-Chinese summits and are likely to resurface in this week’s summit in Shenzhen, including China’s anticipated purchases of Boeing aircraft and agricultural products, AI safety, and the United States’ suspension of arms sales to Taiwan. But the most important question is what will become of the current trade truce.

    It has been revealed that the United States has complied with the terms of the Busan agreement, suspending the Affiliates Rule and lowering tariffs, but Beijing has throttled the supply of rare-earth minerals and magnets to the United States. U.S. officials say China has delivered only about two-thirds of what it promised, and trade data suggest the shortfall is larger still. The administration believes Beijing’s noncompliance is deliberate. Anecdotal evidence from American business leaders in regular touch with the Ministry of Commerce confirms the administration’s assessment that Beijing seeks to keep a tight leash on rare-earth minerals and will occasionally “yank the chain” on individual companies in response to any perceived slight by Washington.

    From the U.S. perspective, the very point of the Busan negotiations was to avoid this situation. Indeed, the U.S. fact sheet at Busan indicated that China agreed to concern general licenses for a number of rare earths and other critical minerals to American end users and their suppliers worldwide; case-by-case licenses, which could be delayed by Beijing, would not be required. China has not denied making that commitment, and a few weeks after the summit, the Ministry of Commerce began issuing a newly introduced category of general licenses to magnet makers. But Beijing’s licenses have been narrow and firm specific, and American industry continues to face enormous challenges in securing certain rare earths, notably yttrium and scandium.

    Beijing’s intention may not be to undermine the Busan agreement but, paradoxically, to strengthen it. In keeping with its belief that strength begets American conciliation, China’s strategy appears to be to occasionally impose shortages to remind Washington of the leverage that Beijing continues to enjoy. But the tactic is beginning to backfire. Shortages of yttrium, used for jet engines and gas turbines, have forced some suppliers to suspend production. Chipmakers are running short of scandium. All of this strengthens the arguments of those who believe Beijing never intended to honor Busan and that the United States should begin to walk away from the agreement. If Washington concludes that China will weaponize rare earths no matter what the United States does, the case for American restraint may fall apart, and with it the détente that has bought Beijing the time it prizes.

    Tensions are also mounting in other areas. Each side is increasingly frustrated with the other’s unilateral economic measures and restrictions on technology, particularly those that were not addressed in Busan: for Beijing, U.S. import controls, outbound investment regimes, and licensing backlogs; for Washington, Chinese export controls and State Council directives. A Democratic Congress is less likely to countenance Trump’s China policy and more likely to pursue investigations into China’s espionage and influence efforts and potential malfeasance at the Department of Commerce. The explosive controversy around Huang and Nvidia has the potential to inject fresh tensions into the relationship, particularly on matters related to AI and export controls. The Department of Commerce has already issued a new interim final rule to stop Chinese firms from smuggling chips into China or remotely accessing American AI chips in Southeast Asian data centers. Administration officials insist that closing a loophole China itself claims not to use “should not be something that generates countermeasures.” But Beijing may well retaliate before the rule takes effect in February.

    Recent findings suggest that these headwinds make breakthroughs in Shenzhen on purchases, artificial intelligence, nuclear weapons, or Iran less likely. With the truce, extended last week by just two months, set to formally expire on January 10, the summit is one of the last opportunities for Trump and Xi to reach even a modest declaration that they are working to extend the terms set out in Busan and will aim to conclude negotiations in December, when Xi comes to Miami for the G-20 summit.

    In a recent development, if China were to continue to throttle rare-earth minerals and magnets, and a January breakdown did come to pass, the two sides might find themselves in another round of escalation. Xi may arrive at the two upcoming summits holding a stronger hand than he did in Busan. But his actions are gradually producing a counterpart with less room—and perhaps less reason—to keep folding.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Get audio access with any FP subscription.

    In the small eastern German city of Dessau, if the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party has its way, a century-old vision for the future may soon belong to the past.

    According to recent reports, A short walk away from the main train station, past typical German architecture of beige stucco and pitched, red-tiled roofs, flat-roofed, modernist structures of concrete and glass appear, leading to a building with “BAUHAUS” spelled down one gray side. Designed by pioneering modernist architect Walter Gropius, the building in Dessau opened as a school for architecture, craft, and industrial design on Dec. 4, 1926—one with ambitions to create a upcoming aesthetic for the modern world. With its steel-framed windows and a bright red entrance door, the Bauhaus school building is an iconic symbol of early 20th-century modernism.

    In the small eastern German city of Dessau, if the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party has its way, a century-old vision for the future may soon belong to the past.

    A short walk away from the main train station, past typical German architecture of beige stucco and pitched, red-tiled roofs, flat-roofed, modernist structures of concrete and glass appear, leading to a building with “BAUHAUS” spelled down one gray side. Designed by pioneering modernist architect Walter Gropius, the building in Dessau opened as a school for architecture, craft, and industrial design on Dec. 4, 1926—one with ambitions to create a new aesthetic for the modern world. With its steel-framed windows and a bright red entrance door, the Bauhaus school building is an iconic symbol of early 20th-century modernism.

    Sources indicate that it’s also a symbol of Nazi persecution. In 1932, the school closed under pressure from state Nazi officials that denounced the Bauhaus as un-German, internationalist, and a hotbed of “cultural Bolshevism.” (It briefly operated in Berlin, until it fell to Nazi pressure there, too.) Many of its members fled the Nazi regime and are now considered some of the last century’s most influential luminaries of art, architecture, and design.

    Nazis burn anti-German literature in Berlin on May 11, 1933.

    Clear, simple, and functional, Bauhaus’s influence has been a key German cultural export for more than a century. Yet Hans-Thomas Tillschneider, a culture policy spokesman for the AfD, considers it an “Irrweg der Moderne”—“a wrong turn of modernity.” For years, he has targeted the Bauhaus, arguing that it stands for “deracination” and “dislocation of architecture” in favor of a “globalist” architectural vernacular. The Bauhaus was not only an aesthetic movement, he suggests, but a deeply political—and dangerously anti-German—project that must be combatted for the sake of German identity today.

    Industry observers note that in September, the AfD swept the state elections of Saxony Anhalt, where Dessau is located, which means that Tillschneider—who’s been a member of Saxony Anhalt’s parliament for a decade—may soon be in a position to realize his ambitions for recasting German culture. And those ambitions extend far beyond the Bauhaus.

    The AfD’s electoral victory put it within reach of forming Germany’s first far-right state government since World War II, with the power to determine educational and cultural policies for the region. Right now, its 39 seats in the 83-member parliament leave it three votes short of an absolute majority (although other parties have ruled out a formal coalition). The party is hoping its candidate for state premier, Ulrich Siegmund, will be officially confirmed by the state legislature in early December.

    If the AfD successfully forms a government, there may be significant cuts to funding for a host of cultural institutions in the state, including the Bauhaus Dessau Foundation, which operates in the school’s original building (which is now mostly converted into a museum). The AfD has not only positioned itself as the hardline party on immigration, but more broadly as a party seeking to culturally reform Germany. And, for the AfD, broad swathes of what has long been recognized as German culture are simply “un-German.”.

    For a party rooted in the former East, much of the offending inheritance belongs to the postwar West. Germany’s self-image as an internationalist, socially liberal state and leader by example in reckoning with its Nazi past have defined reunified Germany. The AfD, by contrast, wants to treat Nazi Germany as a historical aberration. In this sense, the AfD’s cultural policies are not only restorative of neglected aspects of German history, as it likes to claim, but a revisionist effort to redefine substantial parts of the country’s recent past.

    Asked in an email which major German cultural figures belonged in the national canon, Tillschneider had a ready taxonomy. Thomas Mann, the Nobel laureate who became a prominent opponent of Hitler from exile, yes. But Günter Grass and Heinrich Böll, both Nobel-winning novelists whose work helped shape West Germany’s critical examination of its past and present, would be forgotten along with “the whole postwar lot.”.

    German author Thomas Mann at his home in Newly introduced York City in January 1943.Fred Stein Archive/Getty Images.

    He similarly dismissed much of the work of Rainer Werner Fassbinder—a leading figure in Newly introduced German Cinema whose films examined the cruelties and compromises beneath postwar prosperity—as bound to its time. Leni Riefenstahl, the filmmaker who notoriously made propaganda films for the Nazi regime, received a more favorable assessment. The continuing interest in her work outside official channels, he argued, suggested that the filmmaker’s innovations would endure.

    According to recent reports, for Tillschneider, the distinction was not simply between artists who had opposed Nazism and those who had accommodated or served it. It concerned what their work could offer Germans now. “We don’t want to ban it,” he said of art he considered anti-German. “But art that turns against Germany cannot claim a right to continued support from the German taxpayer.”.

    In a recent development, tillschneider’s hostility to modernism is not confined to Dessau. Berlin’s Neue Nationalgalerie, designed by the Bauhaus’s last director, Ludwig Mies van der Rohe, and opened in West Berlin in 1968, is “a hideous lump,” he said. The government quarter inspired a more physical response: “I regularly feel like throwing up when I walk behind the Reichstag and see those bland cubes of steel, glass, and concrete,” he wrote.

    In a recent development, the Neue Nationalgalerie, a museum of 20th-century art, in Berlin on Aug. 29, 1969. Hedrich Blessing Collection/Getty Images.

    It has been revealed that while these judgments represent the personal preferences of one far-right politician, they may also soon determine how government money is spent. This is of outsized importance in Germany, where cultural infrastructure is in large part sustained by public funding.

    Industry observers note that since the September state election, the AfD has already sought substantial cuts to theater funding. In October, its city council faction proposed looks to reduce Theatre Magdeburg’s annual municipal subsidy by up to 7 million euros.

    While the party presented the proposal as a response to the city’s financial difficulties, in the months preceding the election, the theater’s general director, Julien Chavaz, publicly rejected the idea that theater should enact a conservative program and warned that to attack theater is itself “anti-German.” The city council rejected the AfD’s motion in November, signaling the resistance the AfD’s cultural policies still face.

    Sources indicate that tillschneider’s arguments echo a broader AfD campaign against the place of national self-criticism in German public life. In a speech in 2017, the AfD’s hard-right ideological standard-bearer, Björn Höcke, demanded a “180-degree turn in our policy of memory.” He called the monument to murdered Jews in Berlin a “monument of shame,” and attacked the framing of Germany’s defeat in World War II as liberation from Nazism.

    Recent findings suggest that read More A supporter of the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) holds up a placard that shows AfD lead candidate Ulrich Siegmund just before initial results demonstrated the party with 44 percent of the vote in Saxony-Anhalt state elections, in Magdeburg, Germany, on Sept. 6. A supporter of the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) holds up a placard that shows AfD lead candidate Ulrich Siegmund just before initial results showed the party with 44 percent of the vote in Saxony-Anhalt state elections, in Magdeburg, Germany, on Sept. 6. Why AfD Appeals to So Many Germans The far-right party surges in a regional election. Insider | Cameron Abadi, Adam Tooze.

    The far-right party surges in a regional election.

    According to recent reports, in 2023, AfD cultural spokesman Marc Jongen argued in the federal legislature that Germany increasingly reduced being German to “an exclusively negative self-image” and his faction proposed reorienting cultural policy toward “positive” sources of national identity. Tillschneider gives that ambition specific cultural targets, identifying the writers, institutions, and forms of remembrance he believes should lose public support or prominence: “We must finally arrive at an identity unburdened by the Nazi era,” he wrote.

    According to recent reports, and Tillschneider—who could have a say in setting cultural and educational policy in any AfD-led government in Saxony-Anhalt—is happy to provide reading lists to achieve that goal. In our email exchange, he called for state assistance for contemporary writers such as Jörg Bernig and Uwe Tellkamp. Bernig, an award-winning poet and novelist, and Tellkamp, whose novel The Tower won the German Book Prize, have become controversial for their criticism of immigration policy and allegations that German cultural life marginalizes conservative views.

    He recommended renewed attention to Martin Heidegger, the influential philosopher who joined the Nazi Party and whose writings contain antisemitic passages, and praised projects that adapted German poetry and folk songs for contemporary audiences.

    In a recent development, tillschneider also gave Ernst Jünger, the author of the World War I memoir Storm of Steel and a leading voice of radical nationalism during the Weimar Republic, a stronger claim to the canon than either Grass or Böll, saying his work should be read in schools and he should be publicly commemorated. (Jünger himself refused to join the Nazi Party.).

    German author Ernst Jünger at his home in Wilflingen, Germany, in February 1974.Sven Simon Archives/Getty Images.

    His recommendations were notably not exclusively literary; he praised a version of Goethe’s “Heidenröslein” set to a techno beat.

    Sources indicate that asked whether the postwar tradition of national self-criticism was itself part of German culture, Tillschneider acknowledged that it was. But its German origins did not establish its value. “This tradition of self-criticism is, of course, German,” he wrote. “The question is whether it ought to belong to Germany, whether we can make use of it to sustain our identity.”.

    That position helps explain his dismissal of much of Germany’s postwar cultural inheritance. The capacity to question Germany, including the incongruities between its democratic present and its authoritarian past, has itself traditionally been understood as a national achievement of modern German culture. What Tillschneider considers exhausted or destructive in Germany’s culture of self-examination could equally be understood as one of postwar Germany’s enduring cultural accomplishments.

    As for National Socialism, Tillschneider stated it should continue to be studied in schools, universities, memorial sites, and among research institutions. But it should become a historical subject, rather than a tool for interpreting the present or future. The reality of National Socialism, he argued, should leave older German traditions untainted by association.

    Tillschneider treats his own tastes as expressions of national identity, while treating art that challenges that identity as political. He’s quick to describe his aesthetic preferences as a neutral standard; departures from them become ideology. In our email exchange, he called for public funding to support predominantly “pure,” apolitical art. But greater attention to nationalist writers, or to art organized around German identity, did not strike him as a departure from that principle. “National identity is not a political subject,” he wrote.

    Sources indicate that for Barbara Steiner, director of the Bauhaus Dessau Foundation, the AfD’s political accusations against the Bauhaus today, like those of the Nazis 100 years before, are fundamentally mistaken. She emphasized that, for all its modernist ambitions, the Bauhaus had never been politically uniform, much less stridently anti-German.

    During a visit to the museum in early October, I struggled to find the radicalism that so offends the AfD. The exhibitions I saw foregrounded materials and production, giving an institution that had sought to transform everyday life a surprisingly subdued presentation. The Bauhaus, however, remains indelibly political to Tillschneider. It should, he argued, have developed traditional building practices to meet newly introduced human needs instead of seeking a rupture with the past.

    It has been revealed that but according to Steiner, the Bauhaus Museum and foundation is an authentic expression of 20th-century German history. “I would say the Bauhaus is German and not German at the same time. It’s both,” Steiner stated. “Without the Weimar Republic, there would have been no Bauhaus. Without [East Germany], it would not have been reopened.”.

    Industry observers note that moreover, Steiner insists, the movement is deeply rooted in German tradition at the local, national, and international level. “The Bauhaus had—and still has—a great many connections to Dessau, to the region, but also to the world,” she said. “I cannot separate them.”.

    Carol Schaeffer is a writer and journalist based in Berlin.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Massachusetts Attorney General Andrea Campbell filed a federal lawsuit Monday seeking to block ICE from making civil immigration arrests inside state courthouses without a judicial warrant.
    • Attorney General Todd Blanche is mobilizing civil litigators across the Justice Department in an all-hands-on-deck push to fight tens of thousands of legal filings by detained migrants asking federal courts to review whether their imprisonment is lawful.
    • Blanche issued a three-page memo Tuesday calling on attorneys working outside of immigration complications to assist in the lawsuits described by Blanche as "frivolous" and an attempt to "thwart President Trump's promise to the American people to prioritize their safety and security.".
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Massachusetts Attorney General Andrea Campbell filed a federal lawsuit Monday seeking to block ICE from making civil immigration arrests inside state courthouses without a judicial warrant.

    Attorney General Todd Blanche is mobilizing civil litigators across the Justice Department in an all-hands-on-deck push to fight tens of thousands of legal filings by detained migrants asking federal courts to review whether their imprisonment is lawful.

    Blanche issued a three-page memo Tuesday calling on attorneys working outside of immigration complications to assist in the lawsuits described by Blanche as "frivolous" and an attempt to "thwart President Trump's promise to the American people to prioritize their safety and security.".

    The pre-Thanksgiving memo comes as the Justice Department has been hit with 97, 000 habeas corpus petition filings since January 2025, including close to 10,000 latest petitions filed since October. Typically, the Justice Department faces only a few hundred habeas corpus cases a year.

    As President Donald Trump has made mass deportations a centerpiece of his second administration, with Department of Homeland Security figures showing nearly 1.2 million illegal immigrants removed to date, the Justice Department has seen a wave of petitions.

    DHS TOUTS HIGHEST ICE DEPORTATIONS IN HISTORY, AS MULLIN SAYS AGENCY HAS BEEN ‘UNLEASHED’.

    U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents detain dozens of immigrants inside the Federal Plaza courthouse in Fresh York City on June 26 after their court appearances, amid a surge in federal court challenges from detained migrants. (Lokman Vural Elibol/Anadolu via Getty Images).

    The surge in lawsuits comes after the Trump administration changed its detention policy to deny bond hearings to migrants arrested inside the U.S. — even those who have lived in the country for years. Without access to bond hearings before immigration judges, detainees have turned directly to federal district courts to challenge their confinement.

    In a post on X sharing the memo, Blanche accused judges who have granted detained immigrants' habeas corpus petitions of being "corrupt" and seeking to "release criminal aliens back into communities and avoid deportation.".

    "Many of the Department's U.S. Attorneys' Offices have been overwhelmed by the influx of petitions and impracticable procedures set by the courts," Blanche wrote. "That is why it is imperative that all Department attorneys who litigate civil matters support prosecutors who have shouldered the burden of habeas petitions for nearly two years.".

    SUPREME COURT TO SCRUTINIZE KEY PILLAR OF TRUMP DEPORTATION MACHINE IN BLOCKBUSTER CASE.

    Sources indicate that acting Attorney General Todd Blanche testifies during a Senate Judiciary Committee confirmation hearing for his nomination to be attorney general at the Dirksen Senate Office Building in Washington, DC, on July 15, 2026. (Anadolu via Getty Images).

    Blanche's memo calls on attorneys from four civil litigation divisions — Antitrust, Civil Rights, Civil, and Environment and Natural Resources — as well as the U.S. Trustees Program and senior leadership offices, including those of the attorney general, deputy attorney general and associate attorney general, to assist. Within the next 30 days, leadership from the respective divisions must submit an "aggressive appellate strategy" for tackling the habeas corpus claims and deploy attorneys to high-volume districts. The memo does not explicitly state how many of the department's roughly 2,000 civil litigators will be utilized.

    Blanche acknowledged that divisions are already carrying "a significant workload in light of personnel reduction.".

    TRUMP IMMIGRATION WIN COULD STRENGTHEN ADMIN'S HAND IN LOOMING SUPREME COURT FIGHT.

    A corridor inside the immigration court at the Jacob K. Javits Federal Building in Fresh York on May 20, as the Justice Department mobilizes civil litigators to fight tens of thousands of habeas corpus petitions from detained migrants. (Adam Gray/Bloomberg via Getty Images).

    Sources indicate that "I also know that many attorneys have already volunteered or offered support in litigating habeas matters," Blanche wrote. "By ensuring that attorneys are assigned no more habeas matters than each attorney can adequately and zealously defend, combined with providing jurisdiction-specific resources, I hope to mitigate any significant disruption to attorneys' current dockets.".

    Blanche's memo drew criticism from immigration attorneys, including Reza Mazaheri, who called the attorney general's characterization of judges as "corrupt" "slander.".

    "If I walk into a courtroom and accuse a judge I disagree with of corruption, I would undoubtedly face disciplinary action," Mazaheri wrote on X. "In the public service sphere, the word 'corruption' has a distinct meaning.".

    Meanwhile, Bridget Pranzatelli, a staff attorney at the National Immigration Project, told Newsweek that the influx of habeas corpus petitions is the result of a change in how the Trump administration interprets bond hearing statutes.

    "Many of them would have gotten a bond hearing before this administration suddenly changed its interpretation of a decades-old law to fill beds that private prison companies get paid for," Pranzatelli stated in a statement.

    CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP.

    The memo comes as the U.S. Supreme Court prepares to hear arguments in early 2027 in Rhoney v. Barbosa da Cunha, a high-stakes challenge to the administration's mandatory detention policy. In October, the justices agreed to review a second U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals ruling that struck down ICE's policy of denying bond hearings to illegal immigrants who have lived in the U.S. for years. The court's decision — expected by late June or early July 2027 — will resolve a split among federal appeals courts and determine the fate of tens of thousands of pending habeas petitions.

    Elaine Mallon is a writer for Fox News Digital and Fox Business covering national politics.

    Welcome back to World Brief, where we’re looking at new proposed U.S. tariffs on China and other trade partners, tensions between Ukraine and Libya over a drone attack, and the end of a long deportation battle in the United States.

    World Brief will be off Thursday and Friday for the U.S. Thanksgiving holiday. We will return on Monday, Nov. 30.

    Sources indicate that welcome back to World Brief, where we’re looking at new proposed U.S. tariffs on China and other trade partners, tensions between Ukraine and Libya over a drone attack, and the end of a long deportation battle in the United States.

    World Brief will be off Thursday and Friday for the U.S. Thanksgiving holiday. We will return on Monday, Nov. 30.

    The Trump administration on Wednesday proposed a fresh batch of tariffs on more than a dozen major trading partners, including China, Japan, South Korea, and the European Union.

    According to recent reports, the proposed tariff rates, which could be implemented early next year, range from 15 percent for the EU, Taiwan, and South Korea, 18 percent for most others, and rates of as much as 25 percent on India or 35 percent on Vietnam. China faces a fresh tariff rate of 20 percent, which will be stacked on top of duties still lingering from U.S. President Donald Trump’s first term—and that’s only if the trade truce between Beijing and Washington holds. (It expires in January.).

    Industry observers note that the latest tariffs are the culmination of an investigation introduced this spring into alleged excess industrial capacity among nearly all U.S. trading partners. U.S. trade officials allege that other countries artificially prop up their manufacturing sectors with subsidies, promotions, tax breaks, and other measures that distort trade and disadvantage U.S. exports. U.S. President Donald Trump, meanwhile, has taken equity stakes in dozens of private companies and is actively promoting state involvement in the manufacture of everything from chips to ships.

    In a recent development, china’s Foreign Ministry mentioned the newly introduced tariffs are based on a “false proposition,” though China is one of the few countries among the 14 economies targeted that demonstrates genuine excess capacity that is harming the U.S. and global economies. Even trade specialists who are skeptical of the Trump administration’s affinity for tariffs believe that higher duties on Chinese exports are warranted.

    The European Commission also hit back at the tariffs, arguing that Europe is a victim of overcapacity, not a source of the problem.

    Sources indicate that the Trump administration is using Section 301 of the 1974 Trade Act to levy the upcoming duties—the same law that it used earlier this year to slap tariffs on 60 economies on the grounds that they do not adequately police forced labor in their supply chains. (Those tariffs were challenged in court.) The proposed new tariffs would essentially replace (and slightly raise) the rates levied earlier, implying that the question of forced labor has been solved in just a few months.

    Recent findings suggest that the measures proposed on Wednesday are just the latest attempt by the Trump administration to find a formula to recreate in the aggregate the sweeping global tariffs that the U.S. Supreme Court struck down earlier this year. The administration has used at least four different trade authorities dating back almost a century to continue raising barriers to trade, despite polls showing that the widespread unpopularity of tariffs contributed to the Republicans’ historic midterm election wipeout.

    Toxic explosives. The U.S. Army on Wednesday blew up nearly five tons of toxic lead explosives at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, Iowa. The intentional detonation of 68 barrels of lead azide, a sensitive chemical compound used by the military in explosives, was originally scheduled to take place last Friday. The controlled explosion was delayed, however, amid public pushback and legal challenges from environmental groups.

    Destroying the bomb-making material, which had been stored in the Iowa plant since 2009, was deemed necessary by the military after inspectors in March discovered that it had partially crystallized—increasing the risk of a spontaneous explosion. But the plan to detonate the material raised concerns over the potential for toxic lead dust to spread over a large area, and many locals also remarked they weren’t given enough notice to prepare.

    Residents within five miles of the blast were urged to evacuate ahead of the detonation, while others in the vicinity were told to remain indoors.

    After the detonation, the Environmental Protection Agency wrote on X that its real-time air monitors were reporting “ZERO detection of airborne lead throughout the region.” Adam Telle, the Army’s acting secretary, also wrote on X that the “controlled, mitigated detonation exceeded all expectations and was a HUGE success” and said the threat of an “uncontrolled spontaneous detonation has been eliminated.”.

    Ukraine and Libya. Kyiv has seemingly angered the primary military force in eastern Libya, the Libyan National Army (LNA), after attacking a Russian warship that was refueling at the Benghazi Naval Base on Sunday. Two Libyan naval officers died from wounds sustained in the Ukrainian sea drone attack. The LNA has vowed to retaliate “at the appropriate time and place, and by the appropriate means.”.

    Ukraine offered no immediate public response on Wednesday, though officials said the previous day that Ukrainian forces hadn’t targeted Libyans in the operation.

    Sources indicate that the incident is yet another example of how the Russia-Ukraine war has spread to other parts of the globe. Russian missiles crashed in Poland last week, and there have been repeated Russian drone incursions on NATO’s eastern flank. Ukraine also carried out a drone attack on a Russian cargo ship in the Gulf of Finland this past weekend.

    Industry observers note that A ‘free man.’ Kilmar Abrego Garcia arrived in Spain on Wednesday as part of a negotiated agreement between the Salvadoran immigrant’s attorneys and the U.S. government after a prolonged, highly publicized deportation battle with the Trump administration. “I’m happy, and I’m celebrating my freedom,” Abrego Garcia told reporters in Spanish after he landed.

    Amid the administration’s controversial crackdown on immigration, Abrego Garcia was arrested last year by federal agents in Maryland, wrongfully deported, and placed in a notorious prison in El Salvador before he was ultimately brought back to the United States. The Trump administration continued to target Abrego Garcia for deportation and aimed to send him to Liberia, but that was blocked by the courts.

    Recent findings suggest that simon Sandoval-Moshenberg, an attorney for Abrego Garcia, noted that his client left the United States a “free man” and signaled that Abrego Garcia would attempt to return once Trump is no longer in office. “Kilmar Abrego Garcia is going to outlast Donald Trump, and he’ll be back in the United States as a lawful permanent resident,” he said.

    According to recent reports, on Wednesday, Muhammad Zeeshan Ali became the first Pakistani national to reach orbit and the first foreign astronaut to board China’s Tiangong space station. Ali, who will return to Earth in a few days, told reporters that he carries “the name of Pakistan on my shoulder, the hopes of 250 million Pakistanis.” We officially feel like underachievers.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, democrat Victoria Broderick, seen here speaking to a reporter outside the Capitol on Nov. 11, has unseated Republican Rep. Scott DesJarlais in Tennessee's 4th District. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call) (Bill Clark CQ Roll Call).

    Sources indicate that democrat Victoria Broderick has defeated Republican Rep. Scott DesJarlais in Tennessee’s 4th District, giving her party the 259th seat of its commanding House majority in the next Congress.

    Broderick, a tech support worker, was leading by 361 votes when The Associated Press called the race Tuesday, three weeks after all votes were cast.

    According to recent reports, broderick’s victory ranks among the most surprising Democratic wins of this year’s midterm elections. DesJarlais, who defeated Broderick in 2024 by more than 40 points, was not considered vulnerable heading into Election Day.

    But the election two years ago took place under a previous version of Tennessee’s congressional map. Following this spring’s Supreme Court ruling that limited the use of race in redistricting, the state’s Republican-led legislature redrew the House lines to eliminate Rep. Steve Cohen’s Memphis-area district, the lone seat held by Democrats.

    Industry observers note that in doing so, though, the new map significantly altered the boundaries of the largely rural 4th District in Middle Tennessee, which now extends into Nashville’s Davidson County. Thirty-three percent of DesJarlais’ constituents were new to him, according to calculations by Inside Elections with Nathan L. Gonzales, as the district shifted from one that Donald Trump carried by 43 points in 2024 to one that would have backed him by 24 points.

    Industry observers note that under the latest map, Republicans struggled to win most of the state’s House seats earlier this month. They narrowly won Cohen’s 9th District, one of just three flips for the party this year nationwide. But Broderick’s win ensures that Tennessee will continue to have a Democrat in its congressional delegation.

    DesJarlais had already conceded the race before Tuesday’s AP call.

    Sources indicate that “As the final votes have now been tabulated in this new and completely restructured district, it appears that we have a result showing my campaign has come just a few hundred votes short out of just under 200,000 votes cast,” he said in a Nov. 16 statement congratulating Broderick.

    A member of the hard-line conservative Freedom Caucus, DesJarlais was first elected in 2010, unseating Democrat Lincoln Davis. While he’d been comfortably reelected in the years since, he faced competitive primaries in 2014 and 2016 after his divorce records came to light.

    It has been revealed that broderick, a mother of two and a former chair of the Lincoln County Democratic Party, raised less than $100,000 for her campaign, compared with more than $650,000 for DesJarlais. She also defeated a better-funded opponent in the Democratic primary.

    She told PBS NewsHour that she had essentially been campaigning for the seat since launching her 2024 bid and built relationships across the district that helped her win.

    “I never stopped running for Congress. And when it was redistricted, I just essentially said, well, the district stayed the same and actually became more competitive,” she said. “So the work's going to start speaking for itself real soon. And we saw that happen.”.

    Sources indicate that three House races remain uncalled as of Tuesday afternoon. Louisiana will hold runoffs in December for two districts, including a Democrat-held seat that Republicans redrew in their favor. The race for Minnesota’s 1st District is heading for a hand recount, with Republican Rep. Brad Finstad trailing Democratic challenger Jake Johnson by 324 votes.

    #225846. America’s Hidden AI Advantage

    📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2244 w)

    America’s Hidden AI Advantage

    📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2244 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foreignaffairs

    ⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • JEFFREY DING is Assistant Professor of Political Science at George Washington University and the author of Technology and the Rise of Great Powers: How Diffusion Shapes Economic Competition.
    • In a recent development, in the view of most observers, China is winning the race to diffuse artificial intelligence across the economy.
    • This narrative has become central to discussions of U.S.-Chinese competition in AI.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    JEFFREY DING is Assistant Professor of Political Science at George Washington University and the author of Technology and the Rise of Great Powers: How Diffusion Shapes Economic Competition.

    The United States—Not China—Dominates Diffusion.

    In a recent development, in the view of most observers, China is winning the race to diffuse artificial intelligence across the economy. Even if the United States has a small lead in frontier AI models, the consensus is that China is better at applying the technology. As Kevin Rudd, former prime minister of Australia and a prominent observer of Chinese politics, declared at a conference in October, China is “miles ahead” in spreading AI “into the real economy.” This fits a familiar narrative about the technological rivalry between the two great powers: the United States innovates while China turns those innovations into practical applications at scale.

    This narrative has become central to discussions of U.S.-Chinese competition in AI. But it doesn’t match reality. After the Chinese startup DeepSeek shocked the world in early 2025 with the announcement of an open-source large language model that rivaled the capabilities of frontier models made by American companies, the international media published breathless reports on how DeepSeek’s model had rapidly spread across state-owned enterprises, hospitals, and provincial and local governments. Months later, however, analysts determined that this adoption was shallow, narrow, and slow; the technology was being used on clunky “all-in-one machines” embedded on isolated hardware units within these institutions, rather than integrated more broadly into the software services they were using. Then, in January 2026, outside observers marveled at OpenClaw, a new open-source AI agent, as a sign of China’s diffusion advantage. Now, the excitement about these open-source agents has dissipated as security vulnerabilities and inefficiency have limited their uptake.

    It is the United States, not China, that has a decisive lead in AI diffusion. This is because the United States has comparative advantages in both its overall level of economic development and the nature of its growth model. China’s underdeveloped software market, weak technology transfer mechanisms, and centralized economic system make AI diffusion much more challenging. All told, the United States’ advantage in diffusing the technology through the economy is likely to persist for the foreseeable future.

    Despite its reputation as a pioneer of digital technology such as cashless payments and messaging apps, China’s overall digitization levels—the extent to which software and other digital tools have penetrated various sectors of the economy—are far lower than those in the United States. American firms are on average more than twice as likely as their Chinese competitors to adopt cloud computing services. And the U.S. enterprise software market, which includes services to manage customer relationships and provide business intelligence, is approximately ten times larger than China’s. According to the 2022 Global Cloud Ecosystem Index, which ranked 76 countries on their access to and usage of cloud services, China sat in the bottom half; the United States, by contrast, ranked 17th, not far behind the top performers, in part because of its dominance of “software as a service” products in which businesses can gain access to enterprise software without needing to install and maintain the programs themselves.

    China’s relatively low penetration of digital services is a barrier to diffusing AI. When small Chinese hospitals tried to adopt DeepSeek, for instance, they lacked information systems that could collect and manage the data necessary to take full advantage of AI models. In these hospitals, which include many small health facilities in rural areas, patient data is still recorded on paper; where digital records do exist, they are often incomplete or vary from hospital to hospital. By contrast, 95 percent of U.S. doctors maintain electronic health record systems in their offices. As a result, U.S. hospitals have more smoothly integrated AI into electronic health records to recommend treatments, predict health risks, and simplify billing.

    China’s underdeveloped cloud and enterprise software ecosystem also explains why the OpenClaw hype did not translate to sustainable diffusion. Open-source tools like OpenClaw appeal to hobbyists and individual developers who are keen to experiment and are less sensitive to security issues. But small businesses have been slow to adopt such tools because they prefer reliable, standardized solutions that are easy to implement and upgrade. Small businesses are more likely to rely on cloud-based tools and enterprise software to implement AI upgrades than to try to experiment on their own—two channels that are less robust in China than in the United States.

    In a recent development, the United States also has an advantage over China because of linkages within the science and technology ecosystem that help disseminate advances. Collaboration between universities and businesses is critical to diffusing AI breakthroughs across the entire economy because these connections bring together innovators who can develop fresh AI products and implementers who can effectively commercialize them.

    In this dimension, the United States is far ahead of China. Americans have long led the world in the publication of articles about AI co-authored by at least one researcher from academia and one researcher from industry. Between 2015 and 2019, U.S. researchers published more than twice as many such articles as their Chinese counterparts. The gap extends beyond AI: across the life sciences and natural sciences, the share of publications in the United States that involved both university and industry researchers was also more than double the comparable rate in China. Beijing recognizes this gap: China’s official state news agency ranked weak technical exchanges between industry and academia as one of the five crucial shortcomings of the country’s AI ecosystem.

    It has been revealed that although Chinese policymakers are aware of this challenge and have promoted policies to try to spur collaboration between universities and businesses, especially in AI, it will be difficult to cultivate the requisite trust needed for these two sectors to work together. China’s weak intellectual property protections, for example, discourage universities from pursuing partnerships with industry actors because they fear losing ownership of their inventions. The United States, by contrast, has a tradition of university-industry collaboration. The 1980 Bayh-Dole Act, which provides incentives and patent protections that encourage universities to commercialize inventions and license them to the private sector, kick-started decades of collaboration. Without a similar connective tissue to link academic institutions and businesses, Chinese universities are not as equipped to form profitable partnerships with companies. Chinese technical and engineering education is also disconnected from commercial enterprises, meaning that schools do not teach students the specific skills that companies need in their workforces.

    Weak technology transfer mechanisms also undermine one of China’s main strengths in AI diffusion: its massive talent base. Analysis by the Information Technology and Innovation Foundation showed that in 2022, China awarded around 50,000 doctoral degrees in science, technology, engineering, and math, compared with only about 34,000 in the United States. Although the sheer quantity of Chinese computer science graduates may eventually help the country adopt AI advances at scale, the quality of that education determines how quickly or effectively education can encourage AI diffusion. If training is divorced from practical applications, graduates will struggle to adapt cutting-edge advances from industry labs into the sectors in which they work. Consider one commonly used standard to measure the baseline quality of AI education: whether a university employs at least one researcher who has published at least one paper at a leading AI conference. According to data from 2023–24, only 38 universities in China met this standard; the United States accounted for 150.

    China’s centrally planned approach to AI development is also counterproductive when it comes to diffusion. In 2025, China developed an “AI Plus” action strategy that outlines targets for AI adoption over the next decade and released guidelines for government agencies and local officials on how to put the plan into effect across the country. For many observers, the mere existence of a plan showed that the highest levels of Chinese leadership were committed to spreading AI widely and that China was better positioned to win the AI race than the United States, which lacks any kind of similar diffusion blueprint. Rudd’s claims about China’s edge in AI adoption, for instance, cite Beijing’s ambitious policies and targets for AI diffusion as supporting evidence.

    But centralized approaches such as China’s often impede technology diffusion, especially when the state tries to intervene in domains in which the development trajectory is uncertain. One of the planks of China’s AI Plus blueprint identifies “global cooperation” as a priority sector for AI adoption. If local governments were to implement the plan as outlined, it would shift resources from areas in which diffusion has been proven to be effective, such as health care, to the undefined space of “global cooperation.” More broadly, Beijing’s favoritism toward state-owned enterprises and its preference for picking national champions often prop up inefficient technologies that would have been weeded out by market-based competition. Other businesses are unlikely to adopt inefficient technologies, making nonmarket forms of AI development less likely to diffuse widely.

    Counterintuitively, the lack of a clear U.S. policy on AI diffusion is a boon, not a hindrance, to the United States’ attempt to diffuse the technology across the economy. At the height of U.S.-Japanese competition in the 1980s, for instance, when the two countries were racing to train software engineers who could spread computer technology, Japan’s Ministry of Education, Science, and Culture, as it was then known, exercised centralized control over universities. But emerging trends in computer science developed faster than the government could adapt. By concentrating state funds on centers of excellence and imposing one-size-fits-all rules on the computing curriculum, Japan could not match the adaptability of American universities, and the United States surged ahead. Cross-national studies have shown that decentralized science and technology systems are correlated with faster diffusion of latest innovations.

    Industry observers note that another historical case with parallels to China, the Soviet Union, further suggests how centralization is antithetical to diffusion. In the twentieth century, the Soviet Union boasted many prepares for technology development. Yet its top-down approach, which focused on large-scale engineering projects, undercut market-based instruments that encourage technology diffusion through competition. As a result, although the Soviet Union pioneered upcoming technologies in many areas, including the casting of steel, it fell behind the United States in adopting general-purpose technologies such as computers. A prescient U.S. intelligence report published in 1969 deemed the Soviet Union’s mechanisms for technology diffusion as “much more balky” than those of the United States because of the absence of competitive pressures as well as limited linkages between the R & D system and the broader economy.

    The myth of China’s lead in AI diffusion persists despite clear data showing U.S. advantages. In part, this may be because China’s innovation system has facilitated the widespread adoption of certain visible technologies. In less than 20 years, China has built more than 30,000 miles of high-speed rail, for example, blanketing the country with ultra-fast trains that now reach even the most remote provinces.

    Recent findings suggest that but infrastructure presents a very different challenge than AI does. The centralized pressure that officials can use to effectively develop large-scale infrastructure projects is much less effective for general-purpose technologies like AI because it is infeasible to mandate that all small- and medium-size firms, spread across every sector of the economy, adopt artificial intelligence. Those companies would do so only if it made sense from a business perspective, and few have the digital foundations or savvy employees able to harness AI in a way that would help them grow. Moreover, the United States has outbuilt China in the infrastructure most essential to AI development, data centers, in which it retains a ten-to-one edge. In fact, in some cases, the data centers that China has built remain idle because of weak AI demand.

    The misperception that China leads AI diffusion may continue unabated because analysis of the country’s technology ecosystem is overly focused on frontier firms such as ByteDance and DeepSeek and first-tier cities, such as Beijing and Shanghai. Yet AI diffusion ultimately rests on whether adoption occurs in medium size companies, small towns, and inland provinces, where it has been extremely limited. Because these settings rarely feature in outside media coverage, analysis of China’s AI diffusion landscape underestimates the difficulty of translating cutting-edge advances from frontier labs and universities in Hangzhou or Shenzhen to, say, a small firm in a county seat in northwestern Qinghai Province.

    It has been revealed that perhaps the simplest explanation is that such a myth is useful, even if ultimately untrue. In some ways, the United States is trumpeting Beijing’s AI diffusion in the way that Chinese “tiger parents” try to motivate their children to work harder by raising the success of “that other family’s kid.” “Look at how well that other family’s kid performed at the piano recital,” they might say, without listening closely to ensure that the notes were exactly right. In great-power rivalry, too, there is a natural tendency to overhype the other side’s capabilities, in part to spur more effort at home.

    It has been revealed that but such a “useful” myth can backfire if it pushes the United States to overlook its own advantages or even to mimic China’s more top-down approach to AI development. By any measure, the United States maintains a comfortable lead in AI diffusion, and China, despite its impressive successes, has serious challenges. Although the narrative of Chinese dominance endures, for now all signs point to a U.S. lead that will remain strong.

    Ukraine’s Shadow War in Africa

    📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1850 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foreignpolicy

    ⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
