    💡 Key Takeaways
    • The highlights this week: Ukraine attacks Russian vessels in Libya in “response to Russia’s war,” Gambia wins a landmark case at the International Court of Justice, and African nations respond to a disappointing United Nations climate summit.
    • The highlights this week: Ukraine attacks Russian vessels in Libya in “response to Russia’s war,” Gambia wins a landmark case at the International Court of Justice, and African nations respond to a disappointing United Nations climate summit.
    • Kyiv claimed responsibility on Monday for a recent attack on two Russian vessels off the coast of Libya, including the corvette Merkury, one of Russia’s newest warships.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Welcome to Foreign Policy’s Africa Brief.

    The highlights this week: Ukraine attacks Russian vessels in Libya in “response to Russia’s war,” Gambia wins a landmark case at the International Court of Justice, and African nations respond to a disappointing United Nations climate summit.

    Welcome to Foreign Policy’s Africa Brief.

    The highlights this week: Ukraine attacks Russian vessels in Libya in “response to Russia’s war,” Gambia wins a landmark case at the International Court of Justice, and African nations respond to a disappointing United Nations climate summit.

    Kyiv claimed responsibility on Monday for a recent attack on two Russian vessels off the coast of Libya, including the corvette Merkury, one of Russia’s newest warships. The vessels had been docked at the Benghazi naval base when the attack occurred on Sunday.

    Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has described the operation as “exemplary” and noted that it was in “response to Russia’s war.”.

    Yet security experts warn that conducting drone strikes within a region that is not involved in the Russia-Ukraine war could set a dangerous precedent, especially as they fear Africa is becoming a proxy theater in the conflict.

    The United Nations mission in Libya, known as UNSMIL, has called for “an immediate, independent and transparent investigation” into the drone strikes. “Libya cannot afford, and must not become, a battleground for foreign conflicts,” UNSMIL wrote on X.

    Sources indicate that kyiv has confirmed that seven Ukrainian-made naval drones had been debuted from a “mothership” in the region, though it did not clarify how they were transported there. Some unverified Libyan sources have alleged that Tripoli’s U.N.-recognized government may have aided Ukraine, which Tripoli strongly denied.

    Both of Libya’s rival administrations—the government in Tripoli, led by Prime Minister Abdul Hamid Dbeibah, and a Russia-backed government based in Benghazi, controlled by Gen. Khalifa Haftar—have denounced the attacks.

    Following the 2024 fall of the Assad regime in Syria, where Russia operates a naval base, Moscow has sought alternative military footprints in Africa, including by pursuing airbases in eastern Libya. Syria served as a logistical hub for transferring troops and arms to landlocked Sahel nations, where Russia’s mercenary Africa Corps helps fight jihadists.

    With Syria growing closer to the United States and Europe, Libya now serves as that hub, explained Ulf Laessing, the head of the Syria/Iraq program at the Konrad-Adenauer-Stiftung and the author of Understanding Libya Since Gaddafi.

    “Ukraine is trying to hit Russia wherever they can. It’s difficult for Ukraine to hit Russian targets where the Africa Corps is based in the Sahel,” Laessing mentioned. “It’s more efficient and easier to do it where Russia is basically bringing goods.”.

    Zain Hussain, a researcher at the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute, mentioned that “through this attack, Ukraine is showing that it can target Russia’s geopolitical interests as well as fighting a war with Russia at home.”.

    The strikes come amid increasing concern that the war in Ukraine is spreading to other African countries. Ukrainian drone specialists have been deployed to Libya, Mali, and Sudan, according to a September CNN report. A source also told CNN that troops from Chad, Niger, and Burkina Faso had traveled to Mali to receive drone training from Ukrainian soldiers, though several experts told me that the evidence for this is speculative at best.

    Meanwhile, in the Sahel, multiple media reports have accused Ukraine of supporting and training northern Mali’s Tuareg separatists in recent years as a means of wearing down Russian forces there.

    Experts suspect Ukrainian drone assistance in the Tuareg ambush that killed dozens of Russian Wagner mercenaries and Malian soldiers in 2024. At the time, Andriy Yusov, a spokesperson for Ukrainian military intelligence, mentioned that the rebels had been given the “necessary” information to carry out the attacks. Yusov’s comments prompted Mali to sever relations with Ukraine, accusing Kyiv of supporting a “barbaric” attack by terrorists.

    It has been revealed that analysts also suspected Ukrainian involvement in the brief insurgent takeover of Mali’s strategic town of Kidal earlier this year by Tuareg and al Qaeda-linked jihadists. Ukraine’s Foreign Ministry has officially rejected the allegations.

    Ukraine’s latest attacks are unlikely to disrupt eastern Libya’s ties with Russia, Laessing said, especially as Moscow needs “a country on the way to the Sahel.” Still, they add a layer of complexity to long-standing violence and drone warfare in Sahelian nations, said Virginie Baudais, the director of the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute’s Sahel and West Africa program.

    As Baudais put it, the “internationalization of the conflict” in the Sahel will only contribute to “the escalation of violence, with the highest cost for civilian populations.”.

    In a recent development, monday, Nov. 23, to Friday, Nov. 27: The Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention’s public health conference is held in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia.

    Sources indicate that friday, Nov. 27: The deadline for councils in South Africa to elect their leaders.

    Somalia-UAE rift. Last week, Somalia expelled the United Arab Emirates’ ambassador and recalled its own envoy from Abu Dhabi, citing ​violations of the country’s sovereignty that amounted to an “open invasion.”.

    Industry observers note that the dispute stems from growing Emirati ties with Ethiopia and the Somalian breakaway regions of Somaliland and Puntland. Somali President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud also accused the UAE of having played a role in Israel’s recognition of Somaliland last December in a statement to Somalian state news agency SONNA.

    The UAE’s state-owned DP World and its subsidiaries operate ports in those breakaway regions. They have expanded the Berbera port in Somaliland and are developing a road corridor connecting it to landlocked Ethiopia. In January 2024, Addis Ababa signed a memorandum of understanding to eventually recognize Somaliland’s independence in exchange for naval and commercial access to Berbera.

    A Newly introduced York Times report using satellite imagery recently found that the UAE has turned airports in Berbera and Bosaso, a city in Puntland, into military facilities.

    In response to Somalia’s latest move, the UAE stated its embassy in Somalia had been closed since January, after Mogadishu canceled bilateral agreements, and it strongly denounced the “escalatory and hostile approach” by the Somali government amid the latest diplomatic spat.

    It has been revealed that ICJ ruling. Gambia, the smallest nation in mainland Africa, won a landmark case last week when the International Court of Justice (ICJ) ruled that Myanmar committed genocide in its 2017 military campaign that killed at least 10,000 members of the Rohingya Muslim minority community and displaced more than 700,000 into neighboring Bangladesh.

    A Muslim-majority nation, Gambia brought the case to the court in 2019. Now, the ruling has possible implications for South Africa’s ICJ genocide case against Israel for its operations in Gaza.

    In a recent development, both Myanmar and Israel have defended their actions as counterinsurgency operations. But in its decision, the court considered a pattern of mass killings, the razing of homes, and forced exodus. That finding “gives South Africa more avenues ​to argue for genocide” in Gaza, Israeli legal expert Yuval Shany told Reuters.

    Industry observers note that COP31’s failures. This year’s U.N. climate summit, known as COP31, in Turkey ended on Sunday without an agreement after references to phasing out fossil fuels were removed from the draft text. Despite being the most attended COP to date, some observers have called it the “worst” one ever.

    In a recent development, at the summit, African delegations voiced discontent with financial commitments for climate adaptation. Wealthier nations pledged only $50 million in total to the climate adaptation fund, far short of the $300 million annual target. They also largely offered loans rather than grants. The United States, the United Kingdom, Canada, France, Italy, and Australia did not make any funding commitments.

    Africa, which is home to 17 percent of the world’s population, is responsible for just 4 percent of global carbon emissions. Yet the continent faces disproportionate impacts from climate change.

    The African Group of Negotiators (AGN), chaired by Ghana, rejected attempts to weaken both finance targets and the Paris Agreement’s goal of limiting warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius. It said that the debate on fossil fuels had “overshadowed” broken promises on adaptation finance.

    “Those who were arguing about whether we should get fossil fuels in the cover decision or not were producers, exporters, importers and users of fossil fuels,” AGN chair Antwi-Boasiako Amoah stated. “It was hypocrisy.”.

    AFCON verdict. Senegal was reinstated as the 2025 Africa Cup of Nations champion in a much-anticipated ruling by the Court of Arbitration for Sport on Tuesday.

    Senegal initially won the final against Morocco 1-0 in extra time in January. Two months later, however, the Confederation of African Football (CAF) stripped the country of its title, awarding it to Morocco because Senegalese players temporarily walked off the pitch to protest refereeing decisions.

    The court overturned CAF’s decision because the match was allowed to conclude. “By blowing his whistle to restart play, the Referee considered that the conditions for resuming the match had been met,” the court noted in a statement. Morocco plans to appeal the decision.

    Sudanese excavations. Last week, archaeologists unearthed the original floor of the largest medieval church in Nubia, in northern Sudan’s ancient city of Old Dongola. It was part of Makuria, one of three Christian Nubian kingdoms that existed from the sixth to 16th centuries.

    In a recent development, the church was first discovered in 2021, but excavations were suspended two years later following the outbreak of Sudan’s civil war. Operations resumed last year in the abandoned city, which has managed to escape widespread destruction from the conflict so far.

    UNESCO estimated that more than 100 cultural sites have been damaged, looted, or destroyed since fighting began in Sudan in April 2023.

    Recent findings suggest that troll farmers. In HumAngle, Shade Mary-Ann Olaoye reports on U.S.-based social media influencers exploiting false narratives of a Christian genocide in Nigeria for engagement and donations. These accounts have posted artificial intelligence-generated content and videos from elsewhere in Africa, including Somalia, as supposed evidence of persecution in Nigeria.

    Sources indicate that as the creators “continue to spread misinformation, concerns are growing that their online influence could have real-world consequences,” Olaoye writes. “Campaigns like these can deepen ethno-religious fault lines, shape political decisions, and fuel reprisal attacks.”.

    AI bioweapons. In Rest of World, Danai Nesta Kupemba reports on researchers at a small AI lab in Ghana who “jailbroke” their own drug-discovery AI model, which allowed them to quickly design thousands of toxic molecules, to warn about the potential for AI bioweapons misuse.

    “Scholars have long warned about AI’s bioweapons threat, but it is only recently that AI systems have truly outperformed Ph.D.-level biologists,” Kupemba writes.

    #225842. The Model Middle Power

    📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1823 w)

    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Foreignaffairs ↗ Open Full Page

    The Model Middle Power

    📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1823 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foreignaffairs

    ⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • ANDREW YEO is a Senior Fellow and SK-Korea Foundation Chair at the Brookings Institution and Professor of Politics at the Catholic University of America.
    • In the ten months since Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney gave his widely discussed speech at the World Economic Forum in Davos, the question of whether, and how, the world’s middle powers can help rebuild a broken international order has become increasingly urgent.
    • Industry observers note that although the Canadian prime minister’s bold vision was widely applauded, some experts thought his agenda was overly ambitious.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    ANDREW YEO is a Senior Fellow and SK-Korea Foundation Chair at the Brookings Institution and Professor of Politics at the Catholic University of America. This essay is adapted from his forthcoming book South Korea’s Grand Strategy: Narratives and the Rise of a Global Nation.

    What South Korea Gets Right About Geopolitics.

    In the ten months since Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney gave his widely discussed speech at the World Economic Forum in Davos, the question of whether, and how, the world’s middle powers can help rebuild a broken international order has become increasingly urgent. In his remarks, Carney stressed that although the old U.S.-led alliance system was collapsing, middle powers—states that do not have the ability to reshape global politics but that still possess substantial might—were well positioned to pick up the slack. But to do so, Carney argued, they would need to build up their “strength at home” and “act together” to harness their collective power, even in the absence of backing from the world’s hegemon.

    Industry observers note that although the Canadian prime minister’s bold vision was widely applauded, some experts thought his agenda was overly ambitious. They noted, correctly, that it would be very difficult for middle powers to build a grand alliance composed of countries as diverse as Brazil, Canada, South Africa, and Turkey. “The path to unity among middle powers is fraught because this group includes rich and poor countries, as well as small and large ones,” wrote the economist Eswar Prasad in February. Carney, however, is right that middle powers have an opportunity to thrive going forward. Even when aligning with great powers, these countries can still exercise greater autonomy by developing national capacity and diversifying external partnerships.

    South Korea offers a prime example of this flexible approach. For decades, Seoul has pursued a middle-power strategy centered on building domestic strength and forging partnerships with democracies everywhere while deepening its alliance with Washington. South Korea has been adaptable, recalibrating its security alignments, economic strategies, and diplomatic roles as regional and global conditions require. This has enabled a country smaller in size than most of the world’s states to punch far above its weight, exercising substantial influence in Asia and beyond.

    Recent findings suggest that not every government can follow Seoul’s path, and South Korea’s strategy has its limits. As Seoul itself acknowledges, middle powers cannot escape great-power competition. But the country has begun to show what middle powers can accomplish when they leverage their partnerships and their own strength to protect their interests and deter larger threats. And by maintaining and even building its ties to the United States while asserting greater autonomy, South Korea has proven that middle powers can strengthen themselves without building whole new networks—contrary to Carney’s suggestion.

    According to classic international relations theory, grand strategy is the exclusive provenance of great powers. The United States’s effort to contain the Soviet Union during the Cold War is a paradigmatic example; China’s pursuit of global economic primacy is another. Middle powers, by contrast, have little say in such strategies. Instead, these countries are seen as primarily reactive in their foreign policies, navigating around the decisions of the great powers rather than setting the agenda themselves.

    But recent history suggests that the division between great and middle powers is less clear-cut than has been assumed. In practice, middle powers very much have their own affirmative visions that they pursue in the world. They have the leeway to decide which threats matter most to them, which partnerships to prioritize, and where to invest scarce resources. Japan, concerned with the threat posed by China, has been quietly exercising leadership in the Indo-Pacific by improving its ties with neighbors, increasing investment and aid to the region, and strengthening its own defense capabilities—all while remaining closely allied with the United States. India, worried about China, Pakistan, and growing economic headwinds, has successfully bolstered partnerships with the United States and other democracies but maintained its relationship with Russia.

    Sources indicate that much like Japan and India, South Korea is worried about its neighbors. But for Seoul, this is nothing new. South Korean leaders have been concerned with the very thing Carney fretted about in his Davos speech—becoming collateral damage in conflicts between great powers— since at least the late nineteenth century, when it was caught between China, Japan, and Russia. The country has a well-known proverb, “When whales fight, the shrimp's back is broken,” that captures the sentiment that great-power feuds can harm countries caught in the middle.

    Industry observers note that to safeguard against this threat, Seoul has long sought to increase its self-reliance through industrial policy. The country transited from light to heavy export industries in the 1970s, turning it into a major player in the chemical, steel, and shipbuilding sectors. State investments helped it become a major global producer of batteries and semiconductors in the present era. South Korea takes great pride in what historians call “the miracle on the Han”—or the country's rapid rise from a war-torn and impoverished state to a rich one during the late twentieth century. They now use the state’s wealth to promote public goods globally, contributing to international development, global health, climate policy, and multilateral bodies.

    Seoul has also built up a formidable military, one that experts consistently rank as among the strongest in the world. Today, many South Korean analysts argue that Seoul needs a nuclear arsenal for self-defense, even though the country officially remains under Washington’s nuclear umbrella. The state has simultaneously used its armed prowess to deepen relations with U.S. allies. Seoul, for example, has inked multibillion-dollar arms deals with European buyers, making it a key partner in rebuilding NATO’s industrial capacity. In 2025, it was the second largest supplier of weapons to European NATO members (after the United States). South Korea has also forged defense partnerships in the Middle East and Southeast Asia, widening Seoul's options and reducing its dependence on any single market. South Korea, in other words, has been able to convert its economic resources and bureaucratic capabilities into greater influence by expanding its partnerships, strengthening its voice in international bodies, and helping shape global rules and norms.

    It has been revealed that but even as it charts its own path, Seoul has no plans to abandon the United States, at least in the near future. In fact, the sanctity of the U.S.-South Korean relationship is a significant historical Korean narrative. Many South Koreans see the alliance as a bond inked in blood, thanks to the sacrifice both countries made during the Korean War, when they worked to stop North Korea, backed by China and the Soviet Union, from overrunning the south. Most South Koreans correctly believe that the continued U.S. military presence in the country—currently, 28,500 American troops are stationed on the peninsula—has played a major part in deterring North Korean aggression over the past seven decades.

    At first glance, South Korea’s strategy may seem contradictory. On the one hand, the country wants to deepen its cooperation with the United States, on which it still depends for security. But on the other, it seeks greater autonomy.

    Yet these twin goals are not actually at odds. By cultivating ties with Washington, Seoul has gained access to advanced military capabilities and technologies as well as a larger diplomatic platform to expand its regional and global interests. It is in part because of this relationship, for example, that South Korea has had such success at selling weapons to multiple NATO members, including Croatia, Estonia, Finland, Norway, Poland, and Romania. (Seoul has also built up a formidable diplomatic apparatus in its own right.) At the same time, South Korea helps make this compact worthwhile for the United States by providing it with valuable technology, including semiconductor chips. Seoul has also partnered with the Washington to help revive the American shipbuilding industry, agreeing to invest $150 billion in the U.S. sector.

    Still, South Korea’s growing push for more independence in its foreign policy does result in some tensions with the United States that cannot easily be resolved. For instance, the current government’s push to give Seoul, not Washington, operational control over both states’ forces on the peninsula in the event of war has been rebuffed by the U.S. military. American commanders instead favor a conditions-based transfer after South Korea has proven it has the capabilities to lead a joint defense, rather than setting a fixed date. The two sides also have not reached a consensus on what role South Korea would play if Taiwan is attacked or blockaded by China.

    In a recent development, yet so far, Seoul has done an effective job at managing these differences. For example, in his second term, U.S. President Donald Trump has repeatedly accused Washington’s allies, including South Korea, of leeching off the United States and not paying their fair share. To extract more from Washington’s partners, Trump has implemented punishing tariffs. In response, South Korea could have been defiant and slapped on retaliatory restrictions, as other U.S. allies did. Instead, South Korean President Lee Jae-myung avoided rebuking the president and worked to meet American demands in ways that heightened the two states’ mutual dependence. For instance, Lee pledged to invest $350 billion in the United States to advance American economic and national security interests, including by purchasing more U.S. military equipment, and to increase South Korean economic support for locally stationed American forces.

    Seoul’s strategy has not been a uniform success. The South Korean economy remains exposed to American and Chinese pressure despite its growth and diversification. North Korea is expanding its nuclear and missile forces and deepening military ties with Russia, creating new security headaches for which Seoul still needs U.S. assistance. The country is politically polarized, resulting in sharp policy shifts that can undermine long-term strategic planning. It also suffers from the lowest birthrate of any country in the world, threatening its tax base and the size of its armed forces. Beyond that, South Korea may not provide the ideal template for every middle power. Not every country in this category has similar economic resources, networks, or ties to the United States.

    It has been revealed that but on the whole, South Korea’s grand strategy has been effective, and it thus carries broader lessons. For one, it shows how adaptive middle powers can draw on their respective national narratives to find their strengths and to chart a path forward. Perhaps more important, it is proof positive that middle powers can exercise influence and achieve a measure of autonomy even without working together to build a neutral third pole, as Carney urged. It also illustrates that middle powers can remain firmly allied with the United States while developing their own independent capabilities. South Korea, then, demonstrates that states can reduce their vulnerability and widen their political options.

    An earlier version of this article incorrectly stated that the South Korean government was known to be considering developing nuclear weapons.

    #225841. Against an Axis of Anything

    📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1610 w)
    📖 Baca
    General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Foreignpolicy ↗ Open Full Page

    Against an Axis of Anything

    📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1610 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foreignpolicy

    ⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Those picking up a copy of the Economist this week might have been struck with an unpleasant sense of nostalgia.
    • Recent findings suggest that reminiscent of the war on terror and all its fearmongering excesses, this headline was widely mocked on social media as a reminder of the George W.
    • Those picking up a copy of the Economist this week might have been struck with an unpleasant sense of nostalgia.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Get audio access with any FP subscription.

    Those picking up a copy of the Economist this week might have been struck with an unpleasant sense of nostalgia. Readers were greeted with a front cover emblazoned in red and black, with a screaming headline proclaiming the “axis of malice.”.

    Recent findings suggest that reminiscent of the war on terror and all its fearmongering excesses, this headline was widely mocked on social media as a reminder of the George W. Bush era. Those who mocked it were in turn derided as naive; growing connections among Russia, China, Iran, and North Korea surely, others argued, prove the existence of such an axis.

    Those picking up a copy of the Economist this week might have been struck with an unpleasant sense of nostalgia. Readers were greeted with a front cover emblazoned in red and black, with a screaming headline proclaiming the “axis of malice.”.

    Sources indicate that reminiscent of the war on terror and all its fearmongering excesses, this headline was widely mocked on social media as a reminder of the George W. Bush era. Those who mocked it were in turn derided as naive; growing connections among Russia, China, Iran, and North Korea surely, others argued, prove the existence of such an axis.

    But most of this debate missed the point. No one—or at least very few people—would deny that we have seen ties between China and Russia grow in recent years. The use of the axis framing, however, and of language like “malice,” creates a narrative that does not necessarily exist in practice. It suggests that the only response to growing alignment between these states is adversarial, inhibits us from any real debate about the extent and scope of this coordination, and perhaps most importantly, suggests that this process of alignment is inevitable, rather than something that can be molded or changed. Such overly simplistic and Manichaean visions weaken, rather than strengthen, our ability to understand the world.

    None of this is newly introduced. The “axis of evil” first emerged as a term in President George W. Bush’s 2002 State of the Union address, where he referred to Iran, Iraq, and North Korea as countries that endangered freedom around the world. Even at the time, the inclusion of the line in the speech was somewhat strange: It took place just a few months after the Sept. 11 attacks, and shortly after the United States had invaded Afghanistan, yet the three countries representing “evil” had nothing to do with either.

    It has been revealed that but the overblown rhetoric helped to build support for Bush’s Freedom Agenda by reinforcing the idea that dictatorships around the world could endanger daily life in democracies. It attempted to tie the war on terror to the legacy of World War II through implicit comparison to Nazi Germany and imperial Japan. The speech had real-world consequences: It helped the Bush administration build the case for its war against Iraq and undermined the thawing of relations between the United States and Iran that had started shortly after 9/11.

    Since that time, there have been repeated attempts to revive the axis concept to make a political or foreign-policy point. In just the last few years alone, there have been articles about the axis of authoritarians, the axis of upheaval, and the axis of aggressors. All these formulations offer authors the same opportunity: Pick a selection of nations and define them, not on their own terms, but on yours.

    Recent findings suggest that the axis of authoritarians, for example, relies on regime type to tie together its members, though the list of countries involved (Russia, Iran, North Korea, Belarus, and China) includes unreformed Soviet-style totalitarian regimes, kleptocratic dictatorships, and party-rule capitalism. This group includes one of the world’s richest states—and one of its poorest. The axis of upheaval, meanwhile, is defined by countries’ opposition to the United States, or by their shared commitment to “overturn[ing] the global order.” In truth, one could have an axis of almost anything; one is reminded of the old joke from around the time of Bush’s initial speech that suggested groupings including the “axis of just as evil” and the “axis of countries that aren’t the worst but certainly won’t be asked to host the Olympics.”.

    Jokes aside, there is no denying that there are points of convergence and cooperation between the states referenced in these groupings. The reporting that accompanies the axis of malice story, for example, identifies a shared interest in the sanctions-busting “shadow” oil trade as a key area of cooperation among Russia, China, and Iran. Russia and China are cooperating on defense industrial issues, while Russia has built stronger ties with both Iran and North Korea due to its war in Ukraine and the search for cheap drones and easily replaceable domestic labor. There is a very clear case to be made that the bilateral relationships between many of these countries have grown stronger in recent years, to the detriment of U.S. national security.

    Skeptics of the axis notion, however, would argue that many of these areas of cooperation were themselves driven by U.S. sanctions policy, not sought out by the states in question. There are clear tensions between Moscow and Beijing when it comes to North Korea, while China has been remarkably reticent in supporting either Russia’s war in Ukraine or Iran’s war with the United States. The evidence of growing bilateral ties between states is not matched by evidence of a common front among these states. Looked at holistically, many of their actions can just as easily by explained as states that find their interests—at least temporarily—pointing in the same direction.

    Regardless of whether the skeptics or proponents of a more integrated partnership among these states are correct, this is an important debate. Indeed, it’s vitally important for U.S. policymakers to understand the scope and extent of cooperation between potentially adversarial states. The axis framing itself, however, is fundamentally unhelpful in moving these debates forward.

    In a recent development, for one thing, formulations like axis of upheaval and axis of malice are less descriptive than prescriptive: They always suggest the worst, and push policymakers toward the most hawkish options. Consider the description of growing China-Russia trade ties as “collusion.” Were the U.S. to engage in such trade with any of its allies, this would be considered perfectly normal behavior. Indeed, think tank papers are published every day in Washington talking of ways to increase resilience among the U.S. and its allies. The states under discussion here are often bad actors in world affairs, but adjectives like malice or upheaval suggest Manichaean actors implacably opposed to the United States with no nuance involved.

    Sources indicate that the all-or-nothing nature of this framing also makes it more difficult to have discussions about the actual extent and scope of coordination between these states. By portraying them as a unified front—and by framing the debate as whether or not there is an axis—discussion often glosses over more interesting and potentially useful questions: Where specifically are these states cooperating? Are there limits to that cooperation? Are there concerns on which they compete or where their interests diverge?

    Sources indicate that perhaps most importantly, the notion of an axis of unfriendly states overlooks questions about how we got to this point—and whether this set of affairs must necessarily endure. At least some of the recent collaboration between these states has been shaped by U.S. policy choices, from sanctions and export controls on Russia and China, to the war in Iran and its effects in raising global oil prices. U.S. policymakers may still judge these policies to be worth the cost, yet it is fundamentally misleading to suggest that Russia, China, Iran, and others are pulling together purely to oppose the United States, when at least some of that coordination is a response to U.S. actions.

    Recent findings suggest that to put it another way: The idea of an axis of upheaval attempting to overturn global order strips the United States of its agency and replaces it with predestination. This is particularly notable when it comes to the policy responses. An axis of aggression cannot be reasoned with and it cannot be split apart, leaving little for the United States to do other than resist it. A more nuanced understanding of why these states cooperate—and where their common cause might fail—offers opportunities for the U.S. to undermine that alignment. If we understand the causes of adversaries’ alignment, we might be able to predict or even prevent it.

    It’s easy to see why the language of the axis persists: It sells. But there’s a reason why such headlines should be relentlessly mocked. They deny us the ability to have a nuanced debate and reduce our policy options to an unsatisfying binary. For those who take U.S. foreign policy seriously, it’s past time to retire the axis of evil for good.

    Emma Ashford is a columnist at Foreign Policy and senior fellow with the Stimson Center’s Reimagining U.S. Grand Strategy Program. She is also an adjunct assistant professor at Georgetown University and the author of Oil, the State, and War. X: @EmmaMAshford.

    WHITE HOUSE DOUBLES DOWN AFTER TRUMP ANGERS BASE BY FLOATING ILLEGAL ALIEN DEAL WITH DEMS.

    #225839. Trump pardons turkeys but Hill influence isn’t all gravy after midterm roasting

    📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1247 w)

    Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Rollcall ↗ Open Full Page

    Trump pardons turkeys but Hill influence isn’t all gravy after midterm roasting

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1247 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that president Donald Trump, first lady Melania Trump and Speaker Mike Johnson are all smiles at the annual Thanksgiving turkey pardon at the White House.
    • President Donald Trump on Tuesday celebrated what he called one of the “immense powers” of his office, pardoning two turkeys ahead of the Thanksgiving holiday.
    • Joined by first lady Melania Trump and Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., set to lose power in January after he hands the gavel to a Democratic successor, Trump for the sixth time spared the long necks of two American turkeys — this time “Feathers” and “Freedom.”.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that president Donald Trump, first lady Melania Trump and Speaker Mike Johnson are all smiles at the annual Thanksgiving turkey pardon at the White House. (Finn Gomez/Getty Images).

    President Donald Trump on Tuesday celebrated what he called one of the “immense powers” of his office, pardoning two turkeys ahead of the Thanksgiving holiday. But lawmakers say his influence on Capitol Hill has already changed since Republicans’ midterm losses.

    Joined by first lady Melania Trump and Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., set to lose power in January after he hands the gavel to a Democratic successor, Trump for the sixth time spared the long necks of two American turkeys — this time “Feathers” and “Freedom.”.

    “In a few moments, under the immense powers vested in me by the Constitution of the United States of America, I will grant a full, absolute and unconditional pardon — meaning they will live forever — to two magnificent Thanksgiving turkeys, special turkeys,” Trump mentioned, suggesting he could extend his power to spare the birds from the holiday dining table to somehow grant them immortality.

    While voters punished his party’s candidates for doing too little to address high prices and his decision to join Israel in going to war with Iran, Trump on Tuesday remained focused on another area of largely unchallenged authority — his White House projects. He began the event by touting the yearly event, for the first time, being held on the helipad he had built on the White House’s South Lawn. Later, he announced aims for another new location next year.

    “I'm told that per the long-running tradition, these exquisite animals stayed overnight at the nearby Willard Hotel. Unfortunately, for 200 years, the White House lacked appropriate accommodation to host such distinguished guests,” he stated of the turkeys. “I'm pleased to announce that next year we'll be able to have a special location right over there in that rather small ballroom being built. It's going to host a lot of people and a couple of turkeys next year. We're going to do it inside.”.

    Trump also highlighted that the two bright, white turkeys were raised in West Virginia — which he carried more than 40 points when he was on the ballot. The turkeys, now spared, will spend their remaining years in Texas, a state where Democrats scored two of their most high profile wins in the House and Senate races — something Trump left unmentioned.

    The pre-holiday vibes were lighthearted on Tuesday, with the president slated to later travel to South Florida for a Thanksgiving weekend of turkey and time at one of his golf clubs. But when he returns, lawmakers will continue assessing how much sway he still has on Capitol Hill as he begins what, for his predecessors, were their lame-duck eras.

    One Republican Senate ally acknowledged his influence with lawmakers already has changed.

    “I think it's going to be policy-to-policy on that,” stated Senate Republican Conference Vice Chair James Lankford.

    According to recent reports, “But he's the president of the United States all the way to the very end. So he still has his veto pen,” the Oklahoman added. “He still has the ability to be able to direct agencies to engage. We're passing legislation. It takes three to tango: House, Senate, and the White House.”.

    Senate Commerce Committee Chair Ted Cruz of Texas noted Trump’s influence, once the Democrat-controlled House and Senate are seated on Jan. 3, “will, obviously, be different.”.

    “I don't think the incoming Democrat majorities are interested in passing productive legislation and passing pro-jobs legislation,” stated Cruz, a potential 2028 GOP presidential candidate. “I think, instead, they're just going to attack the president all day long.”.

    Still, Cruz predicted “the president will continue to lead.”.

    Sources indicate that trump on Monday demonstrated how he likely intends to use his lame-duck influence on and off Capitol Hill when he successfully pushed for the reinstatement of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. During an interview with CNBC’s Eamon Javers, Trump made an admission that would be stunning from any other sitting American president about a private company, saying he had been “speaking to the board directly and indirectly.”.

    In a Monday statement, Nvidia mentioned its board had “received input from senior levels of the United States government, and based on that input, the board is confident that Mr. Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk.”.

    Such unprecedented moves are a massive reason why Sen. Rick Scott, R-Fla., last week stated he expects Trump to be Trump — despite overseeing a midterms campaign he insisted be about himself and his unpopular second-term record.

    In a recent development, “Any president is going to have a lot of influence because they get to run the executive branch,” said Scott, a former Sunshine State chief executive. “And they have the biggest pulpit in the world. So he's going to continue to have a lot of influence.”.

    Still, some Republican lawmakers have criticized Trump and his team for what they call recent stumbles.

    Sources indicate that sen. Jim Banks of Indiana last week told reporters he had “a lot of questions” about how Trump and his administration handled upgrades to the country’s air traffic control system that prompted a nationwide ground stop on Nov. 13.

    Recent findings suggest that “Somebody needs to be held accountable for what happened,” he said, raising concerns about the president demanding $50 billion in additional taxpayer monies to build a fresh system. “I’m not fully convinced that throwing out more money is going to solve the fundamental problems.”.

    Trump also has taken ample friendly fire on social media from GOP members over his interference in the Huang scandal.

    North Carolina GOP Rep. Pat Harrigan took to X to say the Nvidia founder’s reinstatement was “a mistake.”.

    Recent findings suggest that “For the past two years, I have privately mentioned there is no way Jensen Huang can argue for the exportation of advanced American chips to China without being compromised. Turns out, well, we all know,” Harrigan wrote after Trump contended an administration probe had “exonerated” Huang of any potential wrongdoing. “There may come a time when forgiveness is warranted, but there are still too many unanswered questions and too much unmitigated risk. Today’s coordinated action between the company and this administration is likely to whitewash this risk.”.

    Harrigan, a rare Tar Heel State Republican incumbent to win another term, echoed other GOP lawmakers in calling for an in-depth congressional probe in the Huang scandal and his affair with an alleged Chinese intelligence operative.

    Next week could offer an early test of other Republicans’ willingness to break more publicly with Trump on certain complications, as Huang is scheduled to appear before multiple congressional committees.

    Even before Trump threw his political weight behind Huang’s return, Democratic Sen. Tim Kaine of Virginia said he had sensed a GOP president who had lost clout with his party’s Senate conference.

    “I think the Nvidia glitch has caused some major concerns about the Trump China policy, obviously,” Kaine said. “That is definitely creating some anxiety.”.

    Trump has given clues that he is as concerned with his influence among the incoming Democratic majorities.

    Sources indicate that “If they want to get things done, I want to get things done, too,” Trump remarked during a Friday press conference at the White House. “You know, there are those that say we might get more done because we had some Republicans that were just impossible to deal with.”.

    #225837. Avoiding Colombia’s Escalation Trap

    📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 17m • 📚 Deep Dive (3383 w)

    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Foreignaffairs ↗ Open Full Page

    Avoiding Colombia’s Escalation Trap

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 17 min read (3383 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foreignaffairs

    ⏱️ ~17 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • ELIZABETH DICKINSON is Deputy Director for Latin America at International Crisis Group.
    • How a U.S.-Backed Offensive Could Help Bogotá Reclaim Its Conflict Zones.
    • According to recent reports, on September 21, José Luis Pérez Villanueva, better known as “El Cholo”—the second-in-command and financial architect of the criminal group Autodefensas Conquistadores de la Sierra Nevada—was killed during a Colombian police operation on the rural outskirts of Santa Marta.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    ELIZABETH DICKINSON is Deputy Director for Latin America at International Crisis Group.

    How a U.S.-Backed Offensive Could Help Bogotá Reclaim Its Conflict Zones.

    According to recent reports, on September 21, José Luis Pérez Villanueva, better known as “El Cholo”—the second-in-command and financial architect of the criminal group Autodefensas Conquistadores de la Sierra Nevada—was killed during a Colombian police operation on the rural outskirts of Santa Marta. Within hours, militants from that organization launched a dramatic campaign of terror. The group, known colloquially as Los Pachenca, demanded that businesses across the city shutter. Some 90 percent of shops did, as videos circulated of gunmen shooting up storefronts that stayed open.

    For two decades, Los Pachenca has been the unquestioned criminal authority in the beachfront city and the adjacent Sierra Nevada mountain range, charging extortion payments from businesses and residents and controlling the flow of drugs out of the Port of Santa Marta, en route to Europe and beyond. But the level of control the group exhibited during the strike was particularly jarring, given that Santa Marta is the vacation home of many of the country’s elite and a common destination for international visitors. Colombia’s government responded by militarizing the city, sending in hundreds of soldiers and police officers, who rolled into town on the main highway with tanks and air support. Many shops still stayed closed until the morning of September 25, when the group announced that it was ending the strike. For locals, Los Pachenca’s reaction was a message about who remains in charge.

    It has been revealed that calm has since returned to Santa Marta, but the incident may be indicative of risks to come. Colombia’s newly elected president, Abelardo de la Espriella, has promised a steep military escalation against illegal groups, which have grown precipitously in recent years. As he does so, armed and criminal organizations will undoubtedly respond. Often, their target will not be the state. Instead, they will likely direct their violence against the civilian populations, whom they have spent years coopting and coercing. That is because armed and criminal groups across the country have learned that their true leverage is their ability to govern local communities—and to intimidate and punish them into silence. Even when they do attack state forces, their use of weapons such as improvised explosives and makeshift drones means that bystanders often suffer. In one recent incident in the Pacific coast department of Valle del Cauca, four drone attacks released by an armed group in a single day left five civilians injured.

    In a recent development, these dangers are particularly acute as de la Espriella’s pledge of a zero-tolerance crackdown against armed and criminal groups has won enthusiastic support from Washington. Both countries want big and visible victories against these outfits. They triumphantly announced a upcoming era of cooperation when the president took office in August, including a promise of upgraded military ties. (The United States has not yet publicly pledged new weapons, but it is already providing greater intelligence and logistical assistance on some operations.) After two years of tensions and threats between President Donald Trump and leftist former President Gustavo Petro, the political realignment means that Colombia is once again the United States’ closest defense ally in South America. This is likely to continue, despite major Democratic wins in the U.S. Congress, as the relationship’s focus on security has a long history of bipartisan support.

    This week, during U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s visit to Bogotá, the de la Espriella administration signaled that it would seek congressional approval for joint military operations with the United States in Colombia. This cooperation will likely yield initial results. The Colombian government has mentioned that it aims to ramp up attacks against armed and criminal groups and to go after leaders who enjoyed protection as counterparts in peace talks during the past administration.

    In a recent development, yet Colombia’s true challenge is not how to carry out attacks but what to do afterward. Surgical strikes, which see the military enter and exit rapidly, leave civilians more vulnerable in the aftermath, as armed groups retaliate against alleged informants and tighten their grip in areas they control. Bogotá must ensure that every operation includes contingencies to anticipate criminal groups’ reactions and build on successful offensives by weakening their grasp on communities. The government will need to strengthen the police’s ability to patrol contested areas, a costly but necessary process that the United States and other partners should support.

    Industry observers note that the stakes are high. Bogotá has a chance to leverage its increased military pressure to open the door for the state, rewriting the story of who governs conflict areas. If the government misses this opportunity to consolidate state control, however, Colombia risks entering an escalatory spiral in which civilians pay a mounting price for a campaign intended to protect them.

    Armed and criminal groups have spent the last decade expanding their reach across Colombia. According to the local think tank Pares, the number of municipalities with an armed group presence rose from 212 in 2018 to 518 last year—or about half of all municipalities. This deterioration reversed dramatic and hard-won improvements in security. After the historically violent decades of the 1990s and 2000s, military pressure and negotiations yielded a 2016 peace agreement demobilizing the former Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (FARC), once the country’s dominant rebel group. Colombia’s countryside breathed a sigh of relief as the FARC pulled out of areas where it had been in control, which represented a quarter of the country’s land.

    Industry observers note that the FARC’s exit, however, did not pave the way for Colombia’s highly centralized and bureaucratic state to claim control of those vast geographies. Instead, old armed groups such as the National Liberation Army and newer ones such as the Gaitanista Army of Colombia (also known as the Gulf Clan) saw a chance to expand their access to trafficking routes, coca crops, illegal mines, and, ultimately, vulnerable rural populations. Kidnapping for extortion and mass displacement began to resurface, shattering optimism that progress would move in one direction. Over the last four years, membership in illegal groups has nearly doubled, to some 27,000 fighters today.

    Sources indicate that as a candidate, de la Espriella successfully harnessed public frustration by promising mano dura, or iron-fisted tactics, including aerial attacks and increased incarceration, facilitated by the construction of mega-prisons. He blamed his predecessor’s administration for accelerating insecurity. The first leftist to be elected president in modern Colombia, Petro had entered office in 2022 vowing to de-emphasize the military’s role and instead hold peace talks with various armed organizations. But not every group participated, and many of the ones that did sought to take advantage of cease-fires to cement their control over communities. Midway through his term, Petro pivoted back toward deploying the armed forces. But much of the harm was already done.

    Recent findings suggest that colombia’s newly introduced president has been in office only a little more than 100 days, but the shift is marked. De la Espriella carried out three bombing raids in his first weeks. He has extradited dozens of individuals to the United States, including senior leaders, and the administration has killed or captured many others. The president is doggedly pushing to restart aerial fumigation of coca crops, which the state carried out in the early 2000s to try to reduce the number of hectares under cultivation; the practice has since been heavily restricted by court rulings over concerns about health and environmental consequences. Both in private and in public, military leaders laud the government’s new support for their operations.

    Recent findings suggest that the Trump administration has also welcomed these developments, which align with a regional trend favoring Washington’s approach on counternarcotics. For Colombia, the new era of security cooperation with the United States represents a return to the status quo ante of the last quarter century, which was briefly disrupted by the Petro administration. U.S.-Colombian military ties were forged through antidrug efforts and deepened in 1999 with Plan Colombia, a decadelong $10 billion aid package that funded, among other things, the expansion and professionalization of the security forces and fumigation. The Colombian police and military are deeply integrated with their American counterparts. They use U.S.- and NATO-compatible systems, travel by the hundreds to the United States each year for instruction, and receive American intelligence. In nearly every operation, at least one step (and often far more) in the logistical chain is either coordinated with Washington or relies on U.S. support. That relationship never fully stopped under Petro, but the two sides were notably wary of each other. Now bilateral trust appears to be restored.

    In a recent development, even before the elections, de la Espriella impressed U.S. officials by outlining his plans to reclaim security momentum for the state. The Colombian president is now acting on several explicit U.S. priorities, including extraditions and legislation to designate numerous groups as terrorist organizations. Meanwhile, Bogotá’s coca eradication targets are even more ambitious than Washington’s. At a personal level, relations are strong, too. Two of Colombia’s top military officials previously served as envoys to U.S. Southern Command.

    It has been revealed that bogotá indicates that it intends to deliver results for Washington’s antidrug goals and has explicitly asked for additional support in the form of funding, aircraft, surveillance technologies, and maintenance. Although Colombia’s military remains among the best trained in the region, its logistical needs are critical. Only 13 of Colombia’s 53 Black Hawk helicopters are in working order, and defense spending has shrunk as a share of the national government’s budget, from 22.4 percent in 2003 to just 14.7 percent in 2025, with a growing proportion of those funds spent on salaries and pensions.

    Industry observers note that how much the United States will provide remains to be seen. In August, U.S. Southern Command’s General Francis Donovan discussed ways to shore up the deteriorating air fleet during a visit to Bogotá. The United States has also redeployed surveillance drones from Africa to Colombia and Ecuador, where they are already aiding intelligence collection. But Secretary of State Marco Rubio was reluctant to pledge specific aid while in Colombia in September, and most of this assistance is likely to be in kind or to stay in the hands of the U.S. military and contractors, with little entering the Colombian budget. Much of it appears to be focused on short-term offensive wins.

    Industry observers note that colombia has returned to tactics such as aerial bombardment because they arguably worked against the FARC. Founded as a Marxist rebellion in the 1960s, the group behaved like a conventional army, dressed in uniforms, and sought out combat with the state. This meant that the Colombian military could bomb encampments and that capturing leaders left the organization at times rudderless. Slowly chipping away at the FARC’s hierarchy and control helped push the group to finally negotiate its disarmament, beginning in 2012.

    But today, those same strategies are yielding diminishing returns. The current generation of armed and criminal groups has little interest in confronting the state. Instead, they behave like businesses, seeking to safeguard access to natural resources, supply chains, and trafficking routes. They live within the civilian population and rarely wear uniforms. Leaders are easily replaced and hierarchies are fluid. Critically, Colombia’s armed groups have learned that wars with the military are costly but that controlling local populations—through intimidation and violence, but also by offering economic incentives, jobs, and services—is comparatively cheap. The battlefield has evolved from a conventional conflict to a contest over who can govern territories and the people living there.

    According to recent reports, santa Marta offers an example of how this new model of warfare works. On most days, an outsider in the city would never perceive the presence of Los Pachenca. The group’s members do not patrol or identify themselves. Yet residents know them well from the weekly or monthly extortion payments they are forced to make. Local companies and government officials essentially view the group as an inescapable reality. Pushing back carries a violent price, but paying a protection tax, taking a bribe, or facilitating illegal commerce keeps business running smoothly.

    Industry observers note that the criminal governance of rural areas is even more suffocating. Groups that emerged from splinters of the former FARC, known as dissidents, often force local residents to hold identity cards, issued so that militants have a full census of who lives in the area and can detect possible enemy fighters. In the Amazon region, these groups keep a land registry more complete than that of the state so that they know exactly whom and how much to extort.

    It has been revealed that with this intense surveillance over society, armed and criminal groups frequently deploy the civilian population as human shields against military offensives and police patrols. The most egregious example is the widespread use of forcibly recruited children as bodyguards for senior commanders. De la Espriella’s initial bombardments, which killed at least six children, were even temporarily halted by a court over concerns about minors. Senior officers admit that these types of casualties are inevitable around high-value targets, and that the groups know that the military is far less likely to proceed if it means killing children.

    Armed and criminal groups will also try to use the military operations to their political advantage. When children are killed in bombardments, for example, FARC dissidents spin the local narrative into a story about how the state cares little for rural populations. The argument sticks because there is rarely a credible state presence that can serve and protect these same communities and earn their trust.

    There are more immediate consequences, as well. In the aftermath of bombardments and high-level captures, armed and criminal groups often undertake what amounts to a purge of the population, killing or exiling anyone they believe to have collaborated with the state. And when the state takes out a leader, intra-group violence frequently ensues as former associates compete to take his place. Many residents shelter inside to avoid being caught up in the fighting, leaving children without school and parents without income. If latest splinter groups emerge, the combat for control over neighborhoods can place even more civilians in the crossfire. This fallout widens the gap between immediate tactical results and long-term security gains. Taking out a senior leader wins applause, but conditions may well worsen on the ground.

    According to recent reports, de la Espriella’s administration has rightly identified winning territorial control, permanently dislodging criminal groups, and restoring state governance as its ultimate goals. The dilemma it now faces—exacerbated by U.S. support that focuses on attention-grabbing wins—is how to both achieve short-term results and ensure that these do not unleash latest waves of violence, retaliation against civilians, and, in turn, criminal consolidation.

    Sources indicate that the challenge is twofold. First, the military needs to anticipate groups’ violent reactions and to safeguard the population. In the case of Santa Marta, for example, the government could have increased police presence in the city in the hours after El Cholo was killed. Before the next bombardment or high-level capture, the state should ensure that a ground team of soldiers or military police is ready to hold the ground, protect the community, and prevent the armed group from swiftly stepping back in to reclaim territory.

    The second challenge—establishing lasting territorial control—is trickier. A permanent rural security presence might offer the best chance for Colombia’s government to change the direction of the conflict. The country’s military leadership controls only the tip of the spear, not the rest of the state. Time and again, governments “send only the military to the hardest areas,” a retired senior officer told Crisis Group. Moreover, soldiers are operating under heavy pressure for quick wins, which are measured in the number of combatants and especially high-value targets that are killed or captured. There is a real risk that by focusing largely on these statistics, the state will overlook more comprehensive policies necessary to achieve durable security.

    According to recent reports, pressure to deliver fast results has in the past incentivized unacceptable practices. In the early 2000s, intense political demands for combat kills fueled elaborate schemes in which soldiers murdered thousands of civilians and counted them as guerrilla fatalities, a scandal known as “false positives.” These crimes deeply compromised public trust in the security forces, and the military has worked for years to build a culture and procedures that ensure they do not happen again. Today, the country’s senior military leadership is likely the first and best brake on any attempts to use excessive force. Commanders say that they are cognizant of the need to guard against rules being slowly stretched until they are broken. “We need a stronger security approach, but it also worries us when we hear there is pressure for ‘results,’” one officer said. But U.S. rhetoric and behavior, including its decision to sink what it claims are drug-smuggling boats on the high seas, compound these risks.

    It has been revealed that success, then, may demand a strategy that is ultimately anchored in a much stronger and larger police force, fit for the job of safeguarding civilians rather than merely carrying out offensive strikes. Military operations can generate a window of opportunity by shuffling dynamics on the ground or removing certain dangerous players. Yet those reconfigurations will turn out in the state’s favor only if the resulting vacuum is eventually filled by reliable law enforcement. Take, for example, an operation that temporarily dislodges a group from a rural hamlet. If the military acts alone, it will likely enter and leave in a matter of days or even hours, allowing the armed group to rapidly return. If, however, the offensive is followed up with permanent police patrols, access to the justice system, and social interventions, criminals will have a harder time regaining control.

    Industry observers note that this, of course, is easier noted than done, given the government’s resource constraints. To create effective and permanent patrols, police departments operating in the countryside need more officers and equipment to maintain a presence in the most remote communities. Colombia has roughly 180,000 uniformed police officers, a figure that, per capita, puts it on the lower end of OECD countries, many of which are far more urbanized and therefore easier to patrol. In Colombia’s conflict-affected areas, outgunned officers must often stay inside their local stations for their own safety, limiting their ability to build trust and channels of communication with the population. Other state institutions, such as the justice system, say that they cannot establish a durable foothold in villages without guarantees of protection in the medium term—exactly what rural policing should strive to provide. The U.S. State Department’s Bureau of International Narcotics and Law Enforcement Affairs has funded the building and equipping of rural police stations in the past; it should expand this work. International partners with long-standing expertise in rural policing, such as Canada and France, could provide critical support, as well.

    In cities, the challenge is different. In Santa Marta, for example, the state is present, but it is weak and vulnerable to the pressure and cooptation of the same groups that it must confront. The police need both more officers and better working conditions—including salaries, benefits, access to education, and social support for families—that could help them resist bribes. Regular vetting and counterintelligence checks can help ensure that police are fighting on the side of the state and not its adversaries.

    Sources indicate that expanding the police will be an expensive, long-term undertaking. In the interim, Colombia could prioritize more personnel for critical areas and ensure that officers have a strong grounding in community policing, allowing them to understand the most pressing risks facing civilians. That means regular outreach to communities to build trust and make certain that officers are seen as having a stake in local well-being. The United States, meanwhile, must continue to help Bogotá strengthen its police and courts with direct financial and technical assistance.

    Recent findings suggest that colombia, backed by renewed U.S. support, cannot afford to repeat past mistakes or ignore how the conflict has changed. Bogotá must therefore plan for and capitalize on military pressure to do something no government in Colombia’s history has done: govern well in conflict areas.

    Pedro Sánchez’s Big Bet

    📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1709 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foreignpolicy

    ⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that spain holds elections this weekend—and under normal circumstances, Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez would be cruising to victory.
    • But Sánchez’s standing at home has eroded significantly in recent years.
    • Sources indicate that spain holds elections this weekend—and under normal circumstances, Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez would be cruising to victory.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that spain holds elections this weekend—and under normal circumstances, Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez would be cruising to victory. First elected in 2018, Sánchez has established himself as Europe’s longest-serving social democratic leader. He has made Spain the best-performing economy in the European Union. His willingness to welcome immigrants, challenge U.S. President Donald Trump, and describe Israel’s military campaign in Gaza as a genocide have also turned him into an icon of the international left.

    But Sánchez’s standing at home has eroded significantly in recent years. His government is mired in corruption scandals, his blanket amnesty for separatists involved in Catalonia’s illegal 2017 independence referendum has alienated many voters, and his blueprint to offer a pathway to citizenship to more than 500,000 undocumented immigrants has provoked a right-wing backlash. After more than eight years in office, he is also confronting considerable voter fatigue.

    Sources indicate that spain holds elections this weekend—and under normal circumstances, Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez would be cruising to victory. First elected in 2018, Sánchez has established himself as Europe’s longest-serving social democratic leader. He has made Spain the best-performing economy in the European Union. His willingness to welcome immigrants, challenge U.S. President Donald Trump, and describe Israel’s military campaign in Gaza as a genocide have also turned him into an icon of the international left.

    Sources indicate that but Sánchez’s standing at home has eroded significantly in recent years. His government is mired in corruption scandals, his blanket amnesty for separatists involved in Catalonia’s illegal 2017 independence referendum has alienated many voters, and his proposal to offer a pathway to citizenship to more than 500,000 undocumented immigrants has provoked a right-wing backlash. After more than eight years in office, he is also confronting considerable voter fatigue.

    Now, a worsening housing crisis is threatening to become another political liability for Sánchez. Yet he also sees it as an opportunity: By making housing the defining issue of the election, he may be able to divert attention from his political vulnerabilities while mobilizing the left-wing voters he needs to remain in power.

    In a recent development, last month, Sánchez dissolved parliament and called a snap election for Nov. 29, roughly seven months ahead of schedule. His biggest electoral challenge is not defeating a surging right but mobilizing left-wing voters. If Spain’s center-right and far-right opposition parties take control of the government, it will likely be because many left-wing voters stay home. An estimated 1.4 million left-wing voters are expected to sit out the elections, according to polling.

    That’s what happened in another snap election called by Sánchez in 2023. That year, despite losing the popular vote to the center-right People’s Party (PP), Sánchez and his Spanish Socialist Workers’ Party (PSOE) managed to remain in power through skillful coalition-building with separatist parties from Catalonia.

    The statistics behind Spain’s housing crisis are eye-popping. Between 2015 and 2025, average home prices rose by 80 percent, while rents climbed 87 percent. Nominal wages, by contrast, increased by just 30 percent. An estimated 40 percent of Spanish renters spend an average of 40 percent of their after-tax income on rent and utilities. The burden is even heavier for young people and lower-income households. According to the Bank of Spain, the country currently faces a housing deficit of approximately 750,000 homes, a structural supply gap that could exceed 1 million homes by 2028.

    Spain’s housing crisis has its roots in the 2008 financial collapse, when the burst of a speculative property bubble made the country an epicenter of a global crisis that also engulfed the United States. That year, Spain experienced the steepest decline in construction activity of any EU country, and fresh building virtually ground to a halt. Banks also tightened mortgage lending. The resulting financial crisis, which lasted from 2008 to 2013, brought down thousands of businesses—particularly banks—and pushed unemployment to 25 percent. In 2012, a $124 billion EU-backed rescue package restructured and recapitalized Spain’s financial system.

    Sources indicate that efforts to revive the economy had the unintended consequence of exacerbating the housing crisis. One example is the residence-by-investment program, known as the golden visa. Introduced in 2013, the program sought to attract overseas investment by relaxing restrictions on foreign purchases of Spanish property. It granted Spanish residency to anyone acquiring real estate valued at a minimum of $550,000, or depositing $1.1 million in a Spanish bank.

    Foreign property purchases surged, fueled by Chinese and Russian investors. But much of the investment flowed into areas where housing was already scarce and expensive: the urban centers of Barcelona and Madrid; the coastal areas of Andalusia, Catalonia, and Valencia; and the Balearic and Canary Islands. In these markets, an influx of foreign capital contributed to rising property prices, putting homeownership increasingly out of reach for locals. Responding to public pressure, the Sánchez government abolished the program last year.

    It has been revealed that spain’s efforts to promote tourism have also been a mixed blessing. In 2024, the country welcomed a record 94 million international visitors, making it the world’s second-most-visited destination after France. Tourism now contributes $220 billion to the Spanish economy, accounting for 12.6 percent of GDP. But in many cities, the tourism boom has transformed entire neighborhoods into overcrowded tourist zones that overwhelm and alienate locals.

    Industry observers note that tourism has also increased demand for foreign workers. According to the Elcano Royal Institute, Spain’s immigrant population stands at 9 million, with approximately 600,000 people arriving annually since the end of the COVID-19 pandemic. Many newcomers compete for low-rent apartments that have traditionally been available to young people and longtime residents. Elcano data also reveals that young Spaniards leave their parental homes and begin to establish independent households at an average age of 30.3, four years later than the EU average. More than 80 percent of Spaniards aged 16 to 29 still live with their parents, compared with an EU average of 68 percent.

    For several years, the housing crisis has been convulsing Spanish politics, making the country home to Europe’s most vocal anti-tourism movement. In Barcelona, activists have even sprayed tourists with water guns. City officials have responded with sweeping measures to curb tourism, including some of Europe’s highest tourist taxes, a moratorium on new hotel construction, and a ban on Airbnb-style short-term rentals scheduled to take effect in 2028. But efforts to rein in tourism have set regional and local governments against federal officials in Madrid, who continue to promote tourism expansion by increasing capacity at Spanish airports.

    It was an unexpected human tragedy, however, that propelled the housing crisis to the top of Sánchez’s agenda—and helped set the stage for next week’s election. On Sept. 23, police evicted ​Maricarmen Abascal, an 87-year-old disabled woman, from the Madrid apartment she had called home for 70 years. Urbagestión, the investment manufacturer that purchased her building in 2018 from a real estate firm, had sought to raise her rent by 230 percent. When she refused to leave, authorities removed her on a stretcher. Her eviction sparked a wave of protests that culminated in hundreds of housing activists occupying Madrid’s central square. Maricarmen died on Oct. 7.

    Industry observers note that shortly after her eviction, the Congress of Deputies rejected a PSOE-backed bill that would have introduced rent caps and restrictions on corporate property purchases. The legislation faced stiff opposition from conservative parties, including Junts, a Catalan separatist party that nominally supports Sánchez. Opponents argued that the proposed restrictions would further constrain housing supply. Earlier this month, responding to popular pressure, Spain’s interim parliament passed a separate housing bill aimed at limiting evictions and curbing real estate speculation. The PP opposed the legislation and pledged to repeal it if elected.

    It has been revealed that confident that he will soon be in power, PP leader Alberto Núñez Feijóo welcomed Sánchez’s call for early elections. Polls show a statistical dead heat between the PSOE and the PP. But because neither party is expected to win enough seats to control the Congress of Deputies outright, the far-right Vox—presently Spain’s third-largest party—could emerge as kingmaker. A PP-Vox coalition appears to be a likely outcome of the post-election negotiations. This partnership is not novel: It has been in place at the regional level since 2022 in four autonomous communities: Castilla y León, Aragón, Extremadura, and Andalusia. Vox has used regional governments to advance a nationalist and socially conservative agenda.

    It has been revealed that yet the PP might be walking into a trap of its own making. As in 2023, a snap election is giving Sánchez another opportunity to demonstrate his mastery of the political comeback. Polls that year also predicted a potential governing majority for the PP and Vox, but that outcome failed to materialize. Sánchez ultimately outmaneuvered Feijóo by assembling a governing coalition.

    According to recent reports, there is a powerful political paradox here: Sánchez is politically vulnerable because of the housing crisis. After all, it was under his watch that housing evolved from a growing concern into a full-blown crisis for Spanish voters. But the opposition’s resistance to his proposed remedies may allow him to turn a political liability into a potentially powerful campaign issue.

    In a recent development, framing the election as a referendum on who can best address Spain’s housing woes may offer Sánchez his strongest path to reelection. Rather unexpectedly, the housing crisis has allowed him to shift the campaign’s focus away from corruption and immigration and toward an matter with the potential to mobilize young voters, renters, the elderly, and lower-income households, while also resonating deeply with his Socialist base.

    Omar G. Encarnación is the Charles Flint Kellogg professor of politics at Bard College. He is the author of several books, including Spanish Politics: Democracy after Dictatorship, Democracy Without Justice in Spain: The Politics of Forgetting, and, most recently, Framing Equality: The Politics of Gay Marriage Wars.
